title: Valkyrie combat drone flies in Europe with range topping 3,100 miles
content: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have flown the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft in Europe for the first time. The milestone advances their effort to deliver a combat-ready Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) for Germany and other European military customers by 2029.The aircraft completed a series of maneuvers during testing at an undisclosed facility in Northern Europe. Its performance included rocket-assisted takeoff without a conventional runway, flight at speeds reaching Mach 0.8, and adjustments to mission parameters in the air.The partners now plan more advanced trials involving Airbus’ MARS mission system. The software will help the Valkyrie execute missions autonomously while preserving European control over its critical systems.Valkyrie completes European debutThe U740 Valkyrie measures 9.1 meters (29.9 feet) long and spans 8.2 meters (26.9 feet). It has an internal weapons bay and additional payload stations beneath its wings.The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of approximately three metric tons. Its range exceeds 3,100 miles, and it can operate at altitudes reaching 45,000 feet.These specifications position the Valkyrie for missions that expose conventional aircraft and their crews to significant risks. It can operate independently or coordinate with crewed fighters, including the Eurofighter.Airbus expects the drone to expand the reach and firepower of existing combat aircraft. Its design also offers a way to increase the number of available combat platforms without relying exclusively on expensive crewed fighters.The aircraft supports conventional runway operations, but its rail-launch capability offers another deployment option. Rocket assistance allows it to take off without depending on a traditional runway.MARS brings autonomous controlAirbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure (MARS) system will provide the Valkyrie with its European mission architecture. The system gives European operators control over mission applications, software, data, and hardware.MARS uses AI-assisted software to manage autonomous missions and coordinate groups of aircraft. Human operators will retain oversight of the system, particularly when decisions involve established rules of engagement.That arrangement gives European forces a way to adopt autonomous combat aircraft without surrendering control of their mission systems to an external supplier. Future flight tests will examine how MARS integrates with the Valkyrie’s existing capabilities.Affordable mass drives developmentAirbus Defence and Space CEO Mike Schoellhorn said modern air forces need affordable ways to increase combat capacity in increasingly contested environments.“By pairing Kratos’ proven airframe as a ‘program of record’ with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system, we are able to offer a robust, sovereign, affordable, and combat-ready CCA system by the end of the decade,” Schoellhorn said.Kratos CEO Eric DeMarco also praised the first flight, citing the aircraft’s maturity and the integration work between both teams. He said the partnership could expand opportunities in Germany and other international markets.The 2029 target gives the companies several years to mature the aircraft and its autonomous mission software. Subsequent tests will determine how effectively the Valkyrie can combine affordable production, flexible deployment, and coordinated operations alongside crewed fighters.

title: Staying Active Could Have Two Major Benefits for People With Parkinson’s, Scientists Find
content:
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurological disorder that affects movement, balance, and coordination. It develops as dopamine-producing nerve cells in the brain become damaged or die, leading to symptoms such as tremors, muscle stiffness, and slowed movement. Credit: Stock
Researchers have uncovered a potential connection between the duration and intensity of everyday physical activity and how Parkinson’s symptoms change over time.
People with Parkinson’s disease who stay more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities, according to a study that followed participants for up to seven years. Researchers found that greater activity was consistently associated with more favorable outcomes, although the findings do not establish that exercise directly slows disease progression.
The study, published in
Neurology
, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, examined how different amounts and intensities of physical activity related to changes in Parkinson’s symptoms.
“Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen, leading to disability and a loss of independence,” said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. “Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition.”
How Researchers Measured Physical Activity
The study included 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease, whose average age was 66. Participants reported how much time they spent being physically active each week, including activities at work, around the house, and during recreation. Moderate activities included brisk walking, light swimming, doubles tennis, vacuuming, and mowing the lawn. Vigorous activities included jogging, fast cycling, competitive sports, shoveling, and carrying heavy loads.
Researchers evaluated activity in three ways: total weekly time spent exercising at moderate or vigorous intensity, overall activity volume adjusted for intensity, and time spent performing vigorous activities. For total activity time, participants were classified into three groups: those active for up to four hours weekly, those active for four to eight hours, and those exceeding eight hours. Annual assessments tracked changes in cognitive performance and movement symptoms.
Greater Activity Linked to Slower Cognitive Decline
Differences between the activity groups emerged in tests of thinking and memory. On a 30-point cognitive assessment, where lower scores indicate poorer performance, the least active participants experienced an estimated average decline of 0.478 points per year. The middle group declined by 0.090 points annually, while the most active group showed almost no average decline, at just 0.007 points per year.
Movement assessments also showed different patterns. Researchers used a 132-point scale, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. Participants began with an average score of 23. Over time, the least active group showed an estimated annual increase of 0.143 points, suggesting modest worsening. In contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points annually in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group, indicating more favorable movement outcomes.
The associations remained after researchers accounted for participants’ age, sex, and duration of Parkinson’s disease. Higher values across all three measures of physical activity were associated with slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms, suggesting that both activity duration and intensity may be relevant.
Why the Findings Require Caution
“The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson’s disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time,” said Ryu. “While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed.”
One limitation was that participants reported their own physical activity, potentially introducing inaccuracies in estimates of exercise duration and intensity. Because the study was observational, researchers also could not determine whether greater activity helped preserve neurological function or whether people with less severe symptoms were better able to remain active. Further research is needed to establish whether increasing physical activity can directly influence the progression of Parkinson’s disease.
Reference: “Physical Activity and Motor and Cognitive Progression in Parkinson Disease: A Longitudinal Cohort Study” by Dong-Woo Ryu, Kevin R. Duque, Luca Marsili, Jesus Abanto, Nathaly Chinchihualpa Paredes, Heba A. Deraz, Andrea Herrera Gorriti, Emily J. Hill, Abhimanyu Mahajan, Andrew Duker and Alberto J. Espay, 7 October 2026,
Neurology
DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000218682

title: Scientists Discover Aspirin May Slash Dementia Risk by 70% – but Only for Certain People
content:
Aspirin is a widely used medication known for relieving pain, reducing inflammation, and lowering fever. Credit: Stock
Aspirin was linked to a sharply lower dementia risk in some older adults, and their genes may hold the clue.
Monash University
analysis found that older adults with a particular genetic profile had about a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin. But serious bleeding was also more common in this group, leaving researchers with a promising lead that needs further testing.
The research, published in
Alzheimer’s & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer’s Association
, examined genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Researchers compared genetic scores to investigate whether inherited differences could help explain who might benefit from aspirin.
A Genetic Signal Linked to Platelets
The strongest finding involved a genetic score associated with platelet count. Researchers ranked participants by that score, then compared dementia outcomes among those assigned aspirin or a placebo.
Among participants in the highest 20 percent, dementia developed in 1 percent of aspirin recipients, compared with 3.3 percent of placebo recipients. Although that represents roughly a 70 percent relative reduction, the absolute difference was 2.3 percentage points, equivalent to about 23 fewer dementia cases per 1,000 people.
Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a research fellow at Monash’s School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the finding could help move prevention toward a more personalized approach.
“Previous trials found aspirin didn’t prevent dementia when everyone was considered together,” Dr. Fransquet said. “Our findings suggest there may be more to the story. In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin. It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.”
Lower Dementia Risk, More Serious Bleeding
The potential protection against dementia came with a higher risk of serious bleeding. In the same genetic group, major bleeding occurred in 4.4 percent of aspirin recipients and 2.1 percent of placebo recipients, a difference equivalent to about 23 additional major bleeding events per 1,000 people.
The results draw attention to how platelets may contribute to dementia. Scientists have previously linked platelet activation and aggregation, or clumping, with dementia, but the role of overall platelet count remains less clear.
“What’s particularly interesting is that the signal wasn’t linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease and dementia,” Dr. Fransquet said. “Instead, it’s pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate.”
What Personalized Prevention Would Require
Dementia Australia estimates that 446,500 Australians are living with dementia in 2026 and projects that the number will exceed one million by 2065.
For now, the analysis identifies a group worth investigating rather than establishing a treatment strategy. A trial specifically designed around this genetic profile would help determine whether the apparent dementia benefit is reproducible and how it compares with the bleeding risk.
“We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile. People shouldn’t start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding. If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility.”
Reference: “Platelet count polygenic scores may modify the effect of aspirin in primary prevention of dementia” by Peter D. Fransquet, Chenglong Yu, Cammie Tran, Sultana Monira Hussain, Amy Brodtmann, Andrew M. Tonkin, Mark R Nelson, Joanne Ryan, John J. McNeil and Paul Lacaze, 24 September 2026,
Alzheimer’s & Dementia
DOI: 10.1002/alz.71817

title: Scientists Build a World-First DNA Computer That Runs Without Continuous Power
content:
Researchers have developed a DNA computer that performs mathematical calculations using molecular interactions rather than silicon chips. Credit: Shutterstock
Reusable for up to 25 different calculations, a DNA computer points toward possible uses in energy-efficient computing and long-term data storage.
A DNA computer has added 10 and 3 in 30 seconds, using interacting strands in water instead of a silicon chip. Developed by researchers at Maynooth University (MU), the system can also multiply and divide without a continuous electricity supply.
The work, published in
, presents a first-of-its-kind system described as one of the most complex and fastest molecular computers yet reported.
DNA strands assemble the answer
Dr Abeer Eshra, an assistant professor and computer scientist at MU’s Hamilton Institute who conducted many of the experiments, described what is happening inside the liquid. “A small droplet of liquid contains billions, and sometimes trillions, of DNA strands. These strands interact with one another to produce a result.”
To build the computer, the team combined a small drop of water and salt with short pieces of DNA and a longer DNA scaffold in a test tube. The mixture needs only a little heat to get started and is then cooled, allowing the computation to proceed.
“The molecules interact, form a structure and that structure is the answer,” said Professor Damien Woods of MU’s Hamilton Institute. “One key innovation is that the system naturally finds that answer without needing continuous energy inputs,” he added.
Pictured are three members of the five-person Maynooth University (MU) DNA computing research team: undergraduate researcher Janet Adio, alongside Prof Damien Woods and Dr Abeer Eshra of the Department of Computer Science’s Hamilton Institute at MU. Credit: Maynooth University
Fast for DNA, slower than silicon
The researchers ran ten programs, including 100-bit computations. In one experiment, the computer added numbers in the range of about 11 million to 34 million, taking up to 14 hours to reach a result. The system also demonstrated robustness and reusability, performing up to 25 different calculations in a row.
“The reaction happens fast in the test tube, but not as fast as silicon, nor is it intended to be. But compared to other DNA computers, ours is the fastest,” said Eshra, joint first author of the
study alongside Dr Tristan Stérin. The paper’s coauthors also included Senior Research Fellow Dr Constantine Evans and undergraduate researcher Janet Adio.
Molecular computers could work inside cells
Beyond arithmetic in a test tube, the research points to possible applications in long-term data storage and energy-efficient computation. In time, molecular systems might also operate inside cells for tasks such as disease detection.
Pictured are three members of the five-person Maynooth University (MU) DNA computing research team: undergraduate researcher Janet Adio, alongside Prof Damien Woods and Dr Abeer Eshra of the Department of Computer Science’s Hamilton Institute at MU. Credit: Maynooth University
Woods explained the motivation for exploring other forms of computing. “Silicon-based computers use so much energy – 23% of Ireland’s electricity goes into computing and data storage. We’ve been blinkered by only seeing one type of computer, but there are other examples around us, including our brain.”
Maynooth’s DNA computing research is supported by a €4 million European Innovation Council grant led by Woods. The DISCO project, DNA-based infrastructure for Storage and Computation, aims to develop new ways to compute and store data using DNA technology.
“This is blue skies science. We don’t know where the future is going to take us.” Woods offered that perspective on the broader effort to explore alternative forms of computing.
Reference: “A thermodynamically favoured molecular computer” by Tristan Stérin, Abeer Eshra, Constantine Glen Evans, Janet Adio and Damien Woods, 16 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10996-5

title: Scientists Just Discovered a Major Problem With Lab-Grown Human Embryo Models
content:
Stem cell-derived embryo models offer scientists a promising way to investigate the earliest stages of human development, but their biological accuracy remains uncertain. Credit: Shutterstock
A map built from more than 14,000 embryo cells reveals what stem cell models get right about early human development and where researchers could improve them.
Under a microscope, a cluster grown from stem cells can resemble a human embryo in its first days of development. These structures, called blastoids, offer scientists a way to investigate the biology behind fertility and pregnancy success. Their appearance, however, cannot establish whether the cells inside are developing as they would in a real embryo.
University of Sydney researchers have now looked beyond that resemblance, developing a computational framework to evaluate models produced by four leading methods. Their study, published in
Cell Systems
, found that some reproduced important features of early development relatively well, but none fully matched the biology of a natural human embryo.
Studying donated human embryos involves technical and ethical constraints that have long made the earliest stages of development difficult to investigate. Growing models from stem cells gives researchers another way to explore those stages, provided they understand what the models can reliably reproduce. Blastoids are research models, not actual human embryos, and current models cannot develop into a human embryo.
“If we’re going to use these systems to answer important biological questions, we first need to know what they can reliably tell us,” said lead author Associate Professor Pengyi Yang, an ARC Future Fellow in the University of Sydney’s School of Mathematics and Statistics and Unit Head of Computational Systems Biology at the Children’s Medical Research Institute. Yang also leads the Trans-Regulatory Biology group at the Charles Perkins Center.
Associate Professor Pengyi Yang at his desk. Credit: University of Sydney
Tracing development through 14,000 embryo cells
Yang and his colleagues assembled more than 14,000 single-cell transcriptomes from human embryos at key developmental stages. Each transcriptome records the RNA molecules in an individual cell, providing clues about which genes are active. Bringing these datasets into a common framework allowed the researchers to follow molecular differences that an embryo’s outward appearance alone cannot reveal.
The resulting reference map traces how cells specialize and organize themselves during the days immediately before and after implantation, when an embryo attaches to the lining of the uterus. It gives researchers a detailed biological reference against which to examine the cells in their models.
“Our framework allows researchers to compare these models against a detailed biological reference and determine which cell types and developmental processes are faithfully reproduced, and which are not.”
Some cells have no clear embryonic match
The team compared that reference with blastoids generated using four widely used protocols developed by international research groups. They examined the cells’ molecular identities, the timing of their development, and how they were distributed among developmental branches known as lineages. A model could therefore be assessed on several aspects of its biology, beyond whether its overall shape looked convincing.
Portrait of Associate Professor Pengyi Yang. Credit: University of Sydney
Cells in some models corresponded relatively well to all three major lineages found in a natural human blastocyst, the early embryonic stage that blastoids are designed to resemble. Other models represented certain cell types poorly or contained large numbers of cells that could not be confidently matched to any known embryonic state. The differences meant that each model had its own strengths and gaps.
“But our study also shows that current models are not biologically equivalent to real human embryos, and researchers need to be careful about the conclusions they draw from them,” Yang said.
A shared standard for future blastoids
Researchers worldwide can now examine those gaps using the team’s publicly available reference datasets and benchmarking tools. Testing new models against the same reference could make their strengths and limitations easier to compare. The team hopes that this shared benchmark will also help researchers improve models more quickly and evaluate them more rigorously.
“Our work provides a roadmap for improving embryo models and ensuring scientific claims remain grounded in what the models can actually support.”
As researchers grow the next generation of blastoids, the clusters taking shape under their microscopes will have to meet a more demanding benchmark for how closely their cells reproduce early human development.
Reference: “Systematic transcriptomic evaluation of blastoid models of early human development” by Siqu Long, Hani Jieun Kim, Nazmus Salehin, Hao Huang, Xinran Zhang, Raja Jothi and Pengyi Yang, 2 October 2026,
Cell Systems
DOI: 10.1016/j.cels.2026.101738
The work was supported by a National Health and Medical Research Council Investigator Grant and a Metcalf Prize for Stem Cell Research to Pengyi Yang. Raja Jothi was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health (USA) and National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (USA).

title: The World’s Oldest Land Animal Has a Remarkable Anti-Aging Secret Hidden in Its DNA
content:
Jonathan the tortoise. Credit: St Helena Government Communications Hub
The world’s oldest land animal carries 287 unique gene variants involved in DNA repair and other defenses against aging, offering clues researchers hope to turn into human treatments.
When Jonathan the giant tortoise hatched in 1832, Charles Darwin was still a young explorer and Queen Victoria had yet to take the throne. Nearly two centuries later, Jonathan is still alive – and scientists have discovered something remarkable about his biology. Despite his estimated age of 194, the world’s oldest living land animal has genetic controls for DNA repair and metabolism that closely resemble those of much younger tortoises.
For the past 144 years, Jonathan has lived on the remote South Atlantic island of St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory. He arrived from the Seychelles in 1882 as a gift to the governor, already fully grown, and has spent most of his life roaming the grounds of Plantation House, the governor’s residence.
Youthful patterns in Jonathan’s gene controls
To investigate the biology behind his longevity, a team led by the U.S. longevity research nonprofit Kallel examined both his DNA and the controls that regulate its activity. Their study, published October 7, 2026, in
Science Advances
, is the first to investigate a giant tortoise’s epigenome, the system of switches that helps turn genes on and off.
Jonathan has lived most of his life on the island of St Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean, in grounds of Plantation House – the residence of the governor of St Helena. He arrived from the Seychelles 144 years ago, already fully grown, as a gift to the governor. Credit: Joe Holland
These switches usually change over time, contributing to aging. When the researchers compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of younger Aldabra giant tortoises, however, they found very similar patterns in the switches controlling DNA repair and metabolism.
“We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries,” said Dr. Justin Gerlach of Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.
The team also identified 287 unique gene variants in Jonathan that they say reduce the usual effects of aging. These variants control processes involved in repairing damaged DNA, reducing inflammation, regulating insulin, and suppressing cancer. Together, the DNA and epigenome findings point to a combination of protective genetic features and stability in how key genes are regulated.
Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea), is estimated to be 194 years old. This makes him the oldest living giant tortoise, and oldest land animal, in the world today. Credit: Joe Holland
Gerlach has spent several decades studying giant tortoise ecology and conservation, but this was his first investigation of their exceptionally long lives. The giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are the last survivors of animals that once dominated the ecology of many of the world’s islands.
Jonathan arrived in St. Helena as a gift to Sir William Grey-Wilson in 1882, who later became governor of the island. This image was taken around that time – Jonathan is on the left. Credit: A.L. Innes
“There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject,” Gerlach said.
Tortoise genetics could guide human treatments
“Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan’s genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience,” said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.
Researchers say it’s good genes and lack of genetic wear and tear that have kept Jonathan living for nearly two centuries. Credit: Joe Holland
He added: “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.”

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising Link Between Obesity and Dementia Survival
content:
Dementia is a general term for a group of conditions that progressively impair memory, thinking, behavior, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause, accounting for an estimated 60% to 70% of cases. Credit: Shutterstock
A large study found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia have a significantly lower risk of death than those at a normal weight.
A higher body weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis may be linked to longer survival, according to a large study of older Americans. Researchers found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed had a significantly lower risk of death than those in the normal weight range, even after accounting for other health conditions and lifestyle factors.
The findings, published in the
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
, contrast with evidence that obesity during midlife increases the likelihood of developing dementia. Although the researchers could not determine why higher weight was associated with better survival, their analysis suggests that the relationship cannot easily be explained by several common sources of statistical bias.
Higher Body Weight Linked to Lower Mortality
The survival differences varied by weight category. People who were overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had a 27% lower risk, while individuals with class 2 or 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22% lower risk.
To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed 4,523 participants in the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative study of U.S. adults ages 51 and older conducted by the University of Michigan. All participants were free of dementia when they entered the study but developed the condition later. Data collected between 1998 and 2022 allowed the team to examine weight changes before diagnosis and track survival afterward.
Could Weight Loss Before Diagnosis Explain the Results?
One complication in dementia research is that weight loss often begins long before the condition is formally identified.
Earlier research
Other potential biases could also distort the relationship. Studying only people who develop dementia can introduce misleading statistical associations between weight and mortality. Survivor bias is another concern. Obesity increases the risk of dying from conditions such as cardiovascular disease; people with obesity who survive long enough to develop dementia may be healthier than others who were initially in the same weight category.
The researchers conducted additional analyses to examine these possible distortions but found little evidence that the major biases they evaluated accounted for the observed survival differences.
“Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight,” said Yuan Zhang, assistant professor of sociomedical sciences at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health.
How Energy Reserves May Affect Dementia Survival
One possible biological explanation involves the body’s ability to withstand nutritional decline. Dementia can disrupt brain processes that regulate hunger and eating behavior, while also making it increasingly difficult for people to prepare food or feed themselves. Some individuals experience higher energy expenditure, reduced appetite, and progressive loss of muscle and body tissue.
People with greater fat stores or muscle mass may have more reserves to draw upon when eating becomes difficult. These reserves could potentially help them tolerate periods of inadequate nutrition, although the study did not establish that this mechanism explains the survival advantage.
“Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia,” said Chang. “They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain’s central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.”
What the Findings Mean for Dementia Care
Despite the association between higher weight and longer survival, the findings do not establish that gaining weight improves outcomes for people with dementia. The observational study examined existing differences in body weight and mortality rather than testing whether deliberate weight changes could influence survival.
“This doesn’t mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia,” said Chang, associate professor of social and behavioral sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study’s lead author.
Determining whether fat stores, muscle mass, nutritional status, or other physiological differences account for the association will require further research. Body weight may nevertheless provide useful information about survival prospects when dementia is first diagnosed.
“While our analysis examined several forms of bias, and there are very plausible physiological reasons for the potential benefits of a little extra weight in this context, we still don’t know exactly why people who were overweight or obese had a lower risk of death. Regardless of the underlying mechanism, however, weight status at the time of a dementia diagnosis can still serve as a meaningful prognostic signal,” noted Chang.
Reference: “Body mass index and mortality in incident dementia” by Virginia W. Chang, Eleanor Hayes-Larson, Hui Zheng and Yuan S. Zhang, 25 March 2026,
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
DOI: 10.1177/13872877261491694
This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

title: One-Third of Older Adults With Cognitive Disorders Take Drugs That Could Harm Them
content:
Older adults with cognitive disorders can be especially vulnerable to medications that act on the central nervous system, with potentially serious consequences for health and independence. Credit: Shutterstock
As the population ages, medication safety is becoming increasingly important for people with cognitive decline.
Older adults with dementia and other cognitive disorders are less likely than they were a decade ago to receive medications that can worsen memory, balance, and coordination. But nearly one in three still takes at least one potentially inappropriate drug.
University at Buffalo researchers analyzed data from 2,796 independently living adults age 65 and older with cognitive disorders. Exposure to potentially harmful medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022, according to a study published in the
Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
Why These Drugs Can Be Risky
The medications include drugs used for anxiety, insomnia, psychosis, and other conditions involving the central nervous system. In older adults with cognitive disorders, they can increase the risk of emergency department visits, hospitalization, poorer mental health, and premature death.
“This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used,” says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, the study’s first author.
Benzodiazepines such as Xanax and sleep medications such as Ambien can impair cognition, balance, and coordination, particularly in older adults.
Deprescribing Could Reduce Harm
One strategy is deprescribing, which can involve stopping a medication, lowering its dose, reducing how often it is taken, or replacing it with a safer alternative.
“A central word for patients in this age group is ‘deprescribing,’ which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative,” Hsu says.
The researchers used the American Geriatrics Society’s Beers Criteria, a list of medications that may be risky for older adults. Their analysis represented approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders from 2011 to 2022.
Progress, but Continued Exposure
The study did not examine why prescribing declined. Hsu said increased attention to geriatric medication safety may have contributed.
“We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period,” he says. “However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn’t good.”
The researchers say regular medication reviews and tools such as the Drug Burden Index could help identify patients carrying a high cumulative burden from sedative or anticholinergic drugs.
Further studies are needed to determine whether better medication management can reduce hospitalizations and emergency visits while improving quality of life in older adults with cognitive disorders.
Reference: “Cognitive Potentially Inappropriate Medications, Quality of Life, and Healthcare Use in Older Adults With Cognitive Disorders” by Haowen Hsu, Collin M. Clark, Steven Feuerstein, Robert G. Wahler, Ranjit Singh and David M. Jacobs, 4 August 2026,
Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
DOI: 10.1111/jgs.70607

title: Inflammation May Awaken Dormant Cancer Cells Years After Treatment
content:
Dormant cancer cells may be sensitive to immune-driven changes in their surroundings. New findings reveal one molecular clue connecting inflammation with metastatic reactivation. Credit: Stock
The body’s response to inflammation may disturb cancer cells that have been lying silent for years, giving them an opportunity to grow again.
Researchers at the
Francis Crick Institute
have found that gut inflammation can reactivate dormant breast cancer cells in a mouse model of bone marrow. Their study, published in
Cell Reports
, suggests that changes needed to produce more immune cells can also create conditions that favor cancer growth.
Cancer cells can leave the original tumor and settle elsewhere in the body, a process called metastasis that accounts for most cancer-related deaths. Breast cancer cells frequently reach bone marrow, where an inactive state helps them evade immune defenses and resist chemotherapy.
“Cancer cells that have moved to another part of the body can stay dormant for years after the original tumor has been treated,” explains Crick group leader Ilaria Malanchi, whose lab studies interactions between cancer cells and the body. “It’s a worrying period for people, as they don’t know if these metastatic cells will reactivate, leading to a relapse.”
“We can’t wait five years to see if dormant cancer cells reactivate in mice, as this exceeds their lifespan,” Ilaria explains. “We’ve known for a long time that we need to think creatively about a new model.”
A nest of dormant cancer cells in the bone, in magenta. Bone marrow cells are in blue and blood vessels in green. Credit: Tatiana Rizou, as in Cell Reports (2026).
Recreating Dormant Cancer In Bone Marrow
Building on previous work by Laurie Gay, Stefania di Blasio, and Tatiana Rizou developed an “extramedullary bone model”: bone tissue grown from skeletal stem cells beneath the skin. The replica contains the marrow cells needed to produce blood cells and responds to inflammatory signals much like natural bone marrow.
“We then added cells from a mouse mammary tumor onto the replica bone,” explains Ilaria. “Most entered a dormant state, with only sporadic replication activity.”
Ilaria Malanchi runs the Tumour-Host Interaction Laboratory at the Crick. Credit: The Francis Crick Institute
The model gave the team a way to investigate how events elsewhere in the body affect these resting cells. Fractures and other bone injuries can encourage metastatic cancer growth in marrow, but the researchers wanted to test whether a more distant injury or infection could also disturb dormancy.
Gut Inflammation Changes The Cancer Environment
“We induced intestinal colitis—inflammation in the gut—in the mice with the extramedullary bone hosting dormant metastatic cells. Because the replica bone responds to the immune system, gut inflammation triggered a rapid production of immune cells from the bone,” Ilaria explains.
That response required the marrow environment to reorganize to support greater immune cell production. As it changed, more of the dormant cancer cells began dividing, increasing the chance of a tumor forming. The findings connect inflammation in one organ with changes in the tissue sheltering cancer cells elsewhere.
Examining gene activity in the bone and cancer cells pointed to HMGB2, a molecule that stimulates cell growth. Its levels rose alongside the surge in immune cell production, and it also promoted cancer cell reactivation.
“Even without inflammation elsewhere in the body, just the increased HMGB2 in the artificial bone was enough to stimulate more cancer cells to activate,” Ilaria says. “We also analyzed bone samples from people with breast or prostate cancer—HMGB2 was present where there were actively dividing cancer cells.
“All of these findings suggest that boosting immune cell production in the bone, as part of a normal response to inflammation, comes at the cost of disrupting tumor dormancy, tipping the balance towards reactivation and metastatic growth.”
Why Inflammation Does Not Guarantee Relapse
Ilaria emphasizes that inflammation does not automatically cause cancer to return. “We think it’s a piecemeal situation where each systemic change increases the chance of more metastatic cells waking up each time,” she says.
The research suggests that monitoring infections, inflammation, and injuries after remission might help identify periods when dormant cells are more likely to become active.
“Once cancer cells are actively replicating, they can respond to chemotherapy, so understanding developments affecting the bone marrow could lead to early intervention,” Ilaria concludes.
Reference: “An extramedullary bone model of metastatic dormancy reveals an increased rate of metastatic reactivation upon distant insults” by Stefania Di Blasio, Tatiana Rizou, Laurie J. Gay, Nicolas Rabas, Xuanxuan Fan, Xing-Yu Liu, Victoria L. Bridgeman, Ernesto Rodriguez, Probir Chakravarty, Thomas Snoeks, Adam Karoutas, Felipe S. Rodrigues, Elodie Montaudon, Cristina Lo Celso, Elisabetta Marangoni, Dominique Bonnet, Bin-Zhi Qian, Ander Abarrategi and Ilaria Malanchi, 1 October 2026,
Cell Reports

title: The Fossil Record May Be Missing 200 Million Years of Animal History
content:
Ediacaran sea floor, Namibia, Southwest Africa – 543 million years ago. Credit: Museum of Natural History, University of Oxford / Mighty Fossils
A fossil deposit in Mongolia preserves microscopic organisms in extraordinary detail, down to cells inside specimens that resemble embryos. Yet none of the fossils examined can confidently be identified as an animal, even though fossils from Namibia and South China show that animals already existed when the Mongolian deposit formed.
That gap challenges an assumption researchers have used to date the origins of animal life. If a deposit preserves tiny organisms exceptionally well, can scientists conclude that any animals alive at the time would also have been preserved? A new study led by the University of Oxford, published in
Science Advances
on October 2, suggests the answer is no. Revisiting that assumption pushes the possible origin of animals up to 200 million years before their first unmistakable fossils.
Estimated timeline for the origin of animals based on molecular clock analyses. The grey bar on the right of the image is the origin of animals based on an Ediacaran upper calibration. The grey bar to the left is the origin based on older deposits in the Tonian period, as suggested by the new study. Credit: Orin Lole Durbin
Exceptional preservation can still miss animals
Animal fossils seem to appear relatively suddenly just before the Cambrian Period, which lasted from 539 to 487 million years ago, despite other evidence pointing to an earlier evolutionary history. Researchers have recently used the roughly 590-million-year-old Weng’an Biota in China to limit how far back that history could extend. Its rocks, dating to the Ediacaran, preserve microscopic organisms in exceptional detail, but none are definitive animals. Scientists therefore inferred that animals must have originated after the deposit formed, reasoning that it would have preserved them had they existed.
The Mongolian deposit, known as the Kheseen Biota, offers a way to examine that reasoning. It is more than 40 million years younger than Weng’an, although the two share some species, and dates to a time when animals are known from elsewhere. The research team, which included scientists from the University of California, Berkeley, ETH Zürich, and Yale University, conducted a comprehensive survey of its exceptionally preserved microfossils.
They examined more than 140 samples, including material from previously undocumented localities, using scanning electron microscopy. Alongside the embryo-like fossils with internal cells, they identified new microfossil species, including acritarchs, tiny spherical organisms with spines and branching projections.
Asterocapsoides wenganensis, Kheseen Formation, latest Ediacaran/early Cambrian. Scale bar: 0.1 mm. Credit: Derek Briggs
Senior author Associate Professor Ross Anderson, of the University of Oxford’s Museum of Natural History, said, “The Kheseen Biota breaks the argument that the exceptional microfossils of Weng’an mean we would have seen animal fossils in the assemblage had they existed at the time. The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent—despite the fact we know at that point they existed.”
The earliest animals would have been small and soft-bodied, lacking the shells, bones, and other hard structures that make later animals easier to preserve. Fossilization would have depended on their environment and an unusual combination of chemical conditions after death. The researchers argue that animals either lived in environments different from those represented in the Kheseen Biota or that the chemical conditions there failed to preserve their remains. Either possibility weakens the use of Weng’an’s missing animals as evidence that animal life had not yet begun.
Chemical traces offer another way to look for creatures whose bodies have disappeared. Biomarkers preserved in ancient rocks provide evidence consistent with sponges living at least 650 million years ago, tens of millions of years before the oldest definitive macroscopic animal fossils, those large enough to see without a microscope.
Knollisphaeridium maximum, Kheseen Formation, latest Ediacaran/early Cambrian. Scale bar: 0.1 mm. Credit: Derek Briggs
Molecular clocks point to earlier animals
To estimate how much further back animal origins might reach, the team used molecular clock analysis. This technique compares genetic differences between living species and combines rates of evolution with fossil dates as reference points to estimate when their ancestors lived. The dates supplied by the fossil record help constrain those estimates, so changing them can alter the inferred evolutionary timeline.
Instead of treating Weng’an as the maximum age for animal origins, the researchers drew on several older deposits dating from roughly 850 to 730 million years ago. These included the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway, the Bitter Springs Group in Australia, and the Chuar Group in Arizona, United States. All are rich in fossils and have the potential to preserve animals, although animal fossils have eluded discovery in them. These deposits have previously been used to set maximum dates for animal origins.
Using those older geological constraints shifted the estimated origin of animals back by around 200 million years compared with analyses constrained by the younger Ediacaran Weng’an deposit. The resulting estimate, between 800 and 700 million years ago, places their possible beginnings deep in the Neoproterozoic Era.
Study author Associate Professor Ross Anderson (University of Oxford) in the mountains to the west of Lake Khuvsgul, Mongolia during fieldwork in summer 2017. Credit: Ross Anderson
Animals may predate Snowball Earth
That interval spans the beginning of the Cryogenian Period, around 720 million years ago. During the Cryogenian, enormous glaciers spread across the planet in episodes commonly known as Snowball Earth. Animals could therefore have evolved before some of Earth’s most extreme ice ages or appeared during that inhospitable interval. The findings reopen questions about whether conditions associated with Snowball Earth helped shape the origin and early evolution of animal life.
First author Orin Lole Durbin, now a PhD student at Virginia Tech and an undergraduate at the University of Oxford at the time of the study, said, “Pre-Ediacaran animal body fossils still elude us, and this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago. However, our new fossil evidence from Mongolia undermines one of the main arguments for restricting animal origins to the Ediacaran interval. Meanwhile, our molecular-clock analyses show how much further back their evolutionary history could extend.”
The researchers recommend searching deposits from different parts of the world that represent varied environments and ways of preserving fossils. That search should consider all available evidence, including animal bodies, traces of their activity, and chemical biomarkers.
Anderson added, “Until that evidence becomes available, the precise birth date of the animal kingdom remains uncertain.”
Reference: “Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals” by Orin M. Lole Durbin, Eliel S.C. Anttila, Derek E.G. Briggs, Francis A. Macdonald and Ross P. Anderson, 2 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289

title: Stanford Scientists Discover We’ve Lost Ancient Gut Microbes That Traveled With Humans for Thousands of Years
content:
Our gut microbiome is a complex community of trillions of microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, that help digest food, produce essential vitamins, and regulate the immune system. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists comparing the gut microbiomes of two geographically distant populations uncovered surprising similarities despite thousands of years of separation.
Hundreds of bacterial species missing from modern human guts may have accompanied our ancestors for tens of thousands of years. A
Stanford University
study published October 7 in
found that two populations separated by continents share remarkably similar gut microbes, many with genetic histories linked to ancient human migrations.
The researchers compared the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania with the Tsimane, Indigenous forager-horticulturalists in the Bolivian Amazon. Despite different diets and thousands of years of geographic separation, the populations share 1,231 bacterial species. About 60% are rare or absent in industrialized populations.
Ancient Microbes Shared Across Continents
The researchers identified approximately 1,400 bacterial species in the sampled Tsimane population, nearly 90% of which were also found among the Hadza. This extensive overlap was unexpected because the Hadza primarily hunt and gather wild foods, while the Tsimane cultivate crops and consume substantial amounts of dietary fiber.
“We were really surprised to see that the vast majority of the species in the Tsimane’s microbiome correspond with the Hadza’s,” said Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, Stanford professor of microbiology and immunology and senior author of the study.
“That made us wonder if there really is a core set of bacterial and other species that traveled with the ancestors of the Tsimane as they migrated around the globe,” said Benjamin Good, PhD, Stanford assistant professor of applied physics and senior co-author.
Tracing Bacteria Through Human History
“Could these bugs have been in continual interaction with us since long before the ancestors of today’s Hadza and Tsimane became geographically separated?” Sonnenburg asked. “To answer that, we turned to Ben’s team, and what they found blew our minds.”
Using deep metagenomic sequencing and population genetics methods, the researchers analyzed bacterial DNA to reconstruct evolutionary relationships. For many shared species, estimated divergence times matched major prehistoric human migrations, including movements out of Africa and into the Americas.
“We see evidence that these bacteria were present in the ancestors of both the Tsimane and the Hadza, and therefore presumably the ancestors of all of us,” Good said.
What Modern Lifestyles May Have Changed
“Our study establishes that the hundreds of bacterial species that are rare or missing in industrialized microbiomes were ancient companions of ours as we migrated around the globe, likely passed from generation to generation for millennia,” Sonnenburg said. “This long-term association has implications for how such recent biodiversity loss in our microbiome may impact our biology and thus our health.”
Industrialized populations have substantially less diverse gut microbiomes, potentially reflecting factors such as antibiotic use, processed diets, and highly sanitized environments. Changes in gut microbes have been associated with obesity, Type 2 diabetes, and autoimmune diseases, but whether losing these ancient species directly contributes to illness remains unknown.
“If these microbes hosted by the Hadza and Tsimane really are part of our evolutionary biology, then those of us in industrialized countries are missing a huge part of what our human genome has potentially adapted to over a vast time period,” Sonnenburg said. “We’re interested in more fully exploring these long-standing relationships between humans and our gut microbes.”
Reference: “Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans” by Matthew M. Carter, Zhiru Liu, Matthew R. Olm, Melanie Martin, Daniel D. Sprockett, Parsa Ghadermazi, Benjamin C. Trumble, Hillard Kaplan, Jonathan Stieglitz, Daniel Eid Rodriguez, David A. Relman, Erica D. Sonnenburg, Michael Gurven, Benjamin H. Good and Justin L. Sonnenburg, 7 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11106-1
This study was funded by Open Philanthropy, a Stanford Bio-X Bowes Fellowship, the National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging (grants R01-AG054442 and R35- GM146949), the National Science Foundation, the Wenner-Gren Foundation, the Thomas C. and Joan M. Merigan Endowment at Stanford University, and the French National Research Agency under the Investments for the Future (Investissements d’Avenir) program.

title: Scientists Predicted Humanity Would End on November 13, 2026. Should We Be Worried?
content:
In 1960, scientists published a mathematical model predicting that humanity would face a population catastrophe on November 13, 2026. Credit: Shutterstock
For decades, a doomsday equation predicted population growth better than most experts, until falling birth rates undermined its forecast of catastrophe in 2026.
In 1960,
, one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title:
Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026
. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.
The outlandishness of the claim landed the article in widespread public attention. More surprisingly—because its underlying research and math seemed sound—it also received careful and sustained scientific attention.
The authors—Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert, and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot—argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one.
“Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.”
The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate—until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts.
Today, the global birth rate is
slightly less than half what it was in 1960
. Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to a staggering effect.
Unique human capacities
The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that
whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself
In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional.
Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one.
They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations.
‘Squeezed to death’
Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity.
Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.
Heinz von Foerster in 1963. Credit: University of Illinois, CC BY-SA
This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in
The New York Times
. It became the subject of
a series of
comic strips,
and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.
A population explosion
Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When
Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited—usually at face value—in textbooks on genetics, ecology, and demography.
It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963
Canadian parliamentary committee
, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as the reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971
U.S. Supreme Court abortion case
leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population.
The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate—at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were
better than those
of most demographers
throughout the 1970s and 1980s
Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter, and the global population began falling behind the forecasts—because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
Science and stagecraft
We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13, “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on—prepping for the next doomsday scenario—it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.
For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn, and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.
Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity—that’s a good trick.

title: Qcells plans a gigawatt-scale perovskite tandem solar factory by 2029
content:
Qcells plans a gigawatt-scale perovskite tandem solar factory by 2029
has announced its plans to open a gigawatt-scale factory producing perovskite-silicon tandem solar panels in 2029.
Hanwha Qcells' solar production plant in Cumming, Georgia, USA. /Courtesy of Hanwha Solutions, from:
Qcells is already testing full-size tandem panels in the field, at its own test sites and with potential customers. The panels come from a
40 MW pilot line in South Korea
, launched in 2024, following an earlier pilot R&D line in Germany that opened in 2022. In 2024,
Qcells also announced an independently confirmed efficiency of 28.6% for a standard-size silicon cell topped with perovskite layers
. In July, the company
said its tandem panel had passed testing against UL and IEC quality standards
The location of the future factory has not been decided. A company presentation in Seoul last week reportedly pointed to Jincheon, South Korea. Qcells has also
designed its new vertically integrated factory in Cartersville, Georgia
, to be easily upgraded to tandem production when the time comes. Qcells also implied that industrial policy could be a determining factor in where the tandem factory is built.
Qcells did not share the perovskite composition it uses or any degradation data from the field tests. Company representatives said the 2029 timing allows time to convince large panel buyers to make the switch, and pointed to Qcells’ experience in scaling up gigawatts of solar production.
Qcells is among the companies speaking at
Perovskite Connect 2026
, taking place October 21-22 in Berlin.

title: Perovskite Connect 2026 opens next week in Berlin, join the industry there!
content:
Perovskite Connect 2026 opens next week in Berlin, join the industry there!
The wait is almost over:
Perovskite Connect 2026
opens next week! The event, co-organized by Metalgrass and TechBlick, takes place on October 21-22 at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, with optional tours and masterclasses on October 20. It runs alongside TechBlick’s Future of Electronics RESHAPED conference and exhibition, and together the two events expect over 600 participants, 80 exhibitors and 70 talks.
This is where the perovskite industry comes together under one roof. The program follows the full value chain: materials, inks and quantum dots; printing and solution processing; production and scale-up; testing and measurement; and applications in solar, LEDs, displays and sensors, with tracks for start-ups and market analysis too. To get a taste of what’s coming, take a look at our previews on
new materials and inks powering perovskite manufacturing
testing, reliability and sustainability on the road to bankability
the equipment, processes and applications taking perovskite to production
The speaker line-up includes Oxford PV, imec/EnergyVille, CubicPV, GCL Optoelectronic Material, Microquanta, Tandem PV, Qcells, Caelux, SolarEdge, Eternal Sun, Everlight and ZSW, among others, with talks on topics such as four-terminal tandem manufacturing, accelerated stress testing and perovskite recycling. It’s a chance to hear directly from the companies taking perovskites from lab to fab, and to meet them in person between sessions.
Last year’s inaugural edition drew rave reviews from participants, who pointed to the great turnout, inspiring talks and opportunities to connect researchers with manufacturers. This year promises to be even bigger.
Your pass is worth more than two days in Berlin: every ticket includes 12 months of hybrid access, covering the two onsite days, all of TechBlick’s online events and a library of more than 1,800 on-demand recordings. Tickets are selling quickly and the event is just days away, so now is the time to book your ticket and your travel.

title: 国家能源局召开2026年第三次能源监管工作例会-索比光伏网
content:
10月12日，国家能源局在京召开2026年第三次能源监管工作例会，深入学习贯彻党中央和国务院决策部署，梳理年度任务，宣讲规划政策，交流典型经验，布置下一阶段重点工作。国家能源局党组成员、副局长宋宏坤出席会议并讲话。
会议指出，三季度以来，各能源监管机构坚持以正确政绩观为引领，加压奋进、真抓实干，着力监管保障迎峰度夏能源安全稳定供应，统筹推进全国统一电力市场建设、电力领域综合监管、供电质量提升等重点任务，取得阶段性成效。
会议强调，当前正值全力冲刺的关键阶段，各能源监管机构要锚定年度目标、压实工作责任、持续补短强弱，确保全年工作圆满收官。要完善全国统一电力市场体系，加强电力市场监管执法，维护公平竞争市场秩序。要提早谋划迎峰度冬能源保供监管，加强供需监测预警，完善市场机制促进新能源消纳，及时妥善处置群众各类用能诉求。要扎实做好电力领域综合监管“后半篇文章”，全力推进年度重点监管任务，充分转化运用监管成果。要加大新一轮“获得电力”政策落实力度，压茬推进供电质量提升专项行动，加快非电网直供电小区治理。要严格落实全面从严治党政治责任，巩固拓展树立和践行正确政绩观学习教育成果，持续涵养风清气正的良好政治生态。
会上，国家能源局新能源司、市场监管司、资质中心宣讲有关规划政策要求，东北监管局、南方监管局、浙江监管办、湖南监管办进行交流发言。
国家能源局监管总监梁昌新主持会议，各相关司和部分直属单位负责同志在主会场参会，各派出机构负责同志和有关人员在分会场参会。

title: 国家铁路局：推动风光储微电网规模化应用-索比光伏网
content:
10月12日，国家铁路局印发《铁路科技创新“十五五”规划》（以下简称《规划》）。
在基础研究和前沿技术领域，
《规划》提出“加速绿色智能新材料研发及新技术应用”等重点任务，推动“源-网-车-储”协同、“风-光-氢-储”集成及再生制动等能量管理与实时调度技术研究。
在技术装备领域，
《规划》提出“推动绿色智能装备升级”等重点任务，研发柔性多源接入供电系统、高强高导耐磨线索及智能化高可靠牵引供电成套装备，构建绿色智能供电新模式。
在绿色低碳领域，
《规划》提出“推动绿色建造技术创新、推动运输装备低碳转型、推进绿智融合运营维护、建立健全碳管理体系”4项重点任务，明确“研制大功率氢能干线货运机车和氢能高效补给装备”等重点工程。
《规划》还提出，推动风光储微电网规模化应用，打造“近零碳”绿色施工示范。突破超低能耗建造与光伏/地源热泵技术。强化移动装备低碳化基础理论研究，强化移动装备低碳化基础理论研究，研究新一代永磁直驱牵引、氢燃料电池安全性设计及智能运维等关键技术，攻关燃料电池混合动力机车的能量管理控制技术。推进低排放低油耗内燃机车及动力电池、氢能等多源动力制式机车车辆示范运营，构建覆盖设计-制造-运营全过程的机车车辆能耗与排放的计量、监测评估体系。

title: “蓝片”不列入本土制造！印度发布新版ALMM电池命名标准草案-索比光伏网
content:
印度新能源与可再生能源部（MNRE）发布修订版草案，拟对批准型号与制造商清单（ALMM）List-II 下的光伏电池采用标准化命名体系。草案规定，每个入列电池型号均采用“制造商品牌名 + 14 位字母数字代码”的统一格式，以标识多晶硅、硅锭、硅片和电池的原产地，以及电池技术、硅片尺寸和转换效率等信息。
草案的利益相关方须在 2026 年 10 月 12 日前提交针对该修订草案的反馈意见。
MNRE 拟议的 14 位代码将通过原材料原产地、技术类型、硅片尺寸及转换效率识别 ALMM List-II 电池。（图片来源：MNRE）
本次草案旨在为电池型号建立统一识别基准，并提升光伏全产业链的溯源性。MNRE 规定，该标准化命名体系将适用于备忘录正式发布后印度国家太阳能研究所（NISE）对 ALMM List-II 新申请开展的审查；而已完成审查或已列入 ALMM List-II 的电池型号，则必须在最终备忘录发布后 2 个月内按照新体系完成更名。
按照拟议规则，14 位编码的前 4 位分别代表多晶硅、硅锭、硅片和电池的原产地，本土制造标注为“D”，外国制造标注为“F”；第 5 至 6 位标识电池技术路线，目前涵盖 Mono PERC（MP）、TOPCon（TC）、HJT（HJ）、背接触（BC）以及钙钛矿（PS），同时允许为新兴技术引入额外代码；第 7 至 8 位代表硅片尺寸，其中 MA 代表 M10、MB 代表 M10R、GA 代表 G12、GB 代表 G12R；第 9 至 11 位表示电池转换效率且省略小数点，例如 24.67% 对应编码为“246”，25.55% 则对应“255”；第 12 至 14 位目前作为预留位。
MNRE 曾于 2026 年 8 月提出一版草案，包含产品原产地、电池技术、硅片尺寸、主栅线以及制造商专用识别码。而 10 月更新的修订方案则改为分配给原产地、技术、硅片尺寸和转换效率，并预留最后 3 位。
此外，MNRE 在 10 月版草案中明确，使用已完成 P-N 结形成及减反射膜沉积的“蓝片”（扩散硅片）生产的电池，不得认定为印度本土制造。由于此类硅片更接近未完成的电池而非基础硅片，因此不得用于印度国内含量要求（DCR）项目。
该命名框架还将根据原材料清单（BoM）显示电池的本土或外国原产地属性，以区分 ALMM List-I 与 List-I(a) 光伏组件。MNRE 表示，该标准化命名体系有望成为每个入列 ALMM List-II 光伏电池型号的唯一识别框架，除便利入列外，还可促进产业链上下游的统一识别和追溯，并可能作为监管、商业及其他相关用途的通用产品标识符。
此外，MNRE 于 2026 年 10 月 1 日发布通知，要求光伏组件制造商在其印度标准局（BIS）注册的组件型号中增加 4 位字母 MMCC 国家代码，以标识组件及其 BoM 中所用电池的制造国。根据该程序，前两位字母代表组件制造国，后两位代表所用电池制造国；采用不同国家电池的组件必须申请独立型号，制造商将拥有 180 天时间更新现有注册。

title: 广东2026年新能源机制电价竞价申报全指南：资格｜规模｜报价策略｜风险避坑（粤发改价格函〔2026〕1805 号）-索比光伏网
content:
2026年10月10日，广东省发展改革委、广东省能源局联合发布《关于开展2026年新能源项目机制电价竞价工作有关事项的通知》（粤发改价格函〔2026〕1805号），正式启动2026年度新能源项目机制电价竞价工作。这是继2025年首轮竞价后广东的第二轮年度竞价，也是9月14日竞价登记通知发布后的正式规则落地，标志着广东机制电价体系从 “首轮探索” 进入 “稳态运行” 阶段。
本轮竞价核心呈现 “一扩两稳一细化” 的特征：**规模扩容**，机制电量初始竞价规模达79.34亿千瓦时，较2025年的50亿千瓦时增长 58.68%；**规则稳定**，0.20—0.40元/千瓦时价格区间、80%/70%申报比例上限、12年执行期限、1.2竞争有效性系数四大核心参数全部沿用2025年标准；**主体范围稳定**，继续明确集中式光伏、陆上风电项目不参与本轮竞价，仅面向
开放；**报价精细化**，价格申报基本单位由1%调整为0.1%，报价颗粒度提升10倍。同时竞价项目时间窗口整体后移一年，覆盖2025年6月1日至2027年10月31日投产或承诺投产的未纳入机制项目，为更多在建、规划项目留出申报空间。

业主而言，当前最核心的节点是10月13日的登记截止时间，需优先核对投产时间、项目类型、纳入状态三项资格条件，避免逾期错失年度机会。

title: Alpha Ventus decommissioning tenders halted
content:
Following Ocean Breeze Energy's acquisition of Germany's first offshore
wind farm, Alpha
decommissioning plans previously being progressed by Vattenfall are
no longer moving forward, with the decision attributed to a "change
in needs".
The two tenders, managed by Vattenfall on behalf of Deutsche Offshore-Testfeld
und Infrastruktur GmbH & Co. KG, covered both the wind turbine generator
(WTG) and balance of plant (BoP) scopes.
The WTG tender included the removal of the wind farm's 12 turbines, while
the BoP tender covered the removal of foundations, the offshore substation,
inter-array cables, scour protection and associated infrastructure.
Together, the contracts would have resulted in the full decommissioning
of the Alpha Ventus offshore wind farm. The cancellation of both tenders
suggests that a complete dismantling programme is no longer being pursued.
The development reinforces Ocean Breeze Energy's plans for the project.
As part of the acquisition announcement, the company said it would continue
operating the offshore wind farm.

title: New eCSOV launched by Bibby Marine
content:
Bibby Marine has launched its new electric commissioning service operation
vessel (eCSOV), Staffordshire, at Armon Shipyard in Vigo, Spain. The vessel
entered the water on 10 October, marking a key milestone in its development
ahead of entering service.
Staffordshire is designed to support offshore wind farm operations and
is the first vessel of its kind for Bibby Marine. The launch ceremony was
attended by project partners and representatives from Bibby Line Group.
The vessel is built around a battery-first propulsion system, with onboard
energy storage acting as the primary source of power. Bibby Marine has
partnered with Kongsberg and Corvus Energy on the propulsion and battery
systems and is working with Stillstrom to develop offshore charging compatibility.
According to Bibby Marine, the vessel could reduce operating costs by more
than 40% in self-charging mode and by around 70% when operating solely
with offshore charging. The project has previously received £20 million
in funding from the Zero Emission Vessels and Infrastructure (ZEVI) programme.
Staffordshire is the fifth vessel in the Bibby fleet to carry the name
and forms part of wider efforts to decarbonise offshore wind support vessels
as offshore wind capacity continues to expand globally.

title: EIB increases finance for Burgenland Energie renewable project
content:
The European Investment Bank (EIB) has announced additional financial support
for a renewable energy project in the eastern Austrian state of Burgenland.
Under the latest agreement, the EIB will provide a €20 million loan to
the region's energy supplier, following a €250 million loan granted to
Burgenland Energie last year.
Burgenland Energie, a developer and operator of solar and wind energy projects,
plans to expand its renewable energy capacity to 2 GW as part of efforts
to help Burgenland achieve energy independence by 2030.
EIB Vice-President Karl Nehammer said: "Investments like these are
making Europe's energy independence a reality while strengthening our industrial
base and the fight against climate change."
The financing is supported through the InvestEU programme and contributes
to the objectives of the REPowerEU plan, which aims to reduce Europe's
dependence on fossil fuels while accelerating the deployment of renewable
Total investment in the project currently stands at around €1.5 billion,
with Austrian banks, including UniCredit Bank Austria and Raiffeisen Bank
International, as well as Wiener Städtische and Talanx Group, participating
as financial partners.
Stephan Sharma, Chief Executive Officer of Burgenland Energie, said: "Five
years ago, Burgenland was 50% energy independent. Today, that figure has
already reached 75%. This success demonstrates what is possible when you
consistently believe in a vision and turn it into reality, step by step."

title: Kongsberg Maritime secures deal to support IWS Fleet expansion
content:
Kongsberg Maritime has secured a contract with IWS Fleet AS to support
four offshore wind Commissioning Service Operation Vessels (CSOVs), providing
vessel design and integrated technology solutions.
IWS Fleet recently announced an expansion of its offshore fleet to a total
of 10 vessels. The four new Skywalker class CSOVs will be constructed by
Nantong Rainbow Offshore & Engineering.
The newbuilds will be based on Kongsberg Maritime's UT 5519 DEx design,
building on the operational experience and performance of the six vessels
delivered since 2023.
Designed as walk-to-work platforms, the vessels will enable technicians
to live and work offshore for extended periods. They will also be equipped
with electrical power systems, navigation and bridge systems, propulsion
technology, deck machinery and dynamic positioning systems.
Per Ståle Nykrem, Director of Ship Design Sales at Kongsberg Maritime,
said: "Kongsberg Maritime is proud to continue its collaboration with
IWS Fleet on this next phase of the Skywalker-class programme."

title: CIP acquires 25% stake in Five Estuaries offshore wind farm
content:
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its flagship fund Copenhagen
Infrastructure V, has acquired a 25% stake in the Five
Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm.
The stake in the offshore wind project was previously held by a Macquarie-led
consortium. The agreement follows EDF's announcement last week that it
had acquired a 33.33% stake in the development.
CIP will join EDF Power Solutions, ESB and Sumitomo Corporation in advancing
the project.
Located approximately 40 kilometres off the coasts of North Essex and South
Suffolk, the Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm is expected to have a generation
capacity of up to 1,080 MW. Once operational, it could supply enough electricity
to power around one million UK homes annually.
Kunal Patel, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said: "CIP
is delighted to further expand its UK investment portfolio through the
acquisition of a stake in the Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm. We look
forward to working with our partners to deliver the project."

title: Neocloud Prime Intellect Acquires Startup To Speed Up Inference
content: Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market. For instance, one such neocloud, Prime Intellect , which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on its Nvidia servers, compared to its rivals. Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiring Moondream , a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEO Vincent Weisser . (Weisser wouldn’t share the terms of the deal, but Moondream has raised $4.5 million in funding.) San Francisco- and Seattle-based Moondream is best known for an open-source vision-language model for analyzing and understanding images, like identifying boxes in an image of a warehouse or ads in a livestream. But Prime Intellect is largely acquiring the startup for its employees’ skills in writing software to make models run more efficiently, Weisser said. Specifically, Moondream’s employees have experience with “megakernels,” a technique for speeding up AI inference by combining many separate mathematical operations that happen on a graphics processing unit into a single continuous operation, Weisser said. The process reduces a GPU’s idle time between tasks. Moondream has developed specialized software known as a compiler that can generate megakernels for numerous models, the startup has said. This compiler, as well as Photon, Moondream’s proprietary technology for running models quickly, will be incorporated into Prime Intellect’s tech, Weisser said. Megakernels aren’t a new concept: other inference providers like Together AI have written about their work with megakernels as well. However, writing megakernels historically has been a manual process, engineers say, whereas Moondream says its compiler functions largely automatically. Moondream’s experience in optimizing AI models that work in modalities other than text, like images, is also relatively rare in an industry that is hyper-focused on text-based AI, Weisser said. Prime Intellect thus hopes the new talent will help it cater to customers of AI for robotics and computer-using AI agents, for instance, he said. Those types of customers aren’t as well served by other neoclouds and inference providers today and could represent new sources of revenue for Prime Intellect. The firm said in July that it had passed $100 million in annualized revenue, implying a little over $8 million in monthly revenue at the time. That makes it significantly smaller than other inference providers like Fal , which is generating more than $800 million in annualized revenue, or Together AI, which is generating over $1 billion in annualized revenue. In addition to helping developers run models and providing them with compute for AI training and inference, Prime Intellect offers other software that helps developers tweak their models based on user and customer feedback, otherwise known as post-training or reinforcement learning, Weisser said. It has also trained its own models and other AI software, like coding and AI research agents, he said. If you’re wondering about the trustworthiness of annualized revenue figures in the wake of the OpenAI revenue mishegas last week, we are assured that those figures are real. However, as we have reported time and again, many of these inference providers must pay out a significant portion of their revenue to cloud providers that own and operate the servers, though Prime Intellect is different in that it actually operates its own hardware. AI Deep Dive: AI Will Automate Interpretability Research, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath AI is now solving open math problems by the hundreds, but there’s another field of research that could be even more quickly automated: mechanistic interpretability , which seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, according to Tom McGrath , chief scientist of Goodfire AI , a startup that specializes in the area. “Of all the fields of science, interpretability should be the one that gets most revolutionized—or revolutionized first—by AI,” said McGrath on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive . Compared to pure math, where most of the work happens on paper, interpretability is more like a natural science, such as biology, where experiments have to be run and data has to be collected to form new theories. AI research agents could perform many of those experiments themselves, McGrath argued. “We have the ability to turn a workforce which is orders of magnitude larger than the existing mech interp field loose on these models,” he said. “The thing that I think is going to revolutionize interpretability is deploying the swarm, deploying the swarm to give us orders of magnitude more experimental data, and then using that experimental data to improve our fundamental scientific understanding.” Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Microsoft is overhauling the leadership of its Azure cloud business, cloud chief Scott Guthrie told staff Monday, as the company consolidates units and reorients itself around AI, The Information reported. NTT Data is in final talks to build Anthropic 's first dedicated data center in Japan, a facility in Osaka with power intake capacity of up to 500 megawatts that could cost as much as ¥1 trillion ($6.3 billion) to construct—among the largest such projects in the country. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs , leading a $5 billion loan sale for AI infrastructure startup Volta Infrastructure Holdings , underwrote a $1.3 billion term loan themselves rather than a separate $3.7 billion loan for GPU purchases. Tencent is preparing to raise at least $4.5 billion through US dollar and offshore Chinese yuan bonds, mainly to fund AI capital expenditure, chiefly chip purchases.
