title: Applied Intuition Fields Offers at $30 Billion Valuation
content: For the last three years, AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI have sucked up a lot of investor attention—as well as nosebleed valuations. Now a growing number of startups that make apps, agents or other software powered by AI are fetching valuations of $20 billion or higher. Applied Intuition, a maker of software to train self-driving vehicles, is slated to join this club. Applied Intuition has received investment offers that would value it at least $30 billion, according to people who have spoken to company leaders. The offers are likely to encourage the company to raise at least $1 billion in the next few months, they said. A valuation at that level would double its June valuation and validate the nine-year-old company’s decision to focus on the software component of self-driving—rather than building and operating the cars as well. At the end of 2024, it was generating $400 million in annual recurring revenue , and it has doubled its revenue every year in recent years, investor Andreessen Horowitz said in July. The new funding would also expand the ranks of high-valued startups worth tens of billions. These include coding agent Cognition and Perplexity . Founded by Qasar Younis, former chief operating officer of Y Combinator, and Peter Ludwig, a former Google product manager, Applied Intuition sells software to develop, test and validate advanced driver-assistance and automated driving systems, as well as operating systems for vehicles. It counts Japan’s Isuzu, which uses its software to operate self-driving heavy trucks, as well as Volkswagen and Saudi Arabia’s Humain as customers. It has been expanding into supplying tech for autonomous military vehicles, setting it up for competition with defense tech startups Anduril and Saronic. This summer it launched an AI agent tool, Dana, which employees can use to automate the development of systems for physical AI and software-controlled vehicles. And last week, it announced deals to supply vehicle operating systems and other technology to Honda and Nissan. The success of Google’s Waymo, which has expanded its commercial operation across the U.S., is also encouraging investors to back self-driving car startups. The Sunnyvale, Calif.-based Applied Intuition has raised $1.2 billion from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst, Lux Capital, Kleiner Perkins and others. It hasn’t used most of it, Andreessen Horowitz said in July. title: Applied And Lam Are Overlooked Chip Equipment Stocks
content: The AI chip sector has been picked clean of bargains, as stocks of chip designers, chip manufacturers and chip manufacturing equipment makers have all soared in the past year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t still some opportunities if you know where to look. One example: Applied Materials, which makes machinery used in chip etching and deposition for memory chips—among the most highly sought-after components used in AI chips. As memory chip makers have quickly expanded manufacturing, companies like Applied and its nearest rival, Lam Research, have enjoyed surging demand for their products. The stocks of Lam and Applied Materials have tracked each other closely over the past 12 months, and are up 125% in that time. But there’s a case to be made that investors haven’t appreciated how much their growth could accelerate in the next two years or so. Applied vs. Lam Of the two, Applied may be a better bet for value-oriented investors. It is trading at a discount to Lam, at a forward price-earnings multiple of 28.8 times, well below Lam at 33.7, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. On a revenue multiple, Applied was at 9.1 to Lam’s 11.4. On the face of it, Applied’s discount makes sense. Lam is growing faster than Applied—Lam’s top line grew 24% in fiscal 2025 and slightly faster in fiscal 2026. It is expected to grow 50% in the coming 12 months, according to S&P data. Applied, on the other hand, grew only 4% last fiscal year. It is expected to grow 21% in fiscal 2026 and 35% in fiscal 2027. But some analysts argue that Applied can increase its growth rate to match Lam. They note that Applied is stronger than Lam in the manufacturing equipment used to make DRAM, which is the fastest-growing category of memory chip. DRAM is a faster, more temporary form of memory that has proven especially useful for AI models that need to process large volumes of information quickly. In their most recent fiscal quarters, DRAM accounted for 14.5% of Lam’s total revenue and 20.1% of Applied’s. More broadly, about two-thirds of Applied’s business comes from etch and deposition tools, which lay down layers of material on a chip and then carve them away. Newer DRAM, high-bandwidth memory and advanced logic chips all stack more layers, so chipmakers need more of those steps. Applied has “outsized or overweight exposure to that stuff, which is growing fastest,” said Jim Schneider, a semiconductor analyst at Goldman Sachs. Applied’s pipeline also looks promising, particularly in DRAM. The company has doubled its manufacturing capacity over the last several years, Chief Financial Officer Brice Hill said on an August earnings call, and plans to double the volume of equipment it produces from current levels by 2028 based on “longer-term demand signals” from customers. Executives say they made the decision to increase capacity by evaluating forecasts their large customers provide for the next eight quarters. That lead time has increased in recent years as Applied’s customers have been signing longer-term agreements to sell products to their own customers. That longer-term visibility could help reduce the risk of overproduction. Lam, meanwhile, is stronger in a different type of memory chip, NAND, which more closely resembles a permanent storage vault. In the most recent quarter, Lam said NAND revenue had doubled compared to the March quarter. But in the industry overall NAND revenues are not growing as quickly as DRAM. Analysts at HSBC argued in an August report that NAND supply could reach parity with demand by the end of 2027, potentially slowing Lam’s revenue growth. Lam is also growing fast because it sells tools to package memory wafers together onto a chip, a business executives that have said is driving growth within its foundry segment. While that is helping Lam now, it also means Lam is more vulnerable to a pullback in AI spending that would affect the memory market. Applied, in contrast, is more dependent on slower-growing markets such as automotive and industrial markets. That has hurt Applied’s growth rate in the past couple of years but it could insulate the business from any stumbles in AI. In short, Applied has decent exposure to the fastest-growing part of the memory business, but it also may be less affected than Lam if AI spending retreats and chip makers cut back their orders for chipmaking equipment. The risk for both companies is that they’re heavily exposed to China: each derives around a third of their revenues from that country, and have been affected by trade restrictions, limiting what they can sell. Another risk is that like the memory chip stocks themselves, equipment suppliers like Applied and Lam operate highly cyclical businesses in which years of growth are followed by downturns, as chip makers pull back due to oversupply. “I think both these industries are still cyclical,” said Schneider. But “you’ve got one more year of accelerating growth rate and two more years of growth” at minimum.

title: Researchers Need to Learn How AI Makes Decisions, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath
content: To understand the decision-making of AI, developers often look at the text that models produce as they reason through problems. But these “chains of thought” are increasingly hard to read, which is prompting AI developers to consider other approaches. One alternative, known as “mechanistic interpretability,” seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, rather than just relying on their outward behavior. Leading AI companies have formed mechanistic interpretability teams in recent years, and the field has spawned several startups , the most prominent of which is Goodfire AI, whose chief scientist Tom McGrath joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. ( The full episode is available here .) “Interpretability work is basically a natural science,” said McGrath. “You have this, let’s say, alien mind, and you’re trying to prod it, take it apart.” So far, developers’ abilities to make sense of the internals of AI models, which are made up of trillions of numbers, has been largely limited to understanding narrow tasks, like how they perform certain kinds of math , or detecting the presence of concepts in a model’s thinking, such as Claude fixating on the Golden Gate Bridge . As AI models take on increasingly high-stakes work, interpretability is becoming more pressing. McGrath argues that “brain scan” techniques could help prevent future incidents like OpenAI’s hack on Hugging Face. Goodfire recently went further, kicking off an effort to “fully reverse-engineer” a Qwen language model from China’s Alibaba Group. We also discussed some of the most popular techniques in mechanistic interpretability, how using the approach to train new AI models could backfire and how AI agents could soon automate interpretability research. And what would it look like to fully reverse engineer a model like that? How will we know we’ve achieved that? McGrath: There are a few different definitions. The one that I like best is that I can ask—I’ve got my reverse engineering—I can ask whatever question I want about the model, and I can get a causally verified answer. An answer, perhaps in the form of a paper or a short explanation, that I have good reason to believe, I can test it, I can falsify it. That is the answer that I’m most excited about. One other thing people often propose as the way to measure this is the percentage of the loss you’ve recovered—the loss is just sort of a measure of how well the model is doing at predicting the input text. I’m less keen on that because, sure, in the limit these are the same thing right? But before we reach that infinite limit, I’d prefer to focus our effort on the questions we actually care most about. Drew: Like what? McGrath: So, for instance, let’s stick with reward hacking or deception. I care much more intrinsically about these questions than I care about how it knows where to put the comma. I love the comma—it’s a very impressive thing to be able to put it in the right place. I can’t do it. Drew: It’s the difference between eating your grandma and inviting her to dinner. It’s important. McGrath: Exactly. But while I’m on the way to full reverse engineering, I prefer to get to that part first. The comma occupies dramatically more of the loss reduction than the deception, say, and so it seems like the wrong ordering. I think there’s also something worth saying about “solve X” right is the thing we love saying here in SF. One of the reasons I think we love saying it is it’s actually quite poorly defined. It’s ambitious sounding, but quite poorly defined. I think the best example of doing this well was AlphaFold, where they said they’d solved protein folding. Here they have literally a quantitative threshold, and they can say “we’ve solved protein folding when it’s within such-and-such accuracy.” I forget the units. But that is still an arbitrary threshold, it’s not 100%, at some point you have to say this, this is, it’s sort of a little bit vibey, right? So that’s why I care about where we succeed first, because ultimately the ‘solve interpretability’ destination is quite poorly specified. But I think it’s a great north star. Drew: Okay, and would contrast that—so for current techniques, if you ask “why is a model reward hacking in this environment?” the state of the art is we use these kinds of brain scans, these probes you described, the probes come back saying the model was thinking about deception, and that’s kind of the strongest answer we can get. But when you’re imagining a model that’s fully reverse engineered, when you pose a question like this, the answer that you get back is what? It’s more convincing to you? It’s…? McGrath: It’s more like: the following parts of the model are typically responsible for deception. Here’s a set of experiments that should convince you. If you don’t, I can do more experiments. So it’s more like an interactive experiment—it’s more like an interactive proof, I suppose. These parts of the model typically are responsible for deception. They’re active in this case. They’re active because of these things. If I turn them off, the rollout changes in the following ways that are consistent with these being responsible for deception. If I increase them, if I graft these in to another rollout, it also becomes deceptive, and so on. This is sort of different in type to the kind of explanation where you say, “oh, look, the SAE feature is firing” but I think it’s different in type in a way that is actually good, and is the right way for us to move forward, because the way that it’s different is that it uses a lot of flexible intelligence. It’s not using genius per se, it’s using like, we’ve got these different components, we’ve at some point identified them, perhaps by just pulling apart a bunch of other transcripts. We’ve identified these components, but the actual explanation I’m gesturing at here is one I expect that, given a big database, given an attribution graph, say, or some more exhaustive set of things, I could probably construct that myself in a month or le—yeah, hopefully not a month, hopefully I work a bit quicker than that. But I could, in principle, construct it, and there’s no reason why Astra can’t construct it either. So it feels like the thing I care about here is: how do we make use of this big expansion of agentic intelligence on top of whatever we already have? I think that’s actually a very powerful thing to imagine. Drew: I like this point that ‘solved’ is impressive sounding, but fuzzy enough that it’s easy to claim victory. Another criterion like this is ‘intern-level’—to have intern-level AI. There’s wide variance in the level of interns. I mean, there’s a real experiment you could do, I guess, where you offer people human interns versus AI to see what they do. But still, easy to claim victory on that one I think. McGrath: I think this is just the nature of this kind of relatively fuzzy—things that require fuzzy intelligence. They’re just, you know, it’s fuzzy. Drew: Can you give us a little bit of a market map of the mech intrp world? Who are the different camps or factions? Are there different schools of thought in mech interp? McGrath: Oh, that’s interesting. Yes. I’m trying to put this together and also not upset anybody. Whoever I forget, I apologize, it’s my fault. Okay, so obviously there’s Goodfire, and then there’s Anthropic, where mech interp has a long-standing history: Chris was really the founder of the field. I would say in my mind—I have no real insight into how this works internally—but there seem to be at least two schools of thought, just from reading papers that come out of Anthropic, and one is this sort of dictionary-learning, more a priori decomposition thing, and the other is this idea of natural language autoencoders and what people call meta-models. And we can go into any of these, I’ll just say things and skip over the details for now. There’s Neel’s school—Neel Nanda at DeepMind has this sort of pragmatic interpretability thing, and there I think the idea is more: come up with downstream tasks you might care about, like being able to tell if the model is thinking about apples when I’m not telling you or something, and you don’t so much try to generate broad methods or necessarily broad scientific findings, but you try and solve the task, which I think is a very admirable thing. There’s a more diffuse, I’d say academic cluster, of people doing more specific reverse engineering. People like David Bau at Northeastern comes to mind, Max Tegmark, Martin Wattenberg, who, when I think of someone who’s—if you want to read a really cool account of how a bit of the model works, just go read some of their group’s papers, they’re just candy. And who else who I missed. Oh, Simplex and Resolution. Their technical approaches are different in important ways, but I’d put them both more under the heading of trying to find a fundamental mathematical theory that can account for, that is the right language in which to explain interpretability. And I think I would also put our parameter decomposition team somewhere in that bucket, somewhat more in the decompositions bucket. That’s a pretty exhaustive list, I’m sure I’ve forgotten people, but— Drew: Yeah, that’s very helpful. So these camps differ in terms of their philosophy, or their motivations—what it is that they’re trying to accomplish. Are they trying to build up a comprehensive understanding of how the model works from the ground up, or are they trying to work backwards from a specific goal and use whatever techniques are available in service of that goal? And then as a consequence, these camps also differ in the techniques they favor and the directions that they find most promising. How would you situate Goodfire here? What are the directions Goodfire is pursuing? McGrath: One thing I often say. There’s this idea from the book Pasteur’s Quadrant, which I really like. A lot of people organize science on the basic-to-applied spectrum. I think it’s more like there’s use-case-inspired versus freeform, and then there’s aiming at a fundamental understanding and then there’s like not, I guess. And so the Pasteur’s Quadrant is, in the two-by-two, it’s use-case-inspired basic research. So I would say that the way I describe a lot of what we’re trying to do at Goodfire is thinking about these very ambitious applications of interpretability, having them in mind, and then often doing quite foundational science where that seems necessary. That’s how I’d describe it. Another mental image that I use quite often is this idea of going from—we do a lot of very applied work with customers, which I think is extremely important to get contact with reality, and is ultimately where—whatever we do, ultimately whatever we do only matters if it gets used where it matters. And so this one is in my mind a spectrum: on one side you’ve got freeform, open-ended work, and on the other side you’ve got very customer-facing work, or like things which are driven by precisely the problem, and you know, Fred over there has the problem, and you can go talk to him about it. I like things to be at either end. I think there’s this sort of no-man’s-land in the middle, where you can be doing work with a sort of usefulness flavor. It looks useful, but no one, in fact, has ever used it, and no one is going to use it. And I think that work in the middle is like, sometimes you have to do a bit of that to get from one end to the other, but you don’t want to live there. Drew: Name names. Who’s working on that? McGrath: I am not going to say that. Drew: Do you have an example of a technique that you think falls in that no-man’s-land. McGrath: I think it would not be diplomatic for me to say. Drew: I love academic infighting. So fun. McGrath: Readers are invited to name that, yeah, this is an exercise for the reader. Drew: There you go. McGrath: Or for the comments section, I guess, if this is going on YouTube. Drew: It surely is. Do you feel that the field overall is underinvested in mech interp, or that the AI labs are underinvesting in this research area? McGrath: Yeah. I think—well, obviously, their resource allocations are for them to decide. Drew: Sure. McGrath: I think it should receive an essentially infinite amount of resource investment. It’s hard to imagine—like, if we increased the size of the field by an order of magnitude, I think we would be nowhere near diminishing returns. Drew: If mech interp grew. McGrath: Yeah. Sorry, when you say the field, which field do you mean? Drew: I guess I mean AI as a whole. Or, for the labs, why aren’t they increasing the resources going toward mech interp on the margin? Surely you would have them put more resources toward it. Why don’t they? McGrath: That’s a good question. I think there’s a few answers. One is that some of the returns are more alignment-oriented, some are more moonshot-style, and investing in alignment research is something that I think all of the labs have done, but they’ve done in advance of it being directly important, and so you don’t have as detailed contact with reality as you do now. And I think that we’re going to see a big investment in alignment from all the labs. That’s almost certainly going to be ramping up dramatically, and I expect that investing in interpretability will also be part of that. Another answer is, it’s been a couple of years since I was at a big lab, but I think the pressure to ship a state-of-the-art model every—now more like maybe weeks to months—it’s very good for making models better, but I think it leads to, you’re sort of on the treadmill. It’s very hard to step off the treadmill and do something which is a bit different. It might not be the shortest path to model improvement for the next generation, and I imagine that’s easy to see as the overriding priority, particularly when you have such a competitive landscape. Drew: But you do imagine that interp techniques are going to start to get useful during training. I think you were saying before that sometimes we’ve treated these techniques as the best that they can offer us is an understanding of what’s going on. There’s something here like: mech interp researchers so far have sought only to understand the model; the point is to change it. Something along those lines. McGrath: Yeah. Drew: What would that look like, to incorporate mech interp during training to shape the behavior of models? McGrath: I think there’s a real range. You can go from right outside the loop, where you select environments, for instance based on something like what we did with the predictive data debug, you select some parts of the dataset based on interpretability tools. You can imagine bringing this slightly more inside, where during a training run you detect reward hacking, you do something sensible based on that detection. For instance, if monitoring has told you that this environment is hackable, you send it off to your favorite coding agent with the transcript and a note attached that says “please fix.” Now, that’s something you could do with chain of thought monitoring, but your ability to cheaply and accurately detect these reward hacks, for instance, matters a lot. What would it look like to get it closer in, though? I think the potential prize here is very big, and that is more like a kind of learning principle that can—a sort of, alignable learning principle. Part of the problem—neural networks sort of know what we care about at the start of training, and training gradually causes them to ignore it, because the training process does not incentivize that. There’s no way to say—I’ve been in and around the safety and alignment field for a while now, and one thing I would often say with a bit of exasperation when I was first getting into the field is, “ah, they want backprop, but only in the good direction”—backprop, but only for good things. But I actually think that perhaps the ultimate prize here is like backprop but only for good things. Drew: And can you explain what backprop is? McGrath: Oh yes, backprop is the way that you update the weights in a neural network. Drew: Golden. Yep, that works. But employing our interp techniques as signals during training—some people think of that as very taboo, like that is a controversial proposition, I think for the reason you explained earlier, which is that you worry about just suppressing the bad cognition, pushing it somewhere else in the model, where now you don’t detect it at all. What do you make of those concerns? McGrath: I think they’re very valid. I think we should not deploy these techniques if we’re going to lose the ability to monitor what models are doing. I think about this constantly, and I think the difference between the way I think about it and the way that I think a lot of other people think about this is I think there are algorithms that can use this kind of information without destroying monitorability. We’re doing really a lot of work to understand the dynamics here and try and characterize things much better. Some of that should come out in the next few weeks. Drew: I guess the question that comes up to me is: how will we know? McGrath: Yeah. Drew: How will we know which case we’re in? Did we just cause it to suppress the deceptive reasoning, or did we truly change the motivations of the model? How will we know? McGrath: There’s a few ways, I think. So you might become confident at the level of the algorithm, right? The problem is when your interpretability method is your only way to detect something. So if it’s deception, and for instance let’s say the model is actually good at hiding deception from its chain of thought. If you’re relying on your interpretability technique to say the model is being deceptive, then you can’t tell if you’ve lost this. But this is actually quite a rare property of things that you might try and intervene on. One example I used in the intentional design post is like speaking like a pirate. Has a very clear representational signature, you can pick it up a lot of the time, but it has an even clearer text signature. So I can imagine becoming confident at the level of the algorithm where I’ve used it on 10,000 cases where I can tell from the text. I think that’s probably not sufficient, but it’s a way of telling that you’re on track. There’s also the question how do you preserve a test set, and I think one answer to this is that interpretability is not a monolith, it’s not a single technique. You can do very cheap things, like difference-of-mean vectors we talked about. You can do very expensive things, like deploy a swarm. And I expect that anything you use in training will be very cheap, simply as a matter of, it has to fit in the training process. Whereas your test set can be arbitrarily expensive. So you might imagine that you intervene on representations of deception, but then afterwards you do an extremely exhaustive, agentic effort. There’s also the option to try and restrict computation only to things you understand. You could imagine restricting gradients only to things that you understand. But I think I feel most optimistic about algorithms that we have some mathematical reason to believe don’t do this, and a trust in the algorithm that we’ve built up for theoretical and empirical reasons, but then backed up by this expensive test set that goes, “no, really, you haven’t missed anything.” Drew: And in all of these ways, we’ll be able to basically validate that the method is working— McGrath: Exactly. Drew: The way we intend. How do you square that with what I take to be your position on chain of thought monitoring, which is that we should not train against our chain of thought monitors, for an analogous reason, that if we play thought police, the model will just simply learn a way to suppress the reasoning that we’re training against? What’s different about these two cases? McGrath: Oh, that’s a good point. I think that there’s a status quo in frontier training which seems stable-ish, and what I’m proposing is you could move to a different, and in my opinion better, situation. We haven’t developed it, like I may be wrong. It would be a real shame for us to give up what we currently have on the basis that something else might work. I think that before we do any of the sort of stuff that I’m imagining here, in the context of any genuinely consequential training run, it should be examined to the nth degree. So I think what I’m saying is that, in some ways it’s different because it’s working now, and I’m just a little bit conservative about that. Drew: I see. Okay, that’s a helpful clarification. But that maybe in six months we’ll be in a different situation. McGrath: Maybe. Yeah. I hope so. I believe so. But I recognize that I’m in the minority here, and it’s very different to have demonstrated that you can do something from being optimistic that you can do it. Drew: The last subject I want to make sure that we cover is how you’re going to use AI to help you do your job. I don’t know if you’d say you’re expecting AI to take your job, but how are you thinking about taking advantage of the labor of AI agents going forward? McGrath: Yes, that is a very interesting question. So I think I said to you before we did the show that, of all the fields of science, interpretability should be the one that gets most revolutionized—or revolutionized first—by AI, and it’s disappointing that it hasn’t been. It’s largely our fault. So why do I think that? Because interpretability work is basically a natural science. You have a thing—let’s say an alien mind—and you’re trying to prod it, take it apart. You’re forming hypotheses about, “oh, this neuron does such and such.” When you’re interacting with it, you’re doing little causal experiments. These aren’t things that you can necessarily set off a Python script off to do, because they involve semantics, they involve some sort of coming up with little hypotheses and what are the sensible tests, and that sort of thing. But you can put them more on rails, like the way that Lean guardrails mathematical reasoning, like causal abstraction kind of guardrails scientific reasoning about language models. So we have the ability to turn a workforce which is orders of magnitude larger than the existing mech interp field loose on these models, and I think at the moment the things they will do will be low-level experiments, like how did the model represent variable binding in this case? Or I might ask: how does the model represent variable binding? And then out go the agents: how did it represent it in this case, how did it represent it in the other case? Maybe there’s a little bit of agentic aggregation step on the top, but then some data comes back and we go, “oh, that is how they represent variable binding.” Or you know, we need to do some synthesis ourselves and think about it. So the thing that I think is going to revolutionize interpretability is deploying the swarm to give us orders of magnitude more experimental data, and then using that experimental data to improve our fundamental scientific understanding. Sometimes when I talk about this, people are, they imagine that I think the only blocker is experimental data, like a pile of uranium or something. You pile up enough experimental data in the corner and eventually it undergoes a chain reaction, Drew: Yeah, a critical mass. McGrath: Yeah, that’s not what I imagine. What I imagine is more like what happened with Darwin and evolution, where he went around the world and noticed, “oh, there’s finches, that’s weird; there’s barnacles, what’s up with that?” And eventually, there’s this quote of his that I really like, about his mind having become a machine for grinding laws out of mountains of data or something like that. I think we have the opportunity to assemble the mountains of data, and then it’s on us to do the grinding. Drew: Okay, but the AIs will help at least with creating the mountains of data. McGrath: Yes, exactly. Drew: And maybe with that process of abduction and forming theories as well. I could see it getting to that point. McGrath: Yes, I’m sort of saying, I’m being a little conservative— Drew: A little conservative saying it’s the field that will be transformed the most. McGrath: But the way in which it’ll be transformed Drew: Sure. McGrath: I could give you a galaxy-brain version, where I just press the button and I come back in a week to interpretability.csv, or .pdf, or I don’t even know what format. Maybe the file format isn’t the important thing here. I come back to the giant, million-page textbook on interpretability that tells me everything. There’s the galaxy—there’s the super-RSI-brained version of this. I’m being kind of conservative about which parts of the field get transformed first, simply because I’m actually trying to do it now, and that has a grounding effect, I guess. Drew: Yeah, I can see arguments for why mech interp is going to be differentially accelerated compared to other fields. It has these nice properties: sometimes you’re dealing with a really crisp, well-defined metric, like how much loss you’re able to reconstruct, that you can maybe generate a lot of experiments against very easily. Even so, how much are you expecting the field to accelerate in practice? It could turn out that the models are bottlenecked by research taste, that experiments are slow to run, like actual—in terms of the wall-clock time, they take a while. They have to be run in series because each experiment builds on previous ones. What will it feel like to have a year of mech interp research a few years from now? McGrath: When I’m just saying random vibe things about this, I’m like we should expect a decade’s worth of counterfactual work every year. So you know the field should speed up by an order of magnitude. Two orders of magnitude is hard to imagine, precisely because of the serial time involved in and human time involved in thinking about things at the current level of conceptual ability that I think models have. I’m not worried about experiments taking a long time to run. The advantage is we have them running, they’re tremendously fast. Maybe on big models they’re slower, but I’m not too worried; you can just turn a cluster into a super-high-throughput experimental machine. The question is whether you get the tokens, whether you can make those tokens do something coherent. Drew: I see. Is this happening already? Are you noticing AI speed up your work and start to be useful in these ways? McGrath: Yes. Drew: What does that look like? McGrath: It looks like being able to get in-depth analyses of things that you could have done but never would have done. The parameter decomposition team—I’ll give an example I was talking to them about this morning. Their work produces parameter components, these are little bits of neural network. And you can do the standard auto-interp—automated interetability—where you look at a few examples on which they fired on and come up with a little label. Or you can set an agent running to do the sort of very deep analysis that you might do, and it comes up with a bunch of hypotheses, it proposes inputs that would test these various hypotheses, it looks at the upstream and downstream connections. It does this very painstaking thing, and it’s much more correct. And you or I could have done that. We could have sat there for a week and gone through it, but we just wouldn’t. Drew: I’d rather not. McGrath: Yeah, I quite enjoy it. That sounds like kind of a nice week to me. Drew: That’s why you’re in this line of work. McGrath: Yeah, exactly. But if you look at one of the perhaps the fastest period of theoretical progress in mechanistic interpretability, the early circuits thread, that was a bunch of very smart, very driven people sitting down to do exactly this kind of work. Just there weren’t very many of them. But wherever they looked, they would find something. So we should have 1,000 circuits threads or something. Drew: It’s just worth pausing on, I think, and appreciating how sci-fi this vision is. I mean, many of the interp methods that we’ve talked about are themselves AI models. We haven’t always talked about them that way, but some of them are AI models, which are trained in their own right. We’re describing AI researchers—automated mech interp researchers—training their own AI models to understand the brains of still other AI models. That’s the future we’re headed towards? McGrath: Only in San Francisco. Drew: Truly. McGrath: It’s the only place in the world I would say such a thing. Yes, I think so, with the caveat that training other AI models is one way of doing it. You might imagine they simply just write down matrices; they’re surprisingly capable of just writing parameter components themselves by hand, for instance. But yes, you’ve got a swarm of AIs really trying to deeply understand either another copy of themselves, or a new model, or whatever. It’s a very sci-fi thing, but it’s sort of the only thing that feels appropriate at the moment. Like the world is sci-fi, what else do we—what’s the appropriate response? It’s that, or go into the woods. Drew: I’m getting pretty close to that after this conversation. McGrath: I thought this was optimistic! Drew: It is optimistic, but just so sci-fi. Well, Tom, thank you very much for coming on the show. I really appreciated the conversation. It’s really helpful to have you break down all of these very technical concepts to understand what’s happening in this strange land where people do neuroscience on AI models. So thank you very much. McGrath: Thank you very much for having me. It’s been a pleasure. Drew: You’ve been listening to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. That was Tom McGrath. Tune in next time.

title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?
content: If it’s Monday, it must be time for another AI model release. This time, it was Meta Platforms’ turn, unveiling Muse Wonder, which it claims can “deliver state-of-the-art performance” on certain tasks. It was a triumphant moment for the company, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump that prompted a massive hiring binge over the past 14 months or so. It now claims it is “pushing the frontier” of AI. That would be notable if only everyone wasn’t claiming to be doing the same thing. Two weeks ago, Google unveiled its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which it says “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows” across various subjects (you wouldn’t want it to deliver frontier performance in simple workflows, would you?). In early September, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra , which it said was “state of the art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.” Also in September, Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 , which it claimed to be “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.” We get it—AI executives want to trumpet every advance, hoping it will draw more customers and in some cases investors. You have to wonder, though, whether anyone can keep up with the blizzard of announcements, much less care about them all. As we’ve reported , businesses are increasingly opting for less advanced models to save money for much of their computing needs, reserving any use of the most advanced (and priciest) models for very specific tasks. Indeed, we reported today that only 14% of the AI model usage via OpenRouter ran through the 10 highest-quality models in the third quarter, down from 55% in the first quarter of last year. That’s a result of the falling cost of less advanced models that are “good enough” for most tasks. Consumers, who are the target audience for Meta’s Muse personal agent, certainly don’t need the most advanced AI models for everything they do. Yet Meta said its latest Muse Wonder model will “soon power experiences in Muse.” The only impact of that might be on the company’s costs. One of these days the AI firms will realize the frontier is a lonely place to be. Bumble’s Big Stumble The IPO class of 2021 is gradually getting taken off the public market, very often at a huge discount to where its members entered. The latest is dating app Bumble, which is in talks to go private at a $1 billion valuation, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday. While that implies a higher takeout price than where Bumble’s shares have lately been trading—the stock jumped 50%, or $1.26, to $3.80—it crystallizes the huge drop in the company’s value since it went public. Bumble sold shares in the IPO at $43 each, and the stock nearly doubled in the first few days, giving the company a market capitalization of $9.5 billion. Unfortunately, growth has slowed in the crowded data app market. If this deal gets done, Bumble will be the problem of Ravi Gupta, a former Sequoia partner, and John Hegeman, former chief revenue officer at Meta. The two formed a new company that is looking for acquisitions—starting with Bumble. At least they’ll pick it up at a reasonable price. In Other News • Meta has banned advertisements from ByteDance on its platforms in the U.S. and several other markets, Bloomberg and other media outlets reported. • Bain Capital–owned Bridge Data Centres is in talks with banks to increase the size of a loan from $2.8 billion to about $6.6 billion for its Malaysia operations, Bloomberg reported . The fundraising would be one of the largest debt financing deals in Asia’s data center industry. • Microsoft on Monday announced the latest generation of its homegrown AI chips, dubbed Maia 300, and said it plans to set up “multigigawatt deployments” of the chip starting next year. Today on The Information’s TITV Check out today’s episode of TITV in which Akash Pasricha speaks with Aaron Holmes about his profile of a key Microsoft executive you should be paying attention to. Subscribe now for free to get it delivered straight to your inbox twice a week. New From Our Reporters Pro Report Leading-Edge AI Models Are Losing Their Allure With Developers By Eric Bellomo Exclusive Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst Race to Secure the Chips Their Startups Need By Julia Hornstein, Dakin Campbell and Phoebe Liu Exclusive How Microsoft’s New Office Chief Fixed Copilot and Won Over Nadella By Aaron Holmes AI Agenda OpenAI’s Plan To Revive Sora By Stephanie Palazzolo and Cory Weinberg Upcoming Events Tuesday, October 27 — The Information’s 2026 WTF Summit The Information's WTF Summit returns to Napa Valley, bringing together the women shaping tech, media and finance. title: Trump Administration Plans to Move AI Testing Agency Officials to White House
content: The small agency within the Commerce Department tasked with testing new AI models appears to be getting a refresh. In September, the Trump administration began the process of restructuring the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence so that three of its senior officials report directly to the White House, according to a White House official. For months, administration officials had considered whether to move all of CAISSI into the White House. Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and other senior officials ultimately agreed to the new arrangement in an effort to better integrate CAISSI into the White House’s decision-making process around AI, said the White House official. According to a senior Commerce official, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick invited two White House officials—Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross—to co-manage CAISSI six months ago. The three CAISSI officials, whose names couldn’t be learned because the White House is still processing their move, will report to Kratsios, the Office of Science and Technology Policy Director, and Cairncross, Office of the National Cyber Director, the White House official said. Still, there has been confusion between the White House and the Commerce Department on the CAISSI officials’ move, which is still being finalized. The White House official said the lack of coordination from the Commerce Department demonstrates why CAISSI leadership needs to move to the White House. The new structure is the latest update for CAISSI, which also recently changed its name to reflect President Donald Trump’s preferred new moniker for AI. CAISSI’s new name, its third in less than two years, is a fitting symbol for an agency that has seen more than its share of tumult under Trump’s White House as AI has rocketed to the center of the national agenda. Created by the Biden administration, the agency has been plagued by limited resources, personnel upheavals and bureaucratic nitpicking. The debate over where CAISSI should be housed has left its staff confused in recent weeks about their status, according to two people familiar with the matter. Officials in the Trump administration have for some time debated the best place for CAISSI in the federal government. Some have argued in favor of moving the agency out of the Commerce Department in an effort to provide better resources to its staff, according to people close to the administration. OSTP director Kratsios, for one, has previously advocated for the agency to move to the Department of Energy, where CAISSI could leverage resources such as the department’s national laboratories, The Information previously reported . The uncertainty comes at a crucial juncture for the agency and for the White House’s broader approach to AI regulation. While CAISSI has around just 40 staff and a skimpy $15 million in annual funding, it plays a key role in evaluating new AI models for their capabilities and safety. Despite CAISSI’s diminutive footprint, its technical staff have taken on newfound importance as the Trump administration has reckoned with increasingly advanced cybermodels. As part of a White House framework finalized in August  for testing models pre-deployment, CAISSI works alongside the better-resourced National Security Agency to test frontier models like OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Mythos prior to a broader release, according to four people familiar with the situation. In a blog post published on September 30, Google announced that it had submitted its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, to the White House for the voluntary testing process. Google still has not widely released that model. Especially given its heightened role, CAISSI’s lack of political support and resources under the Trump administration has been a persistent source of concern for AI policy experts and lawmakers, as well as frontier labs and administration officials. When Trump announced the composition of a new SI task force in early October, it included a long list of senior administration officials. However, it didn’t include anyone from the Commerce Department and made no mention of CAISSI. U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who also oversees the NSA, was named head of the task force. Several people close to the White House and the AI industry said integrating CAISSI into the White House would be a welcome step, as it could buoy the agency’s political capital and help streamline the process for evaluating models. More clarity regarding CAISSI’s status would also address industry concerns about the White House’s approach to pre-deployment model testing, especially because it still has not released its framework, and the breakdown of responsibilities between it and other agencies like the NSA remains unclear. Separately, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic recently explored creating their own industry group that would supplement CAISSI’s model evaluation work, partly out of concerns that the agency lacks sufficient resources, The Information previously reported . Political Football The Biden administration initially created the AI Safety Institute as part of a 2023 executive order on AI. It intended to staff the agency with highly technical AI experts and task it with evaluating cutting-edge new models from around the world. The institute was supposed to work hand in hand with a partner agency in the U.K., as well as with industry and policy groups, to create standards for identifying and mitigating AI risk. The incoming Trump administration greeted the agency with skepticism. Under AI czar David Sacks, who favored a hands-off approach to regulating AI, the White House renamed it the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The administration hired Collin Burns, a leading expert on AI testing, to lead CAISSI, but he lasted just a few days on the job. The White House fired him because he had previously worked at Anthropic, which has at times had a hostile relationship with the Trump administration, The Washington Post reported . Though the agency remained at the Commerce Department, the administration often froze it out of broader conversations about AI, according to a former White House official. That remained true following Anthropic’s announcement of its Mythos model in April, a moment when AI’s risks became a more prominent concern within the administration and the Office of the National Cyber Director led policy discussions on the White House’s response. The White House began to lean into CAISSI’s technical expertise more over the summer, including after the administration imposed export controls on Anthropic over security concerns with Mythos and Fable in June. And CAISSI still plays a central role in testing models as part of the White House’s AI framework, according to multiple people familiar with the process. The agency also has forged formal agreements with many of the major AI labs to evaluate their models. CAISSI has dealt with continued turnover, however. In July, its director, Chris Fall, unexpectedly resigned after just three months on the job, and the agency is still looking for a new head, according to two people familiar with the matter. In the interim, Arvind Raman—director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Commerce Department agency that houses CAISSI—is overseeing the AI agency. CAISSI’s cyber lead, Andrew Fasano, left in June to join Anthropic, according to his LinkedIn. And another key staffer, Paul Christiano, joined OpenAI’s nonprofit board in September, though his LinkedIn says he is still an adviser to CAISSI. “President Trump is ensuring America leads the world in Super Intelligence. At the President’s request, the White House is bringing government and industry leaders together to accelerate innovation, ensure the safe and responsible deployment of new models, and protect the American people,” said White House spokesperson Liz Huston.

title: Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst Race to Secure the Chips Their Startups Need
content: As startups scramble to get access to AI servers, more venture capital firms are finding ways to secure compute on their behalf. Andreessen Horowitz, which two years ago set up a cluster of 20,000 graphics processing units for its startups, is in talks to expand its offering, potentially via two data center companies it has backed, according to people familiar with its plans. Meanwhile, General Catalyst is building a data center to supply compute for its startups, said two other people. And several other VC funds have used brokers to find sought-after chips for their companies. “More and more we are working with venture capital firms who are looking to deploy” compute across their portfolios of startups, said Jeff Jewett, chief operating officer at Shadeform, which rents server capacity from various cloud providers and provides it to customers including AI startups. “It’s absolutely going to be a requirement to be able to attract the hottest startups in the world,” he said. The efforts reflect a shortage of the chips designed to handle the complex workloads of training and running AI. These constraints earlier this year led Microsoft and other large cloud providers to divert graphics processing units to their internal teams or bigger customers, making it harder for smaller startups to find a supply. Even for mature startups, compute can be a significant portion of their operating costs. That’s led more venture firms, which typically stick to supplying cash and more ephemeral assets—such as connections to skilled executives and advice on hiring—to wade into hardware. Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman in 2023 were among the first investors to organize a compute cluster, buying advanced Nvidia chips they pooled together and made available to portfolio companies at a discounted price . Their Andromeda Cluster has now pivoted to matching buyers with sellers of compute. Switch, Volta Talks Andreessen Horowitz last year expanded its cluster, initially called Oxygen, into multiple private clusters , including groups of chips rented from different cloud providers. In recent months, the VC firm has discussed partnering with companies, such as Switch, a data center developer and operator, and Volta, a platform that helps build, finance and operate data centers , to expand the cluster, according to people familiar with the talks. Andreessen Horowitz has ties to both. It co-led a $300 million funding round in Volta in August at a $2.4 billion valuation, and it reportedly was in talks to lead a $2 billion round in Switch in July. The investments are part of the firm’s bigger swing at hardware and the infrastructure companies that underpin the AI boom, spearheaded by general partner Martin Casado . It’s unclear how big Andreessen Horowitz’s chip expansion will be. If portfolio companies don’t end up using 100% of the capacity, the firm could resell the capacity to others who want the compute. An Andreessen Horowitz spokesperson said the firm helps founders “navigate finding compute, negotiating contracts and obtaining desirable or special pricing.” General Catalyst, a sprawling investment firm that previously bought a hospital system, is now also delving into chips. In May, the VC firm hired Alexis Black Björlin, who formerly helped run Nvidia’s cloud computing division, as its chief strategy officer. She is focused on infrastructure projects at the firm, or what she has termed “the efficiency frontier of large-scale AI systems” for the firm’s portfolio companies. Earlier this year, General Catalyst CEO Hemant Taneja sent a survey to founders inquiring about their ability to access compute. At the time, the firm was considering ways to help its portfolio companies with supply, potentially by facilitating a shared pool of capacity or negotiating on a startup’s behalf, The Information reported in April. Lately, the VC firm has been working on securing a data center to supply this compute, according to someone with knowledge of the project. It will serve companies from early to growth stage across its portfolio, another person said, suggesting that the cluster could be sizable enough to meet the needs of mature companies that process more tokens than younger startups. These add to other initiatives such as Coatue Management’s launch last year of a data center development company, Next Frontier, which has at least two joint ventures currently underway with neocloud Fluidstack. That effort is in part designed to secure access to scarce compute for its investments, according to someone who spoke with a senior member of the firm. It’s not clear how the biggest VC firms will finance more aggressive forays into chips and data center development, and they certainly could find ways to generate profits from the endeavors. Many of the larger funds have side vehicles they can use to finance such a project, or they could guarantee a loan or sign a lease commitment that would allow a partner to raise the money. Venture Payback Early-stage investor Crucible Capital began building its own cluster last year mostly as an experiment. Now it sells some of the capacity from the 576-chip cluster of Nvidia B300s to a frontier lab, while its portfolio companies use it to test products or run pilot projects, according to a person with knowledge of the firm’s activities. “Our impression is [that] every major fund is attempting to do this,” said Evan Conrad, founder of San Francisco Compute, a three-year-old startup that builds clusters of AI chips and operates a compute marketplace where companies can quickly rent GPUs without requiring long-term contracts. “They’re trying to own the clusters to secure access for their portfolio.” Conrad is currently working with a few VC firms to set up clusters they will control and parcel out to portfolio companies when the startups need the compute. Before that happens, SF Compute plans to sell the VCs’ excess access to other buyers, he said. Sriram Krishnan, a co-founder and general partner at early-stage VC firm Kearny Jackson, in early October posted on X that he had access to “hundreds of AMD mi350s”—AMD’s high-end server chips, which can train and run AI—for lease or purchase, in a cluster he recently set up with a supplier of AI servers. Krishnan said he immediately received an onslaught of outreach from founders hungry for compute: “It was a bit of a hurricane,” he said in an interview. Some founders who messaged him likened having access to GPUs to “having oil during an oil shortage,” Krishnan said. Krishnan will dole out the GPUs in Kearny Jackson’s cluster to portfolio companies and doesn’t plan to turn a profit on the effort. Though he surmises that the prospect of quick access to compute will attract new founders to the firm. “If there’s a mutual fit and an opportunity to invest, then great,” he said.

title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
content:
The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
Plus: A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology.
Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems.
—Grace Huckins
This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power
Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places.
Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out.
—Eshan Raul
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from sustainable cement to shipping containers packed with old EV batteries.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets
Temperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. (BBC)
+ The attack has sparked alarm about cyber threats to food security. (FT $)
+ It joins a recent wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes. (CNBC)
+ AI is exacerbating the threats. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Meta has launched a bunch of new AI models
It hopes the models, built for complex, multi-step tasks, will rival OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s.(BI)
+ They scored well on tests of reasoning, writing, and coding. (NYT $)
+ Mark Zuckerberg says they bring Meta to the “frontier” of AI. (FT $)
+ And will soon power the Muse agent. (Verge)
3 Anthropic warns that AI models may soon self-replicate across devices
Without even requiring access to data centers. (Reuters $)
+ It says models could spread through smart TVs and appliances. (CNBC)
+ We’re putting too much faith in AI saying no. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Police have a new AI tool that finds homes from interior photos
It can match single pictures to Airbnb and Zillow listings. (404 Media)
+ Police-tech giant Flock is tightening its rules. (MIT Technology Review)
5 The world’s first utility-scale enhanced geothermal plant is online
Fervo Energy’s Utah facility will supply carbon-free electricity. (IEEE)
+ AI is uncovering hidden geothermal resources. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Did drone strikes on Yandex data centres blitz Russian bots?
Zelenskyy claims the attacks quietened Kremlin-funded social media accounts. (Euronews)
+ But troll farm experts aren’t convinced. (Verge)
7 NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a Mars driving record
It’s covered 28 miles since landing in 2021. (Reuters $)
+ The rover passed Opportunity after detouring to study ancient rocks. (NYT $)
8 Elon Musk has become the 2026 midterms’ biggest known donor
He gave $158 million to a Republican Senate super PAC. (AP News)
9 Anduril and Palantir founders have backed execution livestreams
Palmer Luckey and Joe Lonsdale support Pete Hegseth’s plan. (Mother Jones)
10 A spacecraft has traced how a mysterious solar switchback formed
The Solar Orbiter’s discovery could improve space weather forecasts. (Gizmodo)
Quote of the day
“Many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.”
—Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar tells CBS News that Silicon Valley’s “social delusion” has convinced researchers to smoke because they expect AI to cure cancer.
One more thing
A brain implant changed her life. Then it was removed against her will.
Sticking an electrode inside a person’s brain can do more than treat a disease. Take the case of Rita Leggett, an Australian woman whose experimental brain implant changed her sense of agency and self. She told researchers that she “became one” with her device.
She was devastated when, two years later, she was told she had to remove the implant because the company that made it had gone bust.
Her case highlights the need for a new category of legal protection: neuro rights. Explore how they could be protected.
—Jessica Hamzelou
We can still have nice things

+ Watch centuries-old Chinese paper-cutting techniques create a spectacular work of art.

title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
content:
MIT Technology Review
Explains:
Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next.
You can read more from the series here
Late last month, Anthropic released a
arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.
These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.
“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.
Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the
Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard
are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a
recent report from Mozilla
. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.
But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”
Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.
Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations.
Mark Zuckerberg himself has said
that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.
“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?
The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a
recent risk report from Anthropic
, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.
There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.
Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.
But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).
In fact, some experts who spoke with
MIT Technology Review
argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.
Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.
Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.
Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.
The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?
A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.
Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a
recent preprint
But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.
Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.
Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.
