title: BMW launches sixth-gen battery production in Shenyang - electrive.com
content:
The BMW Group has begun series production of its Gen6 high-voltage batteries for the Neue Klasse in Shenyang. Following Debrecen and Irlbach-Straßkirchen, the site in northeastern China is the third plant in the company's new battery network. In future, the energy storage systems produced there will power the Neue Klasse models that BMW will manufacture in China for the local market.
Image: BMW
Nowhere is the price competition for EVs as fierce as in China – and it’s well-known that batteries are the most expensive component of an electric car. Manufacturing it close to the vehicle plant thus saves transport routes and inventory costs. This is exactly what BMW is now doing in Shenyang: “The high-voltage battery is a key component of our all-electric vehicles and one of the BMW Group’s most important technologies for the future,” said Production Board Member Dr. Raymond Wittmann. He added: “Production in Shenyang exemplifies our global approach: We manufacture locally, efficiently and close to our markets, in line with uniform global standards and the highest quality.”
Large round cells replace modules
The sixth generation relies on large round cells with a diameter of 4.6 cm, which BMW uses in two heights: 9.5 and 12 cm. Compared to the previous cell generation, energy density increases by more than 20 per cent while charging speed and range even see improvements of up to 30 per cent.
The battery also utilises a novel design. Previously, the cells were housed in modules, which were then installed in the battery housing in a second step. With the cell-to-pack principle, this intermediate level is eliminated, and the cells are placed directly in the housing. This saves material and weight, and the freed-up space can be filled with additional cells. On top of the battery is the Energy Master, a control unit developed by BMW itself. It combines functions of the power supply and battery management. The latter monitors, among other things, the state of charge and the temperature of the cells.
Battery production methods in Shenyang
In Shenyang, the cells are first inspected and then connected to coolers to form clusters. After laser cleaning, the clusters are welded to the cell contact system, which electrically connects the cells. A foaming process mechanically secures the components. The housing is then closed, sealed, and riveted. Finally, the Energy Master is installed, followed by an end-of-line inspection of each individual battery. Quality control for round cells is particularly complex because a pack consists of a very large number of individual cells, and every weld must hold. BMW therefore monitors the laser weld seams with inspection systems directly on the line in real time and also uses digital twins and AI-supported testing methods.
BMW Group’s largest production site
The conversion of the Shenyang site for the Neue Klasse was formalised in a letter of intent between BMW and Liaoning Province in
April 2024
. This involved an equivalent of ~€2.5 billion euros. With an annual capacity of 830,000 vehicles as of 2024, Shenyang is the largest production site in the group. It is spread across the Dadong, Lydia, and Tiexi plants. The site is operated by the joint venture BMW Brilliance Automotive. Just before Christmas 2025, the pre-series of the first Neue Klasse model for the Chinese market, the long-wheelbase iX3, began production there. One of BMW’s Chinese partners is the battery manufacturer
BMW’s production network is also expanding outside China. In the coming months, battery assembly in Woodruff, South Carolina, USA, and in San Luis Potosí, Mexico, is set to begin series production.
The start of battery production in China comes just in time for the long-wheelbase iX3. BMW launched the model for pre-sale at the Chengdu Auto Show in August. Prices range from 269,900 yuan (~€36,100 euros) for the iX3 30L to 339,900 yuan (~€45,400 euros) for the 50L xDrive. According to
CnEVPost
, the first deliveries are planned for November. However,
CarNewsChina
states that larger volumes will not reach customers until 2027, citing the business portal
. BMW sources attribute the long wait to the quality testing of new technologies.

Named for Bob Galyen—a visionary leader, distinguished engineer, and globally recognized thought leader in battery energy storage—this award will honor an individual whose decades-long career has left a lasting mark on the industry through technical excellence, manufacturing leadership, standards development, mentorship, and global vision. Unlike the other categories, this award will not be presented annually by default; it is reserved for truly exceptional individuals whose lifetime contributions merit the battery industry's highest honor.

title: Battery Show Panel Tackles Scaling Energy Storage
content:
Battery Manufacturing
Industry Outlook
Market Analysis
Industry Trends
Peak Energy and B2U Storage Solutions leaders explain how sodium-ion and second-life batteries could help scale energy storage for rising power demand.
October 14, 2026
2 Min Read
Dr. Brandon Kelly, Chief Scientist at Peak Energy and Freeman Hall, CEO and Founder at B2U Storage Solutions, Inc.
Maria Guerra
At The Battery Show North America, the panel titled “Energy Storage at an Inflection Point: Scaling for the Next Era of Power Demand” explored how to move battery storage from strong market interest to real operating scale. The discussion focused on the practical barriers that still slow deployment even as power demand rises from AI data centers, grid modernization, and broader electrification.
made one point especially clear: choosing a battery chemistry is only the beginning. Storage projects still have to be financed, permitted, installed, operated safely, and proven over time. Dr. Brandon Kelly, Chief Scientist at
Peak Energy
, focused on the growing case for sodium-ion batteries in grid-scale applications, while Freeman Hall, CEO and Founder at
B2U Storage Solutions, Inc.
brought the perspective of
second-life battery systems
built from retired EV packs. Together, they outlined two distinct but complementary paths for expanding storage capacity: deploying new chemistries designed for stationary use and extracting more value from batteries that still have useful life after automotive service.
Related:
Inside the 2026 Battery Awards, Where Innovation Took Center Stage
Kelly argued that sodium-ion is much closer to commercial credibility than many buyers assume. He described the chemistry as a strong fit for grid storage, especially because it aligns well with manufacturing approaches already familiar from lithium iron phosphate. Kelly also pointed to China’s role in accelerating development and deployment, noting that sodium-ion already has a growing operational base there. Still, he was clear that industry acceptance will not come from theory alone. As he put it, “What’s really going to drive adoption is just proven deployments, right?” No matter how promising a battery may look on paper, customers want field evidence before they commit.
Hall approached the scaling challenge from a different angle, focusing on batteries that have already completed their first life in electric vehicles (EVs). His company’s thesis is that these batteries often still have substantial value in less demanding grid applications and should not be sent straight to recycling if they can safely deliver additional cycles. Hall described how B2U has spent years building operational proof, not just technical theory, around repurposed battery systems. That work matters because second-life storage has to satisfy the same core requirements as any other infrastructure asset: safety, compliance, bankability, and dependable performance.
In response to questions about market constraints, Hall explained that the challenge has shifted over time. In B2U’s early years, supply of suitable batteries was limited. Today, that is no longer the main obstacle. Instead, the bottleneck is execution. As Hall said, “The constraint isn’t supply anymore. It’s really the ability to get permitted, get financed, and to deploy repurposed projects.”
Related:
Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks, Opportunities, and Innovation
Taken together, the panel offered a grounded view of where storage is heading next. The future will not be won by chemistry alone. Whether through sodium-ion innovation or second-life repurposing, companies that can prove reliability, simplify operations, secure permits, attract financing, and build trust at scale will succeed.
About the Author
Maria Guerra
Senior Editor-Battery Technology, Informa Markets
Maria L. Guerra is a Senior Editor at
Battery Technology
, blending her engineering background with a passion for technology journalism. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Universidad Metropolitana in Caracas, Venezuela, and a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering.
Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. (KBR) in the UK, conducting power system studies and providing technical support for offshore and onshore projects. During her internship at Pequiven S.A. in Venezuela, she trained neural networks using MATLAB (Kohonen Map) to estimate electrical circuit variables for oil wells (e.g., voltage, current, and power).
In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at
Electronic Design
, covering advancements in the semiconductor market, focusing on power/analog electronics systems.
Battery Technology
, Guerra now delivers in-depth coverage of battery manufacturing, EV advancements, energy storage systems, and the evolving landscape of critical minerals and second-life batteries. She is passionate about uncovering the stories that shape the future of electrification, from cutting-edge battery innovations to policy shifts driving sustainable energy.
Guerra is also a member of
The Battery Show North America Advisory Board
, where she contributes her expertise to advising on industry trends and speaker selection for The Battery Show North America, while helping to shape discussions on battery technology and electrification. She was part of the award-winning Battery Technology team recognized with a
Neal Award for Best Coverage of the 2024 Election
Neal Award for Best Explanatory Content
in 2026 for her coverage of battery breakthroughs.
Maria Guerra is based in Brooklyn, NY, and can be reached at

title: GXO Explores Cost Versus Climate on Logistics Transition
content:
GXO Explores Cost Versus Climate on Logistics Transition
Prioritise Us
on Google
GXO has found that cost pressures have overtaken climate ambitions in UK fleet transition. Credit: GXO
Businesses are influenced more by cost pressures than climate ambitions when it comes to fleet transformation, GXO’s Carl Hanson explains
Around the world, businesses are facing increasing pressures to adopt more sustainable operations.
climate pressures increase
, businesses have a growing understanding of their climate impact, but this is no longer the sole driver of transformation.
GXO has released its latest
Future of Transport
research, which reveals that rising costs and the need to save money are a growing factor.
A period of change
The logistics industry is a crucial one, helping businesses grow to scale and connecting organisations around the world. It is responsible for the timely and reliable movement of goods, but its impact is not always a positive one.
supply chain networks grow
, as do the miles travelled. Due to this, freight transportation and logistics account for approximately 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. They are a significant contributor to an organisation’s value chain emissions, which are increasingly falling under scrutiny.
With major climate events becoming a constant disruptor to global supply chain operations, businesses are analysing their supply chain emissions more often. As a result,
the logistics industry
is undergoing a transformation, with a growing demand for alternative fuels and electrification.
GXO’s latest report, however, suggests that the transformation is no longer purely driven by net zero commitments. Instead, rising operating costs are the primary driver of fleet fuel transitions for UK businesses.
The report took insights from more than 1,000 UK supply chain, transport and logistics decision makers. GXO found that 63% of those surveyed said that rising fuel costs are behind the increase in alternative fuel vehicles.
Though emissions reduction is a key priority for many businesses (87%), only 38% are currently operating alternative fuel vehicles. This is partially because businesses desire clear evidence of a commercial return – 76% of businesses say they require clear demonstrations of cost savings or operational efficiencies before they invest in low-transmission transport.
“High upfront costs and the price of infrastructure remain the biggest barriers to adopting alternative fuel vehicles,” Carl Hanson, Transport Managing Director, at GXO UK & Ireland explains to Supply Chain Digital.
Carl Hanson Transport Managing Director, at GXO UK & Ireland. Credit: GXO
Key findings
1,000 UK supply chain, transport and logistics decision makers were surveyed
63% of decision makers say rising fuel costs are speeding up their transition to alternative fuel vehicles
39% of operators are optimising routes in order to increase efficiency
Seven in ten logistic leaders anticipate gas-powered fleets to be a viable option by 2028
Only 25%of businesses have already invested in planning for refuelling or charging infrastructure
Identifying solutions
Operators are increasingly focused on
improving efficiency and cost savings
, which is causing delays in investments and implementation. Due to this, leaders are not only focusing on alternative fuel solutions, but are also changing how they operate their business.
“Businesses are recognising that cutting emissions and costs go hand in hand,” Carl adds. “The most immediate and commercially viable first steps are often the simplest: route optimisation, sharing fleets and improving load fill can reduce their fuel use today.”
GXO’s research demonstrates that the most benefit will come from starting the transformation journey now. As a leading pure-play contract logistics provider,
GXO helps its customers
to identify how they can start their own transformation.
It uses network analysis, phased implementation plans and funding options in order to lead its customers through a practical pathway towards net zero. By starting now, businesses can better manage costs, reduce operational risk and control the pace, rather than speeding to keep up with competitors.
Carl says: “Partnering with a third-party logistics provider like GXO provides businesses with the expertise and scale they need to build a
practical decarbonisation roadmap
, tailored to their specific operational needs as infrastructure continues to develop. Those that get ahead of this will be the ones creating a competitive advantage in the future.”
GXO offers a range of solutions to help streamline operations. Credit: GXO
Future expectations
There are various solutions to moving away from diesel, each with their own benefits. The survey reveals that leaders believe the transition will take place due to a number of technologies and solutions.
“Before committing to a fuel, it’s crucial that businesses fully evaluate their existing operations to understand how their operations perform today and what they want to achieve in future,” Carl explains.
“It’s that insight, not the fuel itself, that should drive the decision – because no single solution fits every operation. The future fleet will be a mix.”
Despite the clear expectations and commitments, the transition is not a simple one. As few as 25% of businesses have begun their investment planning into charging and refuelling infrastructure, while only 30% have started their energy supply procurement planning.
Businesses are anticipating a rise in costs when running transport operations, but GXO has a range of solutions to help drive the net zero transition, including the deployment of electric HGV technology and its EyeQ digital transport platform.
As businesses look to operate more sustainably, they can act strategically to ensure cost savings and efficiency increases alongside the transition.
High upfront costs and the price of infrastructure remain the biggest barriers to adopting alternative fuel vehicles.
Carl Hanson Transport Managing Director, at GXO UK & Ireland
Key companies
CEO: Malcolm Wilson
HQ: Greenwich, Connecticut, USA
GXO is the world's largest pure-play contract logistics provider, operating in 27 countries across six continents. With cutting-edge technology and a commitment to sustainability, GXO delivers customized supply chain solutions including warehousing, distribution, and transport management. The company serves diverse industries through its 970+ locations and workforce of approximately 130,000 team members.

Toby Hay, Managing Director of International Marketing at FedEx Europe, explains how a new portal simplifies temperature-controlled pharmaceutical shipment
FedEx Europe has launched a new data platform to enable pharmaceutical and life sciences companies to book and manage temperature-controlled shipments. The new portal has been launched for
pharmaceutical
manufacturers, biotech companies and clinical trial operators to plan ahead of the increased demands of the year-end
The tool, which covers intra-European and domestic shipments in 26 EU and non-EU European markets, provides access to FedEx’s Temp-Assure Advantage solution.
“Digital tools play an increasingly important role in helping pharmaceutical companies manage complexity. As healthcare supply chains become more interconnected and time-sensitive, customers need easy access to booking, shipment information and operational insights that enable faster decision-making," says Toby Hay, Managing Director International Marketing at FedEx Europe.
The solution leverages FedEx’s specialised healthcare network, which includes more than 130 cold chain facilities, six Life Sciences Centres, dedicated healthcare teams and advanced monitoring capabilities, Toby adds.
FedEx’s specialised healthcare network includes more than 130 cold chain facilities and six Life Sciences Centres. Credit: FedEx
The platform simplifies what has traditionally been a complex and manual process, allowing customers to onboard, order pre-conditioned packaging, schedule shipments and manage returns via the platform.
The platform also provides greater visibility and control for suppliers and manufacturers in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector.
“Solutions such as FedEx Surround provide near real-time visibility and predictive analytics, while our temperature-controlled infrastructure helps safeguard the integrity of critical healthcare shipments throughout their journey.”
“Peak season consistently drives a substantial surge in activity across Europe. Last year, we handled more than 20% higher Peak volumes than the year before, reaching up to 2 million packages on the busiest days,” adds Toby.
Key facts about FedEx Temp-Assure Advantage
Advanced vacuum-insulated packaging and phase-change materials help maintain required temperatures for more than 96 hours
CEIV Pharma-certified facilities and standardised processes provide enhanced control, visibility and compliance throughout transit
Reusable packaging model: containers can be collected, refurbished and redeployed to help reduce waste while maintaining high-performance standards

Frozen: approximately −25°C to −15°C
Refrigerated: 2°C to 8°C

title: PepsiCo: Fragmented Supply Chains & Regenerative Farming
content:
PepsiCo: Fragmented Supply Chains & Regenerative Farming
Prioritise Us
on Google
PepsiCo is aiming to expand its regenerative agriculture program. Credit: PepsiCo
Jim Andrews, CSO at PepsiCo explores how supply chain fragmentation limits the adoption of regenerative agriculture in a new white paper
A September 2026 white paper from PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center examines how supply chain fragmentation limits the spread of regenerative agriculture across US farming systems. The report argues that farm economics, measurement inconsistencies and policy gaps prevent established practices from becoming standard across procurement networks.
The document draws on a 2025 roundtable with consumer goods companies, retailers and farmer-facing organisations to identify where transition risks disrupt supply chain stability. It concludes that sustained public investment, paired with private commitments, could reduce procurement volatility while expanding
regenerative practices across agricultural footprints
Supply chain risks slow adoption
According to PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center, US farmers face high input costs, volatile commodity prices and limited credit access that make transitions difficult to absorb. Cover cropping, reduced tillage and improved nutrient management can lower some costs over time, but initial investments in labour, equipment and capital create exposure for farms operating on narrow margins.
The whitepaper frames this as a supply chain issue rather than a farm-level problem alone. When growers lack the financial capacity to change practices, procurement systems lose resilience and buyers face increased exposure to environmental and price shocks.
The report argues that regenerative agriculture must become a reliable production model to support supply chain continuity. Premium markets and temporary incentives do not provide the stability required for long-term sourcing strategies.
"Regenerative agriculture means you're using the natural ecosystem to make the land better," says Margaret Henry, Vice President of Sustainable and Regenerative Agriculture at PepsiCo.
Margaret Henry, Vice President of Sustainable and Regenerative Agriculture at PepsiCo
"At its heart, it's about helping farmers thrive so they can keep on farming."
Fragmented reporting increases costs
PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center identify measurement and verification systems as a barrier to supply chain coordination. Different programmes require overlapping datasets, separate contracts and inconsistent definitions of regenerative agriculture, raising administrative costs for growers and complicating procurement for buyers.
The report calls for interoperability between measurement frameworks so that data collected on farms can satisfy multiple buyers and public programmes. Without this, supply chain participants face redundant compliance burdens that increase costs and slow adoption.
The document also identifies an opportunity to modernise crop insurance, lending terms and land valuation so they recognise the resilience benefits of improved soil health. When financial systems penalise practices that reduce long-term risk, supply chains remain vulnerable to disruption.
Jim Andrew, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo, explains that the whitepaper followed discussions with organisations across the agricultural value chain.
Jim Andrew, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo at Sustainability LIVE: The Leadership Summit at London Climate Action Week
"The report makes a compelling case that the path to scale runs through better risk management, simpler reporting requirements, stronger farmer support networks and investment models that help reduce barriers to adoption," he explains on LinkedIn.
De-risking transitions for procurement stability
According to Jim, one example in the paper is the Nitrogen Yield Warranty programme with Practical Farmers of Iowa, which has reduced nearly one million pounds of nitrogen while helping de-risk the transition for participating farmers. "It's a reminder that when initiatives are aligned and risks are reduced, meaningful progress can follow," he says.
The warranty model could show how shared risk structures support supply chain stability by removing the financial exposure farmers face when changing practices. This approach could help buyers secure regenerative sources without requiring growers to absorb transition costs alone.
According to Jim, scaling regenerative agriculture does not just depend on farmers being willing to change, but whether they have the economic capacity. The practice may exist, but expanding it to meet procurement demand may not be economically viable without coordinated support.
PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center stress that sharing transition risks across farmers, businesses, financial institutions and government could reduce supply chain disruption while
expanding regenerative sourcing options
PepsiCo and Grimme have teamed up to create digital twin technology for more efficient potato harvests. Credit: PepsiCo
Coordinating investment across buyers
According to PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center, coordinated public and private investment offers one of the most direct routes to
expanding regenerative agriculture
beyond individual pilots. Public funding can attract additional corporate capital, expand farmer participation and help established programmes reach more agricultural land than individual buyers could support alone.
The report advocates co-funding models that allow multiple organisations to support the same farming practices. This gives farmers more stable financial backing and reduces reliance on a single corporate partner, lowering supply chain concentration risk for buyers.
Alongside funding, businesses can invest in technical assistance through agronomists,
farmer-facing organisations and peer networks
. These resources translate sustainability commitments into practical guidance that supports both farm profitability and supply chain resilience.
PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center stress that collaboration should extend beyond food manufacturers to retailers, agricultural input providers, grain handlers and financial institutions. Aligning demand signals across the supply chain could establish regenerative agriculture as a shared commercial priority while supporting rural economies.
PepsiCo numbers
PepsiCo expanded regenerative agriculture to 3.5m acres by 2024 and is targeting seven million acres by 2030, roughly its entire agricultural footprint.
Its climate roadmap now pushes net zero emissions to 2050, with a 50% cut in Scope one and two emissions and a 30% cut in Scope three FLAG emissions by 2030 against a 2022 baseline.
On water stewardship, PepsiCo met its operational water-use efficiency goal in high-risk areas and replenished nearly 29bn litres back into nature in 2025. The company aims to be net water-positive by 2030.
According to PepsiCo, 89% of its packaging is designed to be recyclable, compostable, biodegradable or reusable.
Single-use plastic is being cut through alternatives such as paper multipack rings and reusable models like SodaStream.
Building local support networks
PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center argue that lasting progress depends on embedding regenerative agriculture within farming communities rather than relying solely on financial incentives or corporate targets. Peer-to-peer learning, trusted local advisers and on-farm trials help farmers assess the agronomic and financial implications of new practices under their own conditions.
The report calls for policy reforms that remove disincentives, including land valuation systems that can penalise practices such as establishing wetlands or maintaining cover crops. These structural barriers increase supply chain risk by discouraging practices that
improve long-term resilience
Longer-term public funding, clearer measurement approaches and sustained support for local technical assistance are identified as priorities for the next stage of development. Without these, supply chains remain exposed to fragmented adoption patterns that limit scalability.
PepsiCo and Keystone Policy Center further emphasise the importance of including farmers and farmer-facing organisations in ongoing discussions. This ensures programmes respond to practical needs and changing agricultural conditions, reducing the likelihood of misalignment between procurement goals and farm-level capacity.
Ultimately, the report calls for continued public investment alongside
private-sector funding and collaboration
to make regenerative agriculture a profitable, resilient and widely adopted model of production. This approach could reduce supply chain volatility while supporting environmental outcomes and farm profitability across procurement networks.
It's a reminder that when initiatives are aligned and risks are reduced, meaningful progress can follow.
Jim Andrew, SCO of PepsiCo
PepsiCo partnerships
The Carlsberg Group
is expanding its PepsiCo bottling partnership into Georgia and Armenia through the acquisition of Iberia Refreshments and JI Pepsi Cola Bottler Armenia. This joins Azerbaijan to create a South Caucasus cluster and brings the total to 17 markets.
Wembley Stadium connected by EE
has signed a multi-year partnership with PepsiCo to become the stadium's Official Carbonated Soft Drinks and Crisps Partner until 2030. The agreement will supply brands like Walkers, Doritos, Cheetos and Pepsi MAX with a focus on zero-sugar options.
PepsiCo and Silverstone
have agreed a five-year partnership making PepsiCo the Official Soft Drinks and Official Snacks Partner of the Home of British Motorsport. The deal will deliver immersive food and drink experiences to more than two million annual visitors.
PepsiCo and agricultural machinery manufacturer
have developed VR-based digital twin training for potato harvester operators. The system delivered an 87% increase in bruise-free potatoes and a 1.7 times reduction in severe bruising in pilots, aligning with the broader pep+ agenda and reducing waste across the potato supply chain.

title: CEVA Names Leaders for Freight and Contract Logistics Arms
content:
CEVA Names Leaders for Freight and Contract Logistics Arms
Prioritise Us
on Google
CEVA Logistics announced that it was restructuring its operations into two business units, Freight Management and Contract Logistics, in early October 2026.
CEVA Logistics CEO Patrick Moebel has reorganised the company around Freight Management and Contract Logistics and appointed new regional leaders
CEVA Logistics is restructuring its global operations, simplifying the company’s structure by establishing two business units, Freight Management and Contract Logistics.
The organisational restructure is intended to simplify decision-making, strengthen regional accountability and to bring the company’s operational leadership closer to customers. The changes lay the groundwork for the company’s next phase of growth under CEO Patrick Moebel.
Patrick said: “CEVA has extraordinary people, strong capabilities and an unmatched global network. Our focus is straightforward: empower our people, execute for our customers and deliver sustainable performance. Everything we are doing is designed to help our teams better serve customers around the world.”
The announcement was accompanied by the unveiling of the leaders of the new business units. The former president of Fedex Supply Chain, Scott Temple, has been appointed as the leader for CEVA's Americas regional unit.
Patrick Moebel, CEO of CEVA Logistics (right)
Henri Le Gouis to Lead Freight Management
Henri Le Gouis has been appointed as Senior Vice President for Freight Management, while Chris Walton will lead the Contract Logistics business unit.
Henri Le Gouis has extensive experience in aviation and maritime logistics, and joined CEVA in September 2026. Henri joined from Geodis, where he served as EVP of Global Freight Forwarding at Geodis. Before joining Geodis in November 2024, Henri was employed as CEO Europe at Bolloré Logistics between 2015 and 2024. Henri was previously CEO Western Europe at Bolloré Logistics between 2011 and the end of 2014.
Chris Walton has served in contract-logistics leadership roles at CEVA with increasing responsibility since 2015, with the exception of a three-year spell as Managing Director of UK, Ireland and the Nordics between 2020 and 2023. His most recent position was as Global Head of Contract Logistics at CEVA.

title: BYD's electric luxury GT will get a major update for Europe in 2027
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 15 2026 - 8:58 am PT
used the Denza Z9 GT to showcase its latest breakthrough technology, including its 5-minute Flash Charging. Next year, the luxury GT will get another major update in Europe.
BYD confirms God’s Eye update for Denza in 2027
unveiling the new Z9 GT
in China earlier this year, BYD’s luxury sub-brand Denza claimed it was the “world’s longest pure electric driving range electric vehicle,” offering a CLTC range of up to 1,036 km (643 miles).
launched the electric GT
in Europe in July, its first vehicle in Europe to use its tri-motor e3 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging Technology.
The Denza Z9 GT kicked off “Europe’s Flash Charging revolution,” the company said, enabling drivers to charge up just as quickly as filling a gas tank.
Next year, BYD announced that Denza vehicles in Europe will receive an upgrade to its “God’s Eye” intelligent driving assistance system, adding “a new level” of urban driving ability.
Starting with the Z9 GT in 2027, Denza vehicles will receive City Navigation on Driving Assistant (CNOA) through an over-the-air (OTA) software update.
Denza Z9 GT interior (Source: Denza)
While average ADAS systems can handle straight-line driving on open roads, BYD said CNOA can manage point-to-point navigation in dense city driving.
The update will use the vehicle’s existing hardware, including a LiDAR, 12 ultrasonic radar sensors, three millimeter-wave radar sensors, and 11 cameras.
Once installed, the vehicle can automatically stop at red lights, yield at roundabouts, drive at the posted speed limit, make left turns, and change lanes around double-parked vehicles. It can also detect pedestrians, cyclists, and other objects in narrow city streets.
BYD Denza Z9 GT (Source: Denza)
Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said that “We’re excited to fulfill our promise to bring the benefits of God’s Eye, including City Navigation on Driving Assistant, to the Z9GT.”
The hardware is already pre-installed, and the software is expected to be available in 2027 via an OTA update.
In Europe and the UK, the Denza Z9 GT is available in purely electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.
BYD Denza Z9 GT (Source: Denza)
The all-electric version uses a 122.49 kWh battery pack and three electric motors, delivering a combined 1,140 hp (850 kW) and 892 lb-ft (1,210 Nm) of torque. Under WLTP conditions, the Denza Z9 GT offers up to 599 km (372 miles) of range.
With up to 1,500 kW of charging power, BYD’s Flash Charging stations offer what it calls “Ready in 5, Full in 9, Cold Add 3.”
In 5 minutes, the Denza Z9 GT can charge from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes just 9 minutes, and even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes only 3 minutes longer, replenishing the battery from 20% to 97% in 12 minutes.
The Denza GT is 5,195 mm long, 1,990 mm wide, and 1,480 mm tall, with a wheelbase of 3,125 mm, or about the size of the Porsche Panamera and Taycan.
In Europe, the
Denza Z9 GT EV
starts at €115,000 ($130,000), including VAT. In the UK, it’s priced from £105,000 ($139,000) for the EV variant. The plug-in hybrid (DM) starts at £95,000 ($126,000).

title: BMW's new i3 just drove 753 miles on a single charge
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 15 2026 - 7:21 am PT
BMW put the
to the test to showcase the power of its Gen6 batteries. The long-wheelbase i3 covered 753 miles (1,213 km) without stopping, the longest covered by any BMW EV to date.
BMW i3 50L delivers 1,213 km of range on a single charge
BMW Group
began series production
of its sixth-generation (Gen6) EV batteries in Shenyang on October 15, its third global production site for the new battery tech.
To prove the power of its latest battery tech, set to power its Neue Klasse lineup, BMW put the new i3 50L through an endurance test to see how far it can really drive.
BMW said the new cylindrical cells offer over 20% higher energy density, enabling 30% faster charging and longer driving range than the previous generation.
After unveiling the i3 50L, a long-wheelbase version developed specifically for China at the Chengdu Auto Show in August, BMW said it would deliver a CLTC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km), topping the iX3 50L with a CLTC range of 571 miles (919 km).
During the event, the i3 50L managed over 753 miles (1,213 km) on a single charge, a new record for a BMW electric vehicle, the company said. The electric sedan achieved an extremely efficient 8.8 kWh per 100 km, covering highways, city and rural streets.
While BMW said it was a brand record, not a global one, it was enough to top the Mercedes Vision EQXX, which traveled 1,202 km from Germany to the UK in 2022.
In June, BMW drove an iX3 50L prototype
over 500 miles
(800 km) around the Qinghai Lake grand loop. It achieved an energy consumption of 12.6 kWh per 100 km.
The BMW iX3 Long Wheelbase (left) and i3 Long Wheelbase (right) Source: BMW
The long-wheelbase i3 uses a 113.4 kWh battery that delivers a CLTC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km). Thanks to its 800V architecture, the i3 50L can add 248 miles (400 km) of range in 10 minutes with up to 400 kW fast charging.
BMW opened orders for the iX3 50L at the Chengdu Auto Show in August, starting at RMB 269,900 ($40,000). The i3 50L is expected to go on sale later this year, with customer deliveries set to begin in the first quarter of 2027.
In the US, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is now
available to order
, starting at $61,500. It has an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles.
The 2027 BMW i3 is
also on sale
starting at the same price of $61,500. The electric sedan delivers up to 468 miles of range.

title: Tesla confirms Autopilot/FSD was 'engaged' when car crossed a median and killed a man
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Tesla Full self-Driving
Fred Lambert
| Oct 15 2026 - 7:03 am PT
A Tesla crossed the grass median of Route 55 in New Jersey, hit a tree, slid into oncoming traffic, and struck an SUV head-on. The SUV’s driver, 68-year-old Phillip Eastman, was killed.
Police reported it as a driver who lost control. What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an
ongoing Electrek investigation
matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.
What happened on Route 55
Around 8:31 a.m. on Saturday, August 22, 2026, a Tesla was heading south on Route 55 in Vineland, in Cumberland County, near milepost 34.6. The driver lost control, ran off the left side of the road, crossed the grass median, struck a tree, and continued into the northbound lanes, where the car hit a northbound Chevrolet SUV, according to the New Jersey State Police.
The SUV’s driver,
Phillip “Phil” Eastman, 68, of Springfield, Pennsylvania
, was killed. The Tesla’s driver and a passenger in the Chevrolet were hurt and taken to a hospital with moderate injuries.
Eastman had just been sworn in as a Springfield School District board member, and he spent nearly three decades coaching youth and high school ice hockey, including 17 years as the varsity head coach at Springfield High. His death was widely covered in the Philadelphia area.
And in all of it, no report mentioned Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any driver-assist system. The crash was told as a driver who lost control of his car.
What Tesla told the federal government
Under a NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed. Tesla filed a report on this crash.
In it, Tesla identifies the car as a
2021 Model Y
and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as
“Verified Engaged”
— meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was active. It lists the New Jersey State Police as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from the media.
Then it redacts the fields that would explain what the car did: the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area. All blacked out as “confidential business information,” the
same redactions Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports
What the data doesn’t settle
We want to be precise about what this does and doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds of impact” is the reporting trigger, not proof the system was steering when the car crossed the median. The driver may have been overriding it. And Tesla redacted the software version, so there’s no telling whether this was basic Autopilot or FSD.
Two more gaps are worth flagging. Tesla logs a pre-crash speed of just 37 mph, low for a freeway, which is more likely a single telematics snapshot from the pre-crash window than the speed at which the car left the road. And on this report Tesla checks only that it holds the car’s telematics, not the event-data recorder or video, so there may be less onboard evidence here than in other cases.
What is not in doubt is the one fact the public never got: a driver-assist system was on in a car that crossed a highway median and killed a man. Everything that would explain how is sealed.
Why we keep doing this
This is the pattern the investigation keeps surfacing, and it’s why the redaction matters. Tesla is, more than ever, pushing owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it drives itself. It sells the software as “Full Self-Driving,” Elon Musk keeps promising unsupervised autonomy is close, and the branding invites drivers to trust the car.
But it is still Level 2. The human is driving and responsible at all times, and Tesla’s own actions confirm it: consumer FSD still requires supervision, and its robotaxi service is a small, closely watched fleet. At the moment Tesla is telling owners to trust the car, it hides the records that would show how the system behaves when things go wrong, and a man coaching kids’ hockey one season is a name in a sealed federal file the next.
How we matched it, and why it’s notable:
Electrek flagged this crash weeks ago, from the news, as a fatal Tesla wreck that had no corresponding entry in the federal data, and no public mention of driver-assist. The latest NHTSA release added it, flagged as a fatality with the system verified engaged. The record is unredacted on location (Vineland), state, vehicle (2021 Model Y), the fatality, and the month, and the incident time Tesla logged, 12:29 UTC, converts to about 8:29 a.m. local, within two minutes of the 8:31 a.m. police reported. It’s the same crash. Electrek has reached out to the New Jersey State Police for the crash report and the vehicle data, and asked whether investigators received Tesla’s raw telemetry or only Tesla’s own interpretation of it.
Electrek’s Take
Strip the redaction away and this is a Tesla, running its driver-assist software, that crossed a median and killed a school board member in the oncoming lane. Leave it in place, as Tesla did, and it’s a driver who “lost control.” Those are very different stories, and the public got the one that leaves Tesla out of it.
We’re careful here. The system being on doesn’t prove it caused the crash, the driver may have been overriding it, and we don’t even know if it was Autopilot or FSD. That is exactly the problem. Tesla knows all of it. It has the telematics, it filed the report confirming the system was engaged, and it decided that what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret, down to which software was running. Phillip Eastman’s family, and the troopers still investigating, deserve the full account, not a redacted one.
Tesla is already
under NHTSA investigation
over how it reports these crashes. We’ll keep matching them, one by one, until the record is whole.

title: How federal money is pushing cops towards e-bikes
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 15 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Police departments have been increasingly turning to electric bicycles as a new tool for patrols, and in at least some cases, federal money is helping put officers in the saddle.
The latest example comes from Clinton, where the local Police Department and County Sheriff’s Office recently received five all-terrain e-bikes for use in areas that officers previously had to patrol on foot.
The Recon Power Bikes include three units for the Police Department, including one designated for its mental health co-responder, along with two bikes for the Sheriff’s Office. The bikes and additional equipment were fully funded through the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant.
That program is one of the primary sources of federal criminal justice funding distributed to state and local governments, and in this case, some of that money is being used to give officers a new form of electric transportation.
The e-bikes have already been in service for a couple of weeks. With speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) and a claimed range of up to 50 miles (80 km), they can cover significantly more ground than officers on foot or pedal bikes while still accessing trails, parks, and other areas where patrol cars aren’t particularly useful.
E-bikes are proving popular with police departments, including these BULLS e-bikes serving the LAPD
It’s part of a broader trend we’ve been watching as
police departments increasingly adopt e-bikes
for everything from trail patrols to downtown policing and community engagement.
The appeal isn’t hard to understand. Compared to patrol cars and motorcycles, e-bikes are relatively inexpensive to purchase and operate. They don’t require gasoline, can squeeze through areas inaccessible to larger vehicles, and allow officers to cover considerably more ground than traditional bicycle or foot patrols.
They can also make police more approachable. An officer rolling slowly through a park or downtown area on a bicycle is much easier to interact with than one sitting behind the windows of a patrol car.
E-bikes obviously aren’t replacing police cruisers anytime soon, but they don’t need to. They’re increasingly filling the sizable gap between foot patrols and full-sized vehicles.
And with federal grant money potentially covering the entire cost, it’s not hard to see why more departments are giving electric two-wheelers a try.

title: Tesla loses Cybercab assembly lead to Rivian R2 weeks after launch
content:
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Oct 15 2026 - 5:43 am PT
Tesla’s Senior Manager of Cybercab General Assembly at Gigafactory Texas, Jody Kerns, is leaving the company to become Rivian’s Director of General Assembly for the R2 in Normal, Illinois.
He’s the second Cybercab launch leader to leave Tesla this year. The head of Cybercab new product introduction walked out in April, before the vehicle ever carried a paying passenger.
Kerns announced the move in a
LinkedIn post
this week, thanking his Tesla team for everything “from the WEOL project to the launch of the Cyber Cab.”
His profile shows he joined Tesla in January 2024 as an end-of-line manager and took over Cybercab general assembly in Austin in February 2026. That’s the same month Tesla
rolled the first steering-wheel-less Cybercab off the line
, so he ran final assembly through the entire ramp to commercial service.
At Rivian, he’ll do the same job on the R2. He described the goal as making the R2 “the best electric SUV in the market.”
Kerns isn’t a Silicon Valley hire. He spent 14 years at Volkswagen of America, ending as Director of Assembly from 2021 to 2024, where his profile says he managed about 1,200 people and integrated the ID.4 into a line already building two other models. That’s the Chattanooga plant. Before that, he spent four years in Toyota’s paint shops.
So Rivian is getting someone who has slotted a new EV into a running factory and launched a brand new vehicle from scratch. That’s exactly the R2 problem.
The second Cybercab leader out the door
Kerns’ departure follows Michael So, who was Tesla’s Head of Cybercab NPI from September 2024 to April 2026. So was Giga Texas employee #1 in 2021, helped launch the Model Y and Cybertruck there, and lists the Cybercab’s “unboxed” manufacturing process, brake-by-wire, and butterfly doors among the things he launched.
He left in May to become VP of Product Engineering at Aalo Atomics, a nuclear reactor startup also based in Austin. Under Kerns’ post, So wrote that he “wouldn’t want to launch Cybercab with anyone else.”
The timing isn’t great for Tesla. Commercial Cybercab rides started in Austin on September 3, and NHTSA
hit Tesla with a Special Order
a week later demanding proof, under oath, that a car with no steering wheel or brake pedal meets federal safety standards. NHTSA now estimates the 2026 Robotaxi fleet, Model Y and Cybercab combined, at about 1,000 vehicles.
Rivian, on the other hand, is in the middle of the ramp that decides its future. R2 deliveries started June 9 from Normal, and Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles in Q3 while keeping its 2026 delivery guidance at 65,000 to 70,000. Rivian has already
raised $1.5 billion
partly to de-risk that ramp.

title: Slate Auto opens first ever test drive and experience center in Chicago
content:
Auto dealers
Jo Borrás
| Oct 15 2026 - 4:48 am PT
Jeff Bezos-backed electric truck startup Slate Auto opened the doors to its first-ever brick-and-mortar “experience center” in Chicago’s Near West Side, offering midwest fleet buyers and automotive journalists (Hi!) their first real,
up-close look at what promises to be the most affordable new vehicle in America
It’s true even in the tight, urban jungle of Chicago: Illinois loves trucks. Increasingly,
Illinois seems to love EVs
, too – so it makes sense that a new electric truck startup like Slate would choose Chicago as the home of its first-ever Slate experience center.
Familiar territory
1053 W Grand AVE; image by the author.
The covers are off of the renovations at the old Tesla store on Grand, revealing that the new tenants are, in fact, Slate – and that makes total sense. Not only was the building already laid out for a small showroom, garage and retail space, it was also wired for NACS EV charging. Combine those logistical advantages with the location’s proven track record of getting the EV-curious behind the wheel, and the spot was a no-brainer.
Once potential customers get inside the Slate, they’ll be met with a solid, heavily-sprung door handle that feels expensive, and clicks, pulls, and snaps back with authority. The same is true of the chonky steering wheel, manual seat adjusters, tailgate latch, and charge port cover. The center console, too, despite looking like it was made of
JC Whitney
-spec shiny plastic, didn’t budge, and felt like it might be made of basalt, rather than plastic. Just about everything you touch, in other words, delivers reassuring haptics that shout, rather than whisper:
Slate may be inexpensive, but it’s not cheap
They got the important bits right
That idea carried on through my test ride (I wasn’t allowed to drive), which was quiet, smooth, free of squeaks and rattles on Chicago’s perpetually under construction roads, and felt more than quick enough from where I was sitting.
It was an impressive showing, and my conversation with some of Slate’s tech people about using the same fasteners throughout the vehicle whenever possible gave me a brief glimpse into what is sure to be an absolutely bananas, 3d-printed tuner culture around this thing … but that’s still speculative,
and Slate’s overall success is far from a sure thing
That said, Slate Auto is starting to feel really, really real – and if you’re in Chicago, you now have the chance to see just how real it is for yourself.

title: Xtracycle Swoop ASM review: The nicest cargo e-bike I've tested... so far!
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 15 2026 - 4:03 am PT
I’ve tested a lot of cargo e-bikes over the last decade-plus of reviewing electric bicycles. There are good cargo e-bikes. There are great cargo e-bikes. And then there’s Xtracycle.
More specifically, there’s the new
Xtracycle Swoop ASM,
which might just be a cut above every other cargo e-bike I’ve tested.
ASM stands for “Automatic Smile Machine,” and the name works on two levels. First, this thing is simply a blast to ride, whether you’re the one pedaling or one of the lucky passengers hanging out on the back. Second, it features Shimano’s automatic electronic shifting system, which appeals equally to the engineer and cyclist in me.
To see the bike in action and get my from the saddle thoughts, check out my review video below. Then keep watching for even more details about this impressive full-family cargo e-bike.
Before getting into why that automatic shifting is such a big deal, let’s run through the hardware.
The Swoop ASM is a Class 3 electric cargo bike capable of reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). It uses Shimano’s EP6 Cargo mid-drive motor paired with a 630Wh Shimano battery, with Xtracycle quoting up to 60 miles (96 km) of range. Both the motor and battery are UL-listed, so there’s nice peace of mind built right in.
The bike uses a 24-inch front wheel with a suspension fork and a smaller 20-inch rear wheel, helping keep the rear cargo deck low enough for easier loading and a lower center of gravity. Both wheels wear 2.4-inch Maxxis Metroloads, which offer a nice compromise between comfort and agility.
Stopping power comes from Tektro four-piston hydraulic disc brakes, while the drivetrain is a Shimano CUES Di2 10-speed setup.
And that drivetrain is where things get interesting.
I’ve tested automatic-shifting e-bikes before and haven’t always been impressed. Some systems leave you feeling like you’re fighting against the bike, shifting at moments you wouldn’t choose or seemingly second-guessing what you’re trying to do.
Shimano has this one dialed in.
The system seemingly just knows when I would want to shift and does it for me without getting in the way. After enough time riding the Swoop ASM, I started wishing all my bikes shifted this way.
Automatic shifting makes sense on virtually any bicycle, but it’s especially useful on a cargo bike. When you’ve got a couple of kids riding behind you, the fewer things you need to think about, the better.
There’s nothing quite like coming to a stop on a heavily loaded cargo bike, forgetting to downshift, and then discovering that you’re in a high gear while trying to get several hundred pounds of bike, rider, kids, and cargo rolling again.
The Swoop ASM solves that problem by automatically downshifting when you stop. When the light turns green, you’re already in the right gear.
It also pairs beautifully with the Shimano mid-drive motor. The torque-sensing pedal assist feels natural, and keeping the motor, drivetrain, electronic shifting, and controls within Shimano’s ecosystem makes everything feel cohesive.
Of course, carrying stuff is the entire point of a cargo bike, and Xtracycle has that part figured out too.
I used the rear setup for everything from kids to more than 100 pounds of Jackery solar generators, and the passenger corral works surprisingly well for oddly shaped cargo.
Unlike some companies that advertise an attractive base price and then make you spend hundreds more turning the bike into the family hauler you thought you were buying, Xtracycle generally includes much of that equipment in the package.
The rear passenger carrier is rated as a “2+” setup. I only managed to round up two kids for testing, but there was clearly room back there for a third if I’d been more resourceful – or simply had more nieces and nephews out of school.
Xtracycle’s accessories are also built with the same mentality as the bike itself. The enormous pannier looks like something designed to strap onto the side of a fighter jet rather than a 28 mph cargo e-bike. It is so well made that it looks like it could handle a jet stream.
This stuff feels overbuilt because Xtracycle understands that its customers use these bikes as everyday transportation.
When you’re carrying your kids, groceries, work gear, or whatever else your family can throw at the bike, overbuilt is exactly the right amount of built.
Perhaps one of the best demonstrations of the Swoop ASM’s underlying engineering is something that doesn’t appear on a spec sheet: I can ride it without my hands on the handlebars.
I don’t mean that as a recommendation for your morning school run. Rather, it demonstrates just how stable and well-designed the bike’s geometry is. Xtracycle is a real bicycle company, and it shows. The Swoop tracks beautifully and feels composed instead of giving you that vague, wandering sensation found on some long-tail cargo bikes.
It’s rare that I can actually go no-hands on a cargo bike like I can on my normal city bikes, but this one feels just as stable despite the long, stretched out frame.
There are plenty of smaller touches I appreciate, too. Integrated lighting is included, the adjustable stem helps riders dial in their cockpit position, and there’s even a dropper seat post.
That dropper is particularly useful on a cargo bike. You can ride with the saddle at the proper height for full leg extension, then drop it as you approach a stop so you can comfortably plant both feet on the ground while supporting a fully loaded bike. Start riding again, raise the saddle, and you’re immediately back in the ideal pedaling position.
Interestingly, amid all of this technology, Shimano keeps the display refreshingly simple. You get your battery level, speed, gear position, and selectable information like remaining range, odometer, and trip distance. That’s basically it.
If you want to manually control the Di2 drivetrain, shifting buttons on the right handlebar let you do that. Otherwise, just leave it in automatic and let the bike handle the gears.
The catch, unsurprisingly, is the price.
At $4,495,
the Xtracycle Swoop ASM is unquestionably a premium cargo e-bike. It isn’t competing with $1,500 budget models, nor is it pretending to.
But there are also cargo e-bikes pushing $8,000, so everything is relative.
If your primary goal is spending as little as possible, there are plenty of budget cargo bikes that can get the job done. But if you want higher-end components, an excellent drivetrain, thoughtful geometry, quality accessories, and a bike designed to survive years of hard daily use, this is what paying for a premium model gets you.
And if a bike costs several times more but lasts several times longer while providing a safer, better riding experience for your family, the math starts to make a lot more sense.
Premium cargo e-bikes are a pay-to-play affair. But with the
Xtracycle Swoop ASM
, I can confidently say you’re getting what you pay for.
After testing more cargo e-bikes than I can count, this is one of the best examples I’ve ridden of what happens when a company doesn’t just build an electric bike with a long rack on the back, but actually understands what families need from a true car-replacing cargo e-bike.

title: China’s first 100 MW/1,000 MWh compressed CO2 storage plant connects to grid - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
China Huadian has achieved the first grid connection of its 100 MW/1,000 MWh compressed CO₂ energy storage plant in Xinjiang, marking a major milestone in long-duration energy storage. The facility offers 10 hours of storage and is expected to generate 200 GWh annually, supporting renewable energy integration and reducing carbon emissions.
Vincent Shaw
15 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
China Huadian has completed the first grid connection of a 100 MW/1,000 MWh compressed carbon dioxide (CO₂) energy storage plant in Mulei County, Xinjiang, marking a significant milestone for this emerging long-duration storage technology.
The facility achieved its initial grid connection on Sept. 30, according to China Huadian. Located in the Gobi Desert of Changji Prefecture, the project forms part of a renewable energy development comprising 600 MW of wind and 400 MW of solar capacity.
The storage plant occupies approximately 565,000 square meters and incorporates five gas storage enclosures, 141 liquid CO₂ storage units and 97 thermal storage units. Its rated capacity of 100 MW/1 GWh corresponds to a nominal discharge duration of 10 hours.
Unlike conventional compressed air energy storage (CAES), which typically stores high-pressure air in underground salt caverns or other engineered storage spaces, the Mulei system uses CO₂ as a working fluid in a closed thermodynamic cycle.
During charging, surplus electricity powers compressors that raise the pressure of gaseous CO₂. The heat generated is recovered and stored, while the compressed gas is cooled and liquefied for storage in pressure vessels. During discharge, the liquid CO₂ is evaporated, reheated using the recovered thermal energy and expanded through a turbine to generate electricity. The gas then returns to storage for reuse.
CO₂ can be liquefied at comparatively moderate pressures, allowing more compact high-pressure storage than compressed air. The system also avoids the need for suitable underground caverns, potentially expanding deployment opportunities in geographically constrained locations. However, it still requires substantial above-ground gas storage infrastructure, heat exchangers and specialized turbomachinery.
The technology was developed by a research team led by Professor Xie Yonghui at Xi’an Jiaotong University and commercialized through Shenzhen-based Exax Energy, also known as Bairang New Energy. Dongfang Electric served as EPC contractor and supplied major equipment, including compressors, turbines, generators, heat exchangers and control systems.
According to Huadian, the plant’s CO₂ turbine has a design efficiency exceeding 92%, while the system is designed for at least 30 years of operation, more than 20,000 start-stop cycles and a startup-to-full-load time of less than 20 minutes.
The 92% figure refers to turbine efficiency, not the electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency of the complete storage system. Huadian has not disclosed independently verified system-level efficiency or levelized storage costs.
The company expects annual generation of approximately 200 GWh once the facility reaches full operation, potentially avoiding around 50,000 metric tons of standard coal consumption and 170,000 metric tons of CO₂ emissions annually.
The Mulei project represents a substantial step beyond earlier Chinese demonstrations of the same technology, including a 10 MW/20 MWh verification system completed in 2022 and a 10 MW/80 MWh installation connected to the grid in Anhui province in December 2023. Internationally, Italy’s Energy Dome has also developed commercial-scale CO₂ storage, including a 20 MW/200 MWh facility in Sardinia.
Compressed CO₂ storage is therefore advancing from pilot systems into utility-scale deployment, although it remains considerably less commercially established than conventional CAES. Mulei’s initial grid connection demonstrates engineering integration at the 100 MW scale.

title: BloombergNEF forecasts 584 GW of solar installations in 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
BloombergNEF has cut its 2026 global solar installation forecast to 584 GW, down 10.8% from 2025, driven by a sharper-than-expected slowdown in China. Solar installations outside China are projected to grow to 313 GW, supported by expanding residential and commercial markets.
John Fitzgerald Weaver
15 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
In December 2025, BloombergNEF
projected a pullback
in global solar installations, with China slowing and the rest of the world growing. Ten months later, China has slowed more than expected. The rest of the world has grown slightly faster.
BloombergNEF now projects 584 GW of solar installations in 2026. That is a 10.8% decline from 655 GW in 2025. In December, it forecast 649 GW. In the
first quarter of 2025
, it expected 753 GW. That earlier 2026 figure is 29% higher than today’s forecast.
When asked whether there have been any surprises in the solar industry in 2026 – any
Pakistan’s for instance
– BloombergNEF CleanTech Analyst Jenny Chase said, “Honestly, none so far, a big theme has been no major booms. I don’t think it has anything to do with Chinese politics or pricing.”
BloombergNEF estimates China installed 383 GW in 2025. It now expects 271 GW in 2026, a 29% decline. In the group’s 2025 Q4 projection, China had been forecast for 2026 was 341 GW.
In December, BloombergNEF CleanTech Analyst Jenny Chase said growth in China “cannot continue at its historical breakneck pace.” She now attributes the deeper slowdown to saturation. “We doubt that either batteries or EVs will halt this, they just slow it down a little,” Chase told
pv magazine USA
Last year China deployed 383 GW of solar capacity, of which Chase noted the “breakneck” pace. The nation-state is projected to decline a massive 29% to 271 GW deployed. Through the end of June 2026, China installed about 71.8 GW of PV, down from 212.2 GW in the same period of 2025,
a even sharper decline of roughly 66%
The decline came as part of a shift in policy and a
new five year plan
taking attention off of capacity, and focusing on energy storage.
Outside of China, non-utility, and batteries
The world has slightly outperformed BloombergNEF’s projections. 2025’s deployment capacity of 272 GW was projected to grow to 308 GW – a 13% pop. Current projections put global capacity at 313 GW deployed, well within the end of 2025’s margin of error.
Growth is coming from markets like India, “chugging along”, the Philippines, Nigeria and Malaysia. Regarding both Nigeria and the Philippines, Chase pointed out that the growth in those markets was almost entirely residential and commercial based.
This aligns with a recent report, shown in the above BloombergNEF chart, that with the pullback in utility scale solar in China – non-utility solar is now the largest sector of global renewable energy investment.

title: New image dataset aims to improve AI-based navigation of PV cleaning robots - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have created a dataset of 6,200 solar panel images designed to support AI-based navigation of cleaning robots. The dataset features annotated panel reference lines under clean, synthetically soiled, and laboratory contamination conditions, with the aim of helping developers assess the robustness of visual navigation algorithms.
Lior Kahana
15 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
PV cleaning robots
An international research team developed an
open-access image dataset
to support visual navigation for autonomous PV cleaning robots under different soiling conditions. The dataset comprises 6,200 annotated images of solar panels, including clean images, synthetically generated contamination at five severity levels, and laboratory images of physically soiled modules.
“The novelty of our research lies in developing a photovoltaic image dataset specifically for the visual navigation of cleaning robots, rather than conventional panel defect inspection,” corresponding author Kumeresan A. Danapalasingam told
pv magazine
. “By preserving the same reference-line geometry across different levels of simulated soiling, we provide researchers with a systematic way to evaluate whether robotic vision algorithms can reliably identify navigation cues even when the panel surface is contaminated.”
To construct the dataset, the researchers captured top-down images of PV panels using an HF868-2 camera mounted at the front of a solar panel cleaning robot, approximately 15 cm above the module surface. The camera featured a 2.7 mm wide-angle lens with a 135-degree field of view and recorded video at 320 × 240 pixels and 60 frames per second. The images were geometrically calibrated and resized to 160 × 120 pixels to accommodate the computational constraints of onboard robotic vision systems.
The team manually annotated 800 clean images, identifying three types of structural reference lines used for robot navigation: white cell-gap lines, horizontal frame-cell border lines, and vertical frame-cell border lines. We then processed each image using a synthetic augmentation pipeline that generated five additional versions with increasing soiling, from very light to extreme. The simulated effects included bird droppings, water stains, puddles, glare, water accumulation along module frames, and frame dust, with targeted reference-line coverage ranging from 1% to 50% depending on the severity level.
“One particularly interesting aspect of our research is that different forms of contamination can systematically obscure the same photovoltaic reference lines while their underlying geometry remains unchanged,” co-author Xin Li said. “This allows us to isolate the effects of visual degradation from changes in the robot’s viewing geometry. We believe this provides a useful foundation for understanding how visual navigation algorithms fail under challenging conditions and how their robustness can be improved.”
This process produced 4,800 images for training and validation, divided into 3,846 training images and 954 validation images. For testing, the researchers assembled 1,200 images across six clean and synthetic soiling conditions, supplemented by 200 additional images captured on two separate PV panels physically contaminated with pigment droplets, sand, wastewater, and clean water, as well as exposed to high-intensity lighting to simulate glare. The resulting dataset comprises 6,200 images with corresponding annotation files containing reference-line positions, orientations, endpoints, and class identifiers.
“Our next objective is to move beyond dataset development towards reliable autonomous navigation of photovoltaic cleaning robots,” the academics concluded. “We are investigating lightweight artificial intelligence models for estimating the robot’s heading relative to panel reference lines, as well as localization methods that combine visual information with inertial and wheel-encoder measurements. Ultimately, we aim to validate these approaches on physical robotic platforms under realistic operating conditions.”
The paper “
A robot-view image dataset of photovoltaic panel reference lines with paired synthetic soiling for cleaning robot navigation
” has appeared in
Data in Brief.
Researchers from the University of Technology Malaysia, Canada’s University of Prince Edward Island, Belgium’s Thomas More University of Applied Sciences,
Western Norway University
, and the Indian university
Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham
have participated in the study.

title: Octopus Energy unveils heat pump add-on for home cooling - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
K-based Octopus Energy has introduced Cosy Cooler, a hydronic cooling unit designed to work with its existing Cosy heat pumps. The company says the device can be installed using existing radiator pipework and will cost between GBP 500 ($670) and GBP 600 when it becomes available in 2027.
Emiliano Bellini
15 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The Cosy heat pump
UK energy company
Octopus Energy
has as unveiled Cosy Cooler, a compact indoor cooling unit designed to turn its
Cosy heat pump heating system
into a solution for residential air conditioning.
The device uses chilled water supplied by a compatible Cosy heat pump to cool individual rooms, eliminating the need for a separate refrigerant-based indoor split air-conditioning system. It connects to existing radiator pipework, which the company says can simplify installation in homes already equipped with its heat pumps.
“The portable Cosy Cooler is the size of a tall kitchen bin and plugs directly into radiator pipework to circulate chilled water through the home – with no need for an outdoor hose,” the company said in a statement. “The unit can cool single rooms or run up to two to three units at once across different rooms, depending on the Cosy heat pump model.”
According to Octopus Energy, installation takes approximately three hours. The company expects to offer the unit for between GBP 500 ($670) and GBP 600, with commercial availability planned for 2027.
The Cosy Cooler measures 720 mm × 430 mm × 350 mm and operates as a water-to-air cooling unit. It uses the heat pump’s cooling function to circulate chilled water through an indoor heat exchanger, with a fan distributing cooled air into the room.
Octopus Energy has not disclosed the unit’s rated cooling capacity, electrical consumption, airflow rate or acoustic performance. It has also not published seasonal cooling efficiency figures or detailed operating conditions.
The company said it has already started testing the technology in residential and office environments, although it has not yet announced a firm commercial launch date or published a complete technical datasheet.

title: Dutch startup offers PV mounting solution for fragile roofs - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Dutch startup Rable has developed a self-supporting PV mounting system for fragile roofs with slopes of up to 10 degrees, reducing anchor points by 95% compared with conventional systems. The galvanized-steel structure distributes loads of 6 kg/m² to 15 kg/m² and can reduce installation costs by €0.15 ($0.16)/W, according to the company.
François Puthod
15 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The structure limits the roof load to 7 kg/m² with lightweight solar panels, compared with 13 kg/m² with conventional modules.
Dutch startup Rable has developed a PV mounting system designed to enable solar installations on fragile roofs with limited load-bearing capacity. Called Rable4Roofs, the system uses a self-supporting structure to distribute loads more evenly and significantly reduce the number of anchor points required.
The mounting structure is made from galvanized steel sourced from Belgium and comes with a 15-year corrosion warranty. Its lattice design is central to the system.
“It is a self-supporting, cost-effective solution for fragile roofs, roofs with Class B insulation and parking structures, particularly for east-west configurations,” Mevanly Karamoko, a sales engineer at Rable, told
pv magazine
. “It also requires 95% fewer anchor points than conventional mounting systems, which represents a major advance for the market.”
It can be installed on flat or slightly pitched roofs with slopes of up to 10 degrees without compromising waterproofing. According to Rable, the system can also eliminate the need for roof renovations, which can cost up to €125/m², depending on the building.
Load distribution
The system’s stability relies on a structural design combining compression elements in the supporting framework with tension elements provided by cables. Together, these components form a rigid lattice that distributes loads and withstands environmental forces, including wind and snow.
“The system’s weight is supported by the roof purlins rather than the roof panels themselves,” Karamoko said. “This allows us to achieve loads of between 6 kg/m² and 15 kg/m², compared with two to three times that amount for conventional mounting systems, which can be problematic for fragile roofs.”
The PV modules are installed on dedicated rails designed to ensure alignment, mechanical stability and natural ventilation while allowing rainwater to drain freely. Depending on site requirements, the system can incorporate individual anchor points, typically at its ends, at a rate of approximately one anchor point per 25 modules.
Loads from the mounting structure are transferred to the roof through rubber-granulate pads. The pressure exerted on the roof surface depends on its allowable load-bearing capacity, starting at 3 kPa. Rable offers different pad configurations to accommodate varying structural requirements.
275 modules installed in 2.5 hours
The system is delivered to the installation site preassembled, reducing on-site assembly time.
“The structure simply needs to be unfolded, positioned, secured and screwed into place,” Karamoko said. “Two installers can install the mounting structure for 275 solar panels in just two and a half hours.”
In its first 30 months of operation, Rable has purportedly completed 60 PV projects, ranging from 50 to 5,000 modules per installation.
The company is also involved in two projects in France, including a 260 kW rooftop installation at a supermarket in Châtenoy-en-Bresse, in the Saône-et-Loire department.
“The roof was particularly fragile, with very limited load-bearing capacity. Another challenge was the relatively soft insulation, classified in France as Class B compressibility insulation,” Karamoko said. “Insurers generally refuse to cover installations on this type of insulation, but our mounting system makes it possible to overcome this constraint.”
According to Rable, the project achieved a structural load of 13.7 kg/m² and reduced capital expenditure by €0.15 ($0.16)/W.
Karamoko said the company expects to complete its first 10 installations in France by December. He identified France’s
Décret tertiaire
, which sets energy consumption reduction targets for tertiary-sector buildings, as a potential driver of demand for the company’s mounting technology in the coming years.
The patented system has an ETN (Enquête de Technique Nouvelle), a French technical assessment used to evaluate the suitability of innovative construction products and installation methods for specific applications, valid until 2028. The assessment provides technical documentation that can support acceptance of the system by insurers and construction stakeholders, subject to its scope and conditions.
Rable is also pursuing an ATEx (Appréciation Technique d’Expérimentation), a technical appraisal issued by France’s Scientific and Technical Centre for Building (CSTB) to assess the feasibility and risks of innovative construction solutions before they obtain more established technical approvals
Founded two and a half years ago, Rable is currently expanding its presence across European markets.
