title: Solaria plans 500 MW data center project powered by 350 MW of solar in Uruguay - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Solaria plans to invest $5.7 billion in a data center technology park in Uruguay, including 500 MW of data center capacity and 350 MW of solar PV. The government says it is the largest foreign investment ever announced in the country.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
15 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Americas
Utility-scale
Spanish company
has signed an agreement with the Uruguayan government to develop a data center technology park backed by a planned investment of $5.7 billion.
According to the Uruguayan government, the $5.7 billion project represents the largest foreign investment ever announced in the country.
The project includes $5.5 billion for the construction of data centers with a combined capacity of 500 MW, alongside $200 million for the development of 350 MW of solar PV capacity to supply renewable electricity to the facilities. The planned solar capacity, however, will not be sufficient to meet the data centers’ full electricity demand, meaning additional power sources will be required.
The technology park will be developed in two phases under Uruguay’s free trade zone regime, with facilities spread across the departments of Canelones, San José and Florida.
Construction is expected to continue through 2029, creating an estimated 3,100 jobs. Once fully operational, the complex is expected to employ approximately 1,500 people.
Renewable energy will play a central role in the project’s electricity supply. Uruguay already generates a substantial share of its electricity from renewable sources, and the planned 350 MW of solar capacity will provide additional generation to support the data centers.
The company has not disclosed details of the project’s electrical configuration, grid connection requirements, potential energy storage systems, power supply agreements or the development schedule for each phase.
Solaria has operated in Uruguay for nearly a decade, with solar plants in Young, in the department of Río Negro, and Mercedes, in the department of Soriano. The latest agreement marks an expansion of its activities in the country into data center infrastructure supported by solar generation.

title: Saudi Arabia uses 250 MW solar park to breed threatened gazelles - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman Royal Reserve has introduced 38 Sand gazelles into an operational solar facility following a seven-month trial. The project aims to use existing PV infrastructure as a breeding habitat for threatened wildlife, with the first births expected this winter.
Lior Kahana
15 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Saudi Arabia
Utility-scale
The ReWildingVoltaics initiative
Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman Royal Reserve (Pmbsrr) has introduced a breeding herd of 38 Sand gazelles into an operational 250 MW solar facility, as part of a wildlife conservation initiative. This follows a seven-month proof-of-concept (PoC) exercise that investigated whether solar installations could serve as breeding habitats for threatened wildlife.
“The facility’s size and predator-proof fences allow the gazelles to acclimatize, with few disturbances,” the team said in a working paper seen by
pv magazine
. “The shade beneath solar panels improves animal welfare and reproductive success. There was no damage to infrastructure, operational conflicts, or behavioral issues.”
The solar facility covers 505 hectares across three fenced sections, 370 hectares of which are suitable for animal husbandry. The pilot is taking place in a 157-hectare section housing a 66 MW solar array.
The researchers report that ground temperatures beneath the panels are 5 C to 10 C lower than in exposed areas. The first births are expected this winter, while population modeling suggests the reserve’s Sand gazelle population could increase from 109 to 600 animals by 2031 using the three solar sections.
The reserve’s broader rewilding program, ReWild Arabia, requires large founder populations of threatened species, creating a need for extensive husbandry facilities where animals can acclimatize, breed, and develop natural herd behaviors before release into the wild. The ReWildingVoltaics initiative uses solar parks to provide large, predator-proof enclosures, the team explained, while reducing the need for additional breeding infrastructure and freeing up resources for habitat restoration.
Pmbsrr developed the project in partnership with Amaala Sustainable Company for Energy (ASCE).
“Our collaboration to use our solar plants to reintroduce gazelles continues a longstanding global commitment from shareholders to integrate biodiversity conservation with renewable energy generation,” said former ASCE CEO Daniel Blanco.

title: Germany deploys 12.76 GW of solar in first nine months of 2026 - pv magazine Global
content: The anticipated recovery in Germany’s rooftop solar market has yet to materialize, while utility-scale solar installations have declined sharply, according to the Federal Network Agency’s latest figures for September. Germany added 1,226 MW of new PV capacity in September, down from 1,644 MW in August and up from 920 MW in September 2025 . Only February 2026 recorded a lower monthly total over the past 12 months. The Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) based its figures on commissioning and decommissioning data submitted to the Market Master Data Register (Marktstammdatenregister) by Oct. 13. The agency applied a 15% adjustment to account for installations that have yet to be registered, as operators have four weeks to report new systems. Utility-scale solar additions fall to lowest level of 2026 The Federal Network Agency recorded 38,859 new rooftop PV systems with a combined capacity of 554 MW in September, slightly above the 539 MW registered in August. Monthly additions reached 814 MW in July and 672 MW in June. The figures suggest that the expected rush to install rooftop PV systems ahead of planned changes to Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) has yet to materialize. The federal government’s draft legislation proposes phasing out feed-in tariffs for small PV systems after a transition period. The changes are scheduled to take effect in early 2027. Utility-scale solar additions fell sharply in September, with just 103 ground-mounted projects totaling 479 MW – the lowest monthly figure of the year. In August, 166 solar parks with a combined capacity of 1,054 MW were commissioned. Plug-in solar installations also declined. The agency recorded 28,647 new systems totaling 42 MW in September, compared with 41,978 systems and 61 MW in August. At the end of September, Germany had 6.34 million operational PV systems with a combined capacity of 130.7 GW. Since the beginning of 2026, 660,445 systems totaling 12,762 MW have been commissioned, while 29,898 systems with a combined capacity of 136 MW have been decommissioned. As a way of comparison, in the first nine months of 2025 the country installed 12.56 of new PV installations. EWS reports unexpectedly weak solar growth in September German PV wholesaler EWS also reported relatively weak installation figures for September. Its analysis of Market Master Data Register figures showed 1,026 MW of newly installed PV capacity based on data available at the beginning of the week. The figure remains preliminary, as operators have one month to register new installations and additional reports are expected. EWS expects September additions to remain below those of previous months, even after late registrations are included. Its latest figures show 1,941 MW of new capacity in July and 1,651 MW in August. However, the company expects September installations to exceed those recorded in the same month last year, when additions totaled 1,024 MW, including late registrations. EWS also compared Germany’s solar market performance over the first three quarters of 2025 and 2026, highlighting a shift toward larger installations despite relatively stable overall deployment. “After three quarters, the German photovoltaic market is statistically tracking remarkably closely to the levels seen in previous years. The total photovoltaic capacity added so far is slightly higher than that of the first three quarters of 2024 and 2025. At the same time, the market structure is undergoing a significant shift. While project-based business and the traditional specialized trade segment were still evenly balanced in 2025, new capacity is increasingly shifting toward large-scale installations – a trend that began as early as 2024,” EWS said. PV systems larger than 750 kW continue to gain market share, accounting for approximately 57% of all new solar capacity installed in Germany so far this year. By contrast, installations in market segments traditionally served by specialist installers continue to decline. The downturn affects both commercial PV systems and residential rooftop installations of up to 10 kW. According to EWS, newly installed capacity in these segments has fallen by more than 40% since 2024. title: India’s solar industry faces workforce readiness gap - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A Mercom India study has found that solar industry employers across project development, manufacturing, rooftop solar, and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) often need to spend months training fresh graduates before they are ready to contribute effectively.
Uma Gupta
15 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
India’s rapidly expanding solar industry is facing a growing workforce readiness gap, with employers across utility-scale project development, manufacturing, rooftop solar installation, and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) reporting that fresh graduates require substantial training before becoming productive, according to Mercom India’s newly released survey report
Bridging India’s Solar Talent Gap – Aligning Academia with Industry Needs.
Based on responses from more than 100 industry participants across four major solar segments—utility-scale, manufacturing, rooftop, and engineering, procurement, and construction—the study found the challenge extends beyond individual technical skills. Employers identified gaps across practical exposure, project execution, manufacturing processes, system design, regulatory understanding, commercial knowledge, troubleshooting, and site readiness.
“India’s solar industry is expanding rapidly, but the talent pipeline is not keeping pace with what companies need,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO of Mercom Capital Group. “Employers are spending significant time training fresh graduates before they can contribute effectively in project development, manufacturing, rooftop solar, and EPC roles. Academic programs need much stronger exposure to current technologies, operating projects, factories, site conditions, regulations, and the commercial realities of the evolving industry. Greater cooperation between industry and academia is critical to closing this gap.”
According to the report, nearly three-quarters (74%) of manufacturing respondents said fresh graduates take 3 to 12 months to become productive, while another 7.4% said the process takes more than a year. Forty percent (40%) of respondents said 25% to 50% of new hires need retraining, while 29.6% said 51% to 75% require retraining.
Nearly two-thirds of utility-scale solar respondents (62.5%) said more than half of their new hires need significant retraining before becoming productive, including 37.5% who said this applies to over 75% of new hires. Half of the respondents (50%) believe fresh graduates do not understand grid congestion and curtailment risks. EPC companies also reported extended ramp-up periods.
Fifty-four percent (54%) of rooftop solar companies said fresh graduates take more than three months to become productive, including 16% reporting six to twelve months and 13.5% reporting more than a year.
The survey shows the skill gap varies across the solar value chain. Among utility-scale developers, 75% reported a lack of practical exposure as the biggest hiring bottleneck. Respondents also highlighted gaps in project feasibility assessment, grid and regulatory processes, and commercial understanding, indicating limited exposure to how projects move from development to commissioning.
Solar manufacturing companies reported different challenges. About 37% of respondents cited a lack of practical exposure as the biggest hiring bottleneck, followed by a lack of basic industry knowledge at over 33%. Respondents also reported gaps in troubleshooting, quality assessment, production processes, and understanding factory performance metrics.
Rooftop solar companies highlighted gaps in field exposure, practical system design, customer interaction, and regulatory processes. Nearly 60% identified either a lack of field exposure or weak practical design knowledge as the biggest hiring challenge.
EPC companies similarly emphasized practical site readiness. About 88% identified lack of field exposure, weak technical knowledge, or limited understanding of project development as the leading hiring challenges. Only about 42% said graduates can work effectively on live project sites, indicating difficulty translating engineering knowledge into real-world construction, commissioning, and project execution.
More than 83% of respondents in every segment said they would or may support internships, site exposure, factory visits, or training partnerships. Manufacturers showed the strongest interest at 96%, indicating substantial scope for structured industry-academia collaboration centered on practical and industry-relevant training.
“The industry is clearly willing to participate in solving this problem. Companies across all four segments are open to internships, site exposure, factory visits, and training partnerships. What is missing is a structured mechanism and effort that brings industry and academia together regularly, so curricula and practical training keep pace with how quickly the solar market is changing,” Prabhu added.

title: Finland demands grid-forming support for new wind, solar in weak grids - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Fingrid will require new wind and solar plants in Finland’s weakest grid areas to provide grid-forming capability, which developers can meet with co-located batteries sized at up to 30% of plant output.
Brian Publicover
15 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Nuveen Infrastructure operates a 30 MW battery in Finland and is developing around 700 MW of energy storage projects in various regions.
Finnish transmission system operator Fingrid has published technical requirements obliging new large wind and solar plants in converter-dominated parts of its network to provide grid-forming control, either through their own inverters or through separate equipment built at or near the site.
Fingrid announced the measure in late Setpember and published the detailed requirements earlier this month, under its VJV2024 grid code for power plants. They apply to type D plants connecting where the equivalent short-circuit ratio (ESCR) at the connection point is below 1.0. Existing plants and projects that already hold a connection agreement are exempt.
Wind generation in Finland is concentrated in such areas, notably along the west coast, and grid security can be disrupted where there is too little synchronous generation, Fingrid said. Its requirements document says grid-following converters in these areas can cause poorly damped voltage oscillations, weak fault ride-through and overvoltages during three-phase faults, risking the disconnection of plants at scale, and that tuning control parameters alone can’t solve the problem.
Developers can choose between batteries, energy-storage-equipped static synchronous compensators (ES-STATCOMs) and synchronous machines such as synchronous condensers. Minimum sizing rises as the grid weakens. A battery must be rated at ±10% of the plant’s capacity where the ESCR is between 0.9 and 1.0, ±20% between 0.7 and 0.9, and ±30% below 0.7. The equivalent thresholds are 7%, 13% and 20% for an ES-STATCOM, and short-circuit power of 33%, 66% and 100% of plant capacity for a synchronous machine.
The equipment must be online whenever the plant runs at 50% of its rated output or more, and in service before the plant first exports power. It must sit within 60 km of electrical distance from the plant, either inside the plant, at the same substation or on the same 110 kV line, so that a single fault on Fingrid’s meshed network cannot separate the two.
Batteries installed to meet the requirement may trade in electricity and reserve markets, provided that market activity never cuts into their minimum stabilizing capability. A battery providing system services must also comply with Fingrid’s storage grid code. One that does not participate in markets can instead be treated as an ES-STATCOM and sized at the lower thresholds.
Fingrid will present the requirements in a webinar on Oct. 16.
Fingrid already requires grid-forming capability from large batteries under its storage grid code, and
Merus Power’s 30 MW/80 MWh project in Rovaniemi
is among the systems being built to that standard. The four Nordic transmission system operators said in a
joint position paper
in November 2025 that grid-forming requirements for wind and solar would follow the evolution of European network codes. India’s Central Electricity Authority has separately
proposed mandatory grid-forming inverters and co-located storage
for new solar and wind projects.
Pairing batteries with wind is not new in Finland. Ilmatar’s 30 MW/41 MWh Ainola battery, co-located with the Piiparinmäki wind farm in North Ostrobothnia, went online in June 2025, when the country had about
250 MW of battery capacity in operation

title: Skapion's counter-drone system claims to stop over 100 drones at once
content: Defense technology startup Skapion has unveiled a new air defense system designed to intercept large numbers of attacking drones simultaneously, addressing a growing challenge for militaries: stopping coordinated drone swarms without exhausting interceptor supplies or defense budgets.The company described its platform as the world’s first “Native Counter-Swarm” defense system, built from the outset to engage multiple aerial targets at once rather than treating each drone as a separate engagement. Skapion announced the system on October 14, as defense companies gathered for the Association of the U.S. Army’s 2026 Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, D.C.Skapion said the mobile, kinetic system is designed to engage more than 100 targets simultaneously, with an interception rate exceeding 97 percent. Those are company-reported performance targets, however, and the system has not yet publicly demonstrated those results in a live-fire test. Skapion plans to conduct its first live-fire test in the coming weeks.A different approach to drone swarmsConventional air defense systems can struggle when large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones arrive together. Even when defenders can detect and intercept individual threats, a coordinated attack can strain available interceptors and create more simultaneous engagements than a system was designed to handle.Skapion’s approach centers on what it calls a many-to-many architecture: multiple interceptors can be assigned to multiple targets at the same time. An AI-based command-and-control system is designed to combine information from the company’s own sensors or third-party detection systems, prioritize incoming threats, allocate interceptors, and manage engagements in real time.The system is intended to operate autonomously or with a human operator supervising engagements, depending on customer policy, according to the company. Its open architecture is also designed to integrate with existing command-and-control systems and other counter-unmanned aircraft systems.Skapion noted that its interceptors use a fully kinetic approach, meaning they physically engage targets rather than relying solely on electronic jamming. That could be relevant against drones that operate autonomously or don’t rely on communication links that can be disrupted.Vertical-launch architecture is designed to provide 360-degree engagement coverage. The company said it can deploy the system on ground and maritime platforms, although various reports indicate Skapion is not currently pursuing airborne deployment. Interceptors designed to cost lessCost is central to the system’s pitch. Militaries may end up using expensive air defense weapons against drones that cost far less to build, creating an unfavorable resource exchange during prolonged attacks.Skapion aims to bring the cost of each interceptor down to approximately $10,000 at scale. The outlet also reported that the interceptors are designed to engage drones at distances of roughly 1 to 7 kilometers (0.6 to 4.3 miles) and may use either electro-optical or radio-frequency seekers.The company envisions distributing launch systems across mobile vehicles and other platforms rather than concentrating all defensive capacity at a few fixed sites. Such a network could potentially protect military forces, critical infrastructure, and other installations against coordinated attacks. These applications remain prospective, rather than evidence of an established operational deployment.Live-fire testing is the next milestoneSkapion was founded by a team with experience in defense and engineering. Its founding architect, retired Brig. Gen. Pini Yungman, previously led Rafael’s Air and Missile Defense Systems division and contributed to Israel’s Iron Dome and David’s Sling programs. That background informs the company’s approach, but it alone does not establish the new system’s performance.The startup raised $36 million in seed funding earlier in 2026, with UP. Partners and Khosla Ventures led the round. The funding is intended to support engineering development, validation, and expansion of the company’s capabilities. The planned live-fire test is expected to involve up to 50 interceptors targeting small Class 2 and Class 3 drones, using a proximity-based kill mechanism. The company is also aiming for an operational test evaluation in 2027, with a hoped-for operational capability in the second half of that year.For now, Skapion’s unveiling presents a proposed answer to the economics and complexity of drone-swarm attacks, not a proven replacement for existing air defense systems. Live-fire results and subsequent evaluations will be important in determining whether its approach can deliver the scale, reliability, and cost advantages it promises.

title: US engineers create wearable solar tech to cut soldiers' battery loads
content: Engineers at Florida International University (FIU) have developed a thin, wearable solar device that can generate electricity from sunlight and also produce light. Called SOLED, the device combines the functions of a solar panel and a light-emitting diode (LED) in a single, flexible structure. The technology could be integrated into soldiers’ uniforms or equipment to power electronic devices in the field, potentially reducing reliance on batteries, generators, and resupply missions. The research aims to support lightweight wearable power systems and could also lead to new applications in displays, sensors, and other optoelectronic devices.Dual-function solar deviceSOLED combines a solar cell and a light-emitting diode (LED) in a single, lightweight structure that could eventually be integrated into uniforms, wearable equipment, and other portable power systems.The device is made using perovskite, a semiconductor material that can absorb sunlight and convert it into electrical energy. The researchers report that SOLED achieves a power-conversion efficiency of up to 22 percent when operating as a solar cell, a performance level competitive with commercial solar technology. When operated in reverse, the same device emits light with nearly 11 percent efficiency, an improvement over earlier versions of the technology.SOLED combines energy harvesting and light emission within a single thin structure. In its solar-cell mode, the device captures sunlight and converts it into electricity that could help power electronic equipment. In its light-emitting mode, it uses electrical energy to produce light.According to the team, this dual functionality could make the technology useful in applications where space, weight, and energy availability are important considerations. Soldiers can carry up to 20 pounds (9 kilograms) of batteries to operate communications equipment and other electronic systems during missions. Integrating solar devices into uniforms or equipment could provide an additional power source, potentially reducing dependence on conventional batteries, generators, and supply deliveries.The panels could also offer an alternative to generators in remote environments, where noise, heat, and bulky equipment can create operational challenges. However, the technology remains under development, and its practical performance in field conditions will depend on further improvements and testing.Wearable solar innovationAlthough SOLED can produce light, its current output is not particularly bright to the naked eye. Its peak emission occurs at a wavelength of 818 nanometers, just beyond the visible spectrum in the near-infrared region. The emitted light can appear as a faint pink glow, but wavelengths in this range can be detected by specialized equipment.Potential applications include night-vision sensors, biometric scanners, and medical imaging systems. Combining light emission and energy generation in one component could support compact optoelectronic devices that perform multiple functions without requiring separate components for each task.The research team is working to increase the panels’ visible brightness while expanding their size. Scaling up the technology is challenging because the device consists of multiple thin layers that must maintain performance as the overall panel grows.The researchers showed that SOLED can maintain strong performance even in the smallest samples commonly used in early-stage solar-cell research. A device measuring 1.1 square centimeters retained a power-conversion efficiency above 20 percent. The team also tested a larger 2.1-square-centimeter version and reported continued strong performance.These results indicate that the technology can be developed beyond very small laboratory samples. However, larger panels will require further engineering and evaluation before they can be incorporated into practical products.The next stage of development will focus on scaling SOLED toward panel sizes suitable for real-world applications. If the researchers can preserve its efficiency and light-emitting capabilities at larger dimensions, the technology could provide a compact platform for wearable energy generation, specialized sensors, and other devices that combine solar power with light emission.

title: US could get 650 MW nuclear power plant in Virginia by early 2030s
content: A stretch of farmland along Virginia’s James River is under evaluation for a small modular reactor facility that could deliver up to 650 megawatts of electricity to the regional grid.Geenex Power’s proposed Beck Creek Energy Project would occupy part of the Traver Family Farm property in Amherst County’s District 1, near the Joshua Falls Appalachian Power substation. The developer estimates the facility could create more than 200 permanent local jobs.Existing transmission infrastructure helped draw the company to the location, offering a potential connection to the PJM regional power market. Construction and operation are tentatively targeted for the early 2030s, although the proposal remains in early-stage site evaluation.Existing power lines guide site selectionThe proposed facility’s electricity would enter the PJM market rather than serve Amherst County exclusively or supply a dedicated customer.Geenex is assessing how much generation the property could accommodate. Its preliminary estimate puts potential capacity at up to 650 MW, but further investigations could change that figure.“What we’re seeing right now is that we think that the land and area would be able to support up to 650 megawatts,” said Delaney Bolton, a development project manager with Geenex Power. “That number may change based on some more of our technical due diligence studies,” he added.Although the proposal identifies small modular reactors as its technology category, Geenex has not selected a specific reactor technology or finalized the facility’s layout.Studies examine river and safety considerationsTechnical and environmental studies are underway to determine the project’s design and potential effects on the surrounding area, including the nearby James River.“We’re still kind of developing what the site could look like through preliminary and conceptual site designs. So I don’t have an answer for you on what it ultimately will look like,” Bolton said.Bolton said the company plans to meet state and federal environmental requirements and share findings with residents as its studies progress.She also said advanced nuclear technology incorporates improvements developed through decades of industry experience. If the project advances, Geenex plans to coordinate emergency preparations with local, state, and federal officials.“There is extensive emergency response planning and first responder training that goes into building one of these sites,” Bolton said.Local jobs depend on project approvalsGeenex hopes to work with a future technology partner to operate the plant and train local workers for nuclear industry positions. An economic impact analysis is also underway.“We really want to keep the jobs local and kind of bring the whole community along with us as we build this plant,” Bolton said.Amherst County Administrator Jeremy Bryant told 10 News that Geenex has not submitted an application to the county.The company hopes to begin discussions about land-use and rezoning applications in early to mid-2027. State and federal permitting, including nuclear regulatory approvals, also stand between the proposal and construction.The early-2030s schedule remains tentative as planning and regulatory requirements evolve. Residents can submit questions and concerns through the Beck Creek Energy Project website while the evaluation continues.

title: Tesla Powerwalls help California home batteries set new 745 MW record
content: Home batteries operated by Sunrun and Tesla delivered a record 745 megawatts of peak power to California’s electricity grid on October 6, helping meet elevated demand during a prolonged heat wave.The dispatch surpassed the 669 MW delivered a day earlier, setting consecutive records for residential distributed power plants in the United States, according to Sunrun’s October 14 announcement.At the request of the California Energy Commission and utilities, the companies discharged batteries installed in homes during multi-hour evening peak periods. Sunrun said the coordinated releases increased the grid’s operating margin and put downward pressure on real-time electricity prices.Home batteries meet evening demandThe October 6 dispatch delivered enough peak power to supply all households in San Francisco and San Jose combined, according to Sunrun. It demonstrated how batteries spread across individual properties can collectively provide a substantial source of electricity when demand rises.Both evenings involved California’s Demand Side Grid Support (DSGS) program. Dispatches were triggered after the California Independent System Operator’s day-ahead locational marginal electricity price exceeded $200 per megawatt-hour.The October 5 event also marked the first time this year that DSGS and the Emergency Load Reduction Program called for concurrent dispatches across all participating investor-owned utility service territories. By coordinating residential batteries, the programs tapped energy infrastructure already installed in homes to support the wider electricity network during periods of heightened demand.Two dispatches raise the recordThe back-to-back events exceeded the previous residential distributed power plant record of 580 MW, set on September 9, 2026. That dispatch had surpassed the 539 MW delivered on July 29, 2025.The latest peak of 745 MW represented an increase of 165 MW over September’s record, or approximately 28 percent.“These record-setting events prove that the energy infrastructure already installed in people’s homes can deliver power at a scale that makes a real difference for the grid,” said Sunrun CEO Mary Powell.“Instead of relying solely on costly new power plants to meet peak demand, California is putting existing home battery infrastructure to work when electricity is needed most, and customers are being compensated for helping strengthen grid reliability,” she added. Sunrun alone has more than 120,000 residential batteries enrolled to support California’s grid. The company did not provide separate contributions from Sunrun and Tesla for either October dispatch.Google-backed project targets local needsThe records come as another distributed power initiative takes shape around San Jose, with a focus on providing localized grid support.In September, Sunrun, Tesla, and Everyday Electric, formerly Renew Home, announced plans to enroll nearly 21,000 existing flexible energy devices in a Google-funded distributed power plant with utility PG&E.The initiative is designed to test how distributed energy resources can relieve local grid constraints and help meet rising electricity demand. Initial dispatches are expected in October, according to the announcement.Together, the projects illustrate the expanding role of household energy equipment in utility operations, giving customers opportunities to receive compensation while helping electricity providers manage peak demand and make better use of existing grid infrastructure.

title: DeLorean flying car: Tesla flying car faces surprise rival in race for electric flight
content: DeLorean Motor Company is entering flying car racing, joining the Airspeeder International Series as the championship’s first American constructor.The DeLorean Airspeeder Team is scheduled to debut when the 2026–27 season opens in November 2026.Announced at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the entry puts the brand behind an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOL, competing against national teams. DeLorean starts with a standardized racing aircraft before pursuing its own design with engineering students from UC Berkeley and Georgia Tech.The partnership gives a brand closely associated with the fictional flying time machine in Back to the Future a role in developing electric aviation through competition.From movie skies to a racing grid“People have pictured a DeLorean in the sky for 40 years. We decided it was time to stop picturing it,” said Cameron Wynne, DeLorean’s chief brand officer.The announcement brings DeLorean into a championship created by Australian entrepreneur Matt Pearson. Airspeeder positions its racing series as a testing environment for electric flight technology, using competition to advance aircraft development.“DeLorean is the original flying car brand. Long before anyone had built one, the whole world already knew what a flying DeLorean looked like,” said Pearson, Airspeeder’s founder and CEO.“Every great racing series is defined by the constructors who choose to compete in it. To have an American icon line up on our grid in our first international season tells you where this sport is going,” he added.The entry also extends DeLorean’s identity beyond its recognizable road car, bringing the name to an international motorsport built around electric aircraft.Electric aircraft race through virtual gatesFor its opening season, the DeLorean team is set to compete with the Airspeeder Mk3C, the standardized aircraft package used by other entrants.Its initial involvement centers on the team’s visual identity rather than a DeLorean-developed airframe. The shared platform gives competing teams the same underlying aircraft package for the 2026–27 campaign.Instead of following an asphalt circuit, competitors navigate three-dimensional courses defined by virtual gates. Onboard sensors and collision-avoidance systems support racing safety as the aircraft move through the course.The format adds a vertical dimension to competition, with the racing route extending through airspace rather than remaining on a conventional track.Tesla has also explored the idea of a hovering sports car through its long-delayed Roadster project. Its Model X features ‘falcon-wing’ doors, while the Cybertruck uses a stainless-steel exterior, drawing comparisons with DeLorean’s signature design.University teams support a custom racerDeLorean plans to expand its engineering role for the 2027–28 season by developing its own racing aircraft alongside students from UC Berkeley and Georgia Tech.The collaboration brings university engineering resources into the aircraft’s design and analysis before a DeLorean-specific racer reaches competition.Wynne also linked the program to the wider development of advanced air mobility. He said racing offers an opportunity to help shape “the regulatory, safety and compliance frameworks required” alongside the technology.Several details remain undisclosed, including the team’s pilot lineup, the custom aircraft’s design, and the full sporting program for its debut season.The announcement concerns a racing entry, with no consumer flying car announced. DeLorean said further details about the partnership’s direction are due in the coming months.

title: Inside Boston Dynamics' push to build Atlas humanoids in just one hour
content: Boston Dynamics released a video offering a closer look at the prototype operations team that builds and maintains its Atlas humanoid robot.The nearly six-minute film shows how the team combines precision machining, assembly, and repair to accelerate robot development. The company said its team can currently build a robot in about a day, with a target of reducing the process to roughly an hour next year. The approach applies manufacturing practices to research and development, allowing engineers and machinists to modify components and processes quickly as designs evolve.Atlas assembly overhaulThe company released a nearly six-minute video showing how its manufacturing processes support rapid hardware development, letting engineers move from design changes to physical components and assembled robots faster.The company currently takes about a day to build a robot, with the goal of reducing the process to approximately one hour next year. Longer-term ambitions include bringing build times down to minutes. However, these targets refer to the robot-building process described in the video and do not establish a production-line output rate or a timeline for commercial deliveries.Boston Dynamics‘ prototype operation brings engineers and machinists together to develop, manufacture, assemble, and maintain robotic hardware. Rather than relying entirely on external suppliers for specialized components, the facility performs precision machining in-house, allowing teams to modify parts and manufacturing processes as designs evolve.The work includes producing components with tight dimensional tolerances and carrying out specialized operations such as gear cutting. These capabilities are important for humanoid robots, which require precisely manufactured mechanical parts to support coordinated movements, repeated operation, and reliable performance.Keeping machining close to engineering also shortens the feedback loop between design and testing. Engineers can discuss component requirements directly with machinists, make adjustments, and evaluate revised parts without waiting for a lengthy external manufacturing process. Components can move from machining to assembly on the same day or the following day, enabling teams to test design changes on physical hardware sooner.The facility also develops the manufacturing methods needed to produce new components efficiently. This includes selecting suitable cutting tools, refining machining procedures, and incorporating robotic arms into assembly tasks. The approach allows manufacturing techniques to evolve alongside the robot’s mechanical design.Atlas build efficiencyThe emphasis on manufacturing efficiency extends to the design of Atlas itself. Its components must balance dexterity, durability, cost, and ease of maintenance, particularly as the robot moves toward wider industrial use.The company recently introduced four-finger hands for Atlas, underscoring the need to design robotic hardware around practical requirements. Hands must perform varied tasks while remaining sufficiently robust and serviceable for repeated use. Faster prototype development allows engineers to evaluate these trade-offs through physical testing and refine components before they enter broader production.The integrated workflow also supports maintenance and repair, helping the team identify hardware issues and return robots to testing faster. This is particularly relevant during research and development, when repeated experiments and design revisions can place additional demands on prototype hardware.The push to shorten Atlas build times comes as humanoid robotics companies increasingly focus on manufacturing scale. However, the time required to assemble an individual robot differs from the rate at which a production line can manufacture multiple units.Other manufacturers have reported hourly production targets, weekly output figures, and cumulative production milestones. These measurements describe different stages of manufacturing and cannot be compared directly without additional information about assembly procedures, automation, testing, and the status of completed robots.Boston Dynamics’ approach focuses on improving the connection between engineering and manufacturing, with faster component production and assembly intended to support more rapid development. The video also serves as a recruitment effort, highlighting the technical work involved in building and maintaining Atlas.

title: New tool targets rare-earths' shortages to boost electric motor manufacturing
content: A major laboratory in the United States has developed a new tool, which can guide manufacturers’ motor technology decisions amid critical material shortages. Called Motor Decide, the tool is designed to help industries evaluate electric motor technologies and make informed decisions under uncertain market conditions.“Many companies make technology decisions based largely on market momentum or competitor activity,” said ORNL’s Praveen Kumar, lead researcher on the project. “We wanted to create a tool that helps organizations make more informed, data-driven decisions for the long term.”Researchers also highlighted that critical materials such as copper and rare earth magnets are essential components in the electric motors that power transportation, manufacturing systems and energy infrastructure. As industries work to reduce dependence on vulnerable supply chains and manage rising geopolitical and market uncertainty, selecting the right motor technology has become increasingly complex.SI-driven platform can help companies evaluate electric motor technologiesThe Super Intelligence (SI)-driven platform can help companies evaluate electric motor technologies before market conditions shift.The team also highlighted that electric motors power a wide range or technologies, from hybrid or electric vehicles, to industrial systems and household appliances. Many depend on critical minerals such as copper and rare earth elements that face growing supply chain pressures. Motor Decide was created to help companies consider possible alternatives.The system combines SI, advanced modeling and large-scale scenario analysis to evaluate how motor technologies could perform under fluctuating material costs and supply chain disruptions. Researchers can model what happens if copper prices increase sharply or if a newer technology becomes commercially viable years from now. The result is a ranked set of motor technology options with insights into cost, performance, critical material use, manufacturability and long-term risk.“We define the operating environment in which the decision is being made. That includes procurement sources, manufacturing readiness, technology maturity and application requirements. Then we test how those factors change under different scenarios,” said Kumar.Platform also accounts for how organizations make decisionsThe platform also accounts for how organizations make decisions, helping users evaluate tradeoffs and quantify risk when comparing emerging technologies. “People ultimately own the decision,” Kumar said. “We are trying to quantify uncertainty and incorporate it into the decision-making process.”Motor Decide is also designed to work alongside another ORNL-developed platform, Motor AI, which uses SI-assisted engineering tools to accelerate detailed motor design. While Motor Decide helps identify the best motor technology pathway, Motor AI performs the detailed motor design work needed to bring those concepts to life, according to a press release.Once a company selects a preferred motor approach, researchers can transition the results into Motor AI to generate detailed design configurations and engineering specifications. Together, the tools could help accelerate the development of more resilient electric motor systems while reducing the risks associated with critical material shortages, volatile supply chains and rapidly changing global markets. The effort reflects ORNL’s broader mission to combine super intelligence, advanced manufacturing and energy research to help strengthen U.S. competitiveness and industrial resilience. Researchers are continuing to evaluate and expand the platform’s capabilities for future applications, as per the release.

title: AUKUS' nuclear-powered attack submarines' designs to be shaped by US firm
content: The U.S. Navy has awarded Huntington Ingalls Industries’ (HII) Newport News Shipbuilding division a contract worth approximately $56 million to support submarine engineering and design activities under the trilateral Australia-United Kingdom-United States (AUKUS) security partnership. The agreement includes an option that could increase its total value to approximately $91 million, further expanding American industrial involvement in the programme.The contract covers engineering, technical assistance, technology integration, supply-chain development, workforce training and digital transformation initiatives. It also includes support for the design of the future SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered attack submarine, which is intended to be built by the United Kingdom and Australia.Longstanding nuclear experience benefits the AUKUS mission“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management. “We are honored to leverage that experience and contribute even more to the AUKUS partnership.”Under the agreement, Newport News Shipbuilding will continue providing technical and industrial support to both AUKUS partners through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales framework. A key element of the contract is the United States Industry Support initiative, under which American engineers and designers will contribute their expertise to the development of the SSN-AUKUS submarine.The work is intended to help transfer specialized nuclear-submarine design knowledge, improve technical coordination and strengthen the industrial capabilities required to build and sustain advanced submarines over their operational lifetimes.Nuclear-powered submarine constructionHII’s experience in nuclear-powered submarine construction is expected to play an important role in this effort. Newport News Shipbuilding is one of only two shipyards in the United States that build nuclear-powered submarines, giving the company substantial expertise in complex submarine design, construction and maintenance.According to HII, the contract reflects the company’s continued commitment to supporting AUKUS and advancing shared security objectives among the three participating countries.The contract award is the latest in a range of initiatives HII is actively engaged in to advance the AUKUS partnership. HII’s Mission Technologies division in Australia was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program, which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base, according to a press release.HII is also working with Australian industry and academia in Australia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise. This includes educating and training thousands of engineers, maritime specialists, nuclear tradespeople and other professionals to support the enterprise across its full lifecycle, as per the release.The $56 million contract signals another step in the development of the industrial and technical framework underpinning AUKUS. By involving Newport News Shipbuilding in SSN-AUKUS design activities and supporting wider engineering and workforce initiatives, the agreement strengthens the connection between American submarine expertise and the future capabilities of Australia and the United Kingdom.

title: New chip gyroscope measures rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour
content: Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and Caltech have developed a chip-scale optical gyroscope that can detect rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour, nearly 2,000 times slower than an earlier silicon nitride design.The result brings the sensor closer to measuring Earth’s rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour. It could eventually help develop compact navigation systems for aircraft, vehicles and spacecraft operating where GPS signals are unavailable.Unlike conventional gyroscopes that rely on mechanical movement, the new device uses light traveling through a ring-shaped optical circuit to detect rotation. The researchers say the approach could offer high-precision sensing in a smaller, more durable package.The experimental gyroscope uses silicon nitride, a material compatible with standard CMOS chip-manufacturing processes. Its sensing circuit measures about 24 millimeters across, while the packaged device is only a few centimeters wide.Light detects tiny rotationsThe researchers combined two previously developed technologies: a Brillouin laser gyroscope from Caltech and a low-noise laser-on-a-chip platform developed at UC Santa Barbara with support from the Air Force Research Laboratory.Inside the device, two semiconductor lasers send light in opposite directions around a ring-shaped circuit. Interactions between the light and vibrations in the material generate two stable laser signals.When the device rotates, the frequencies of these signals shift slightly relative to each other. Measuring that difference allows the gyroscope to determine the rotation rate.The ring’s ability to retain light is central to its sensitivity. Its quality factor, a measure of how efficiently an optical resonator stores light, exceeds 163 million.This allows the device to isolate a narrow 2-megahertz bandwidth from an optical signal operating at approximately 200 terahertz. Photons remain inside the resonator for nearly 100 nanoseconds, allowing light to circulate repeatedly.The larger ring also improves sensitivity because optical gyroscopes can detect smaller rotations when the light encloses a greater area.“Our new gyroscope combines several advanced technologies to achieve a high level of sensitivity in a format that can be made with standard CMOS chip-processing methods and uses just milliwatts of optical power,” said Daniel J. Blumenthal, who led the UC Santa Barbara research team.Testing near Earth’s rotationTo evaluate the device, researchers mounted the packaged chip on a piezoelectric rotation stage that moved it back and forth at controlled frequencies.A separate optical interferometer measured the stage’s actual movement, providing a reference against which the gyroscope’s readings could be compared.The sensor produced a linear response and detected rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. That compares with 72,000 degrees per hour measured by the researchers’ earlier silicon nitride Brillouin gyroscope.The improvement demonstrates how low-noise lasers and high-quality optical resonators can increase rotation sensitivity on a photonic chip.However, the new device has not yet demonstrated direct measurement of Earth’s rotation. It also remains a laboratory prototype rather than a fully integrated navigation sensor.Researchers are working to reduce unwanted light scattering, which can affect measurement stability. They also plan to integrate the lasers, photodetectors, and other components into a single compact system before testing it outside the laboratory.The findings were published in Optics Letters.

title: Mayhem 10 drones get upgrade to combine satellite, cellular and radio
content: AeroVironment is preparing to strengthen communications on its Mayhem 10 autonomous military drone system with technology from Australian firm Elsight. The partnership aims to keep the platform connected when military operations disrupt or degrade individual network links.The companies will integrate Elsight’s Halo technology into Mayhem 10. The system combines available communications links into one connection, helping operators maintain control as network conditions change.Halo combines multiple connectionsHalo can bond satellite connectivity with private or public cellular networks. It can also use point-to-point radio links to maintain a communications path when conditions change.The technology automatically adjusts to network availability. If one connection weakens, Halo can use other available links to preserve connectivity. This reduces the need for operators to switch between networks manually. The integration could be particularly valuable for launched effects operating beyond reliable line-of-sight radio coverage, where maintaining a control link becomes more challenging.The approach could prove useful in environments where military forces cannot rely on consistent communications coverage. Terrain may obstruct radio signals, while damaged infrastructure can limit cellular access. Electronic warfare can create additional challenges for systems that depend on wireless links.However, network bonding does not guarantee uninterrupted communications. Its effectiveness depends on which links remain available and how well they perform under operational conditions. The companies have not disclosed test results or quantified Halo’s performance against deliberate electronic interference.Modular design enables upgradesMayhem 10 features an open architecture that allows AeroVironment to incorporate third-party technologies without redesigning the entire platform. Its modular design supports different mission configurations.The system can carry payloads for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Other potential roles include electronic warfare and communications relay. Mayhem 10 also supports precision-strike missions across air, ground, and maritime operations.Halo adds a communications capability to this existing framework. Reliable links could help operators direct the system and receive information when network conditions become unpredictable.Austin Miller, AeroVironment’s vice president and general manager of loitering munition systems, said dependable connectivity remains essential during contested operations.“Mayhem 10 was built to evolve with the mission,” Miller said, pointing to the platform’s open architecture as a way to incorporate new capabilities quickly.The integration could give military users greater flexibility when mission requirements or communications conditions change. Neither company has disclosed specific changes to the platform’s hardware or software for the integration.Integration work is underwayElsight CEO Yoav Amitai said Halo was designed to maintain connectivity as network conditions fluctuate. He said the integration should also reduce the burden on operators managing communications links.The partnership addresses a persistent challenge for remotely operated and autonomous military systems. Even a capable platform can lose effectiveness when its communications links fail.Multiple connections can provide alternative routes for transmitting data. Their usefulness still depends on network availability, signal quality, and the ability to withstand interference.AeroVironment and Elsight are advancing the integration, but neither has announced a completion date. The companies have also not confirmed when the combined capability could enter operational service.

title: Scientists make brain-like device remember and forget using current
content: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have demonstrated a way to control how an experimental electronic device forms and erases memory, using electrical currents to change the behavior of a material called vanadium dioxide.The device, known as a neuristor, mimics certain electrical switching behaviors of biological neurons. The researchers found that they could influence whether its switching became more predictable or returned to a less predictable state.The discovery could help scientists design brain-inspired computing hardware that stores information through changes in its physical structure. Such systems aim to perform some computing and memory functions more efficiently than conventional approaches that move data between separate processors and memory units.Led by physics professor Oleg Shpyrko, the UC San Diego team used coherent X-ray diffraction to observe nanoscale changes inside the material while electrical current passed through the device. This allowed them to investigate how its internal structure affected its switching behavior.Electrical pulses reshape memoryVanadium dioxide can undergo a transition between electrically insulating and conducting states. This change is accompanied by structural changes in the material, making it useful for studying electronic devices that imitate some features of neurons.In the experiments, researchers examined how repeated electrical stimulation affected the arrangement and movement of tiny regions within the material. These regions, called domains, can interact as the device switches between states.The team identified a process known as jamming, in which the movement of these regions becomes increasingly restricted. Rather than behaving independently, their interactions begin to constrain how the material changes.Repeated electrical stimulation above a threshold drove the material toward this jammed state. As a result, the device’s subsequent switching became more predictable, indicating that its earlier electrical activity had influenced its future behavior.The researchers also found that lower-current stimulation could reverse this effect, restoring a less predictable switching state. This provided a way to control the device’s memory-like behavior through electrical inputs.The experiments tracked structural changes over periods lasting thousands of seconds, allowing the researchers to connect the device’s electrical history with changes inside the material.Controlling when memory fadesThe findings offer a physical explanation for how a neuristor can retain information about previous electrical activity without requiring a separate conventional memory component.In this case, learning does not mean that the device understands information or independently solves problems. It refers to a measurable change in switching behavior caused by previous stimulation. Forgetting describes the reversal of that change.This distinction matters for neuromorphic computing, which seeks to build electronic systems inspired by how neurons and synapses process and retain information.A device capable of adjusting its response based on earlier electrical signals could eventually contribute to circuits that combine memory and computation. However, the researchers have demonstrated the mechanism in an experimental material system, not a complete brain-inspired processor.Further work would be needed to determine how reliably the behavior can be controlled across multiple devices, how quickly memory states can be changed and whether the approach delivers measurable energy savings in practical circuits.The research also provides a method for studying how nanoscale structural changes influence electronic switching in materials with coupled structural and electrical transitions.The findings were published in Nature Communications.

title: 80,000-ton aircraft carrier to serve as key vessel of NATO’s naval force
content:
Vessel has secured certification for daytime helicopter operations
The vessel has secured certification for daytime helicopter operations after completing a series of training activities designed to demonstrate the ship’s readiness to support aviation missions at sea. The carrier is expected to hold NATO command ship responsibilities until mid-2027, positioning it to lead a multinational naval force if activated during an international crisis.
HMS Queen Elizabeth departed Belfast today after becoming the first Royal Navy aircraft carrier to visit Northern Ireland’s capital for more than 60 years.
“It has been a huge honour for us to be the first Queen Elizabeth-class carrier to visit Belfast and is a real proof of concept for future visits,”
HMS Queen Elizabeth’s Commanding Officer, Captain Claire Thompson.
“Our visit has highlighted the strong maritime heritage the Royal Navy shares with the community and with industry in the city, and has provided an opportunity for a significant number of my sailors to have their first port visit since joining the ship.  The city’s reaction to having us here has been outstanding; warm and very welcoming, for which we are very grateful.”
It was HMS Centaur in the summer of 1965 that was the last carrier to make the stop in Belfast, the city in which Second World War carriers HMS Eagle and Glorious were built, as well as namesake warship HMS Belfast. Those traditions continue today with the historic Harland & Wolff shipyard playing a central role in building the Royal Fleet Auxiliary’s new Fleet Solid Support ships.
This autumn’s training – split between UK waters and the eastern Atlantic – lays the groundwork for more complex workouts in 2027, including NATO’s Steadfast Defender.
The carrier is NATO’s command ship – the alliance’s crest is emblazoned on her forward island – until mid-2027, and would lead a multinational naval force in a global crisis; a staff has been embarked for the past few weeks getting used to life on board and determining how they would operate if activated.
For the ship’s company, the key task of the autumn is to turn 80,000 tons of military hardware into a working aircraft carrier sbeginning with resuming air operations.
Before the ship could consider hosting any air power, however, crew had to prove they could deal with emergencies: a crash on deck and recovery of a pilot, and, in the bowels of the carrier, a raging inferno with casualties in one of the engine rooms.
Commissioned into the Royal Navy on 7 December 2017, HMS Queen Elizabeth is the lead ship of the Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers. Its construction involved multiple shipyards across the United Kingdom, with sections assembled at Rosyth Dockyard.
The carrier measures approximately 280 metres in length and 73 metres across its flight deck. Its design supports an air group of up to around 40 aircraft, including F-35B fighters and helicopters, depending on the operational configuration.
The United Kingdom operates two carriers of this class: HMS Queen Elizabeth and HMS Prince of Wales. Together, they provide the Royal Navy with a substantial platform for projecting air power, supporting allied operations and responding to emerging security challenges.
The ships also represent a major investment in Britain’s maritime industrial base, drawing on expertise in naval engineering, aviation support and complex warship construction.

title: Used EV batteries get a second life powering hungry data centers
content: Power shortages are becoming a serious obstacle for American manufacturers and data center operators. New grid connections can take years to secure, leaving businesses searching for faster ways to get electricity. Redwood Materials wants to use retired electric vehicle batteries to help close that gap.The company is working with Rivian to install battery storage systems at its manufacturing facilities. The arrangement gives used EV batteries another purpose after they leave vehicles. It also connects battery recovery directly to the growing demand for reliable industrial power.Giving batteries second lifeEV batteries can lose the capacity needed for driving without becoming useless. Some packs retain enough energy storage potential to serve stationary applications, where weight and packaging constraints matter less.Redwood collects used batteries from Rivian and evaluates how to handle them. Packs suitable for another application can support energy storage. Others can go through recycling to recover valuable materials.Rivian already operates a 10-megawatt-hour second-life battery system at its factory in Normal, Illinois. Redwood identifies the installation as the first of its kind at a US automaker’s manufacturing plant.Rivian’s service centers also offer a steady source of batteries removed during maintenance and repairs. Recovering those packs gives Redwood access to materials that might otherwise create additional handling and transportation costs.The arrangement creates a useful link between vehicle servicing and factory power. Batteries returning from the road could eventually help supply the facilities producing new vehicles.Making old batteries workIntegrating retired EV batteries into one dependable power system presents a significant engineering challenge. Packs vary in chemistry and age, and their performance changes with use. A storage system must account for those differences to deliver electricity reliably.Redwood says its battery recovery work provides valuable information about how packs deteriorate over time. Engineers can use that knowledge when deciding how to incorporate different batteries into energy storage systems.The company also develops its own DC-DC converters and control software. These components help manage electrical power across the system, allowing batteries with different characteristics to contribute to a shared installation.Controlling more of the technology could help Redwood avoid some equipment procurement delays. It also gives the company greater flexibility when designing systems for individual customers.Beating the power bottleneckThe opportunity extends well beyond automotive factories. Data centers supporting AI workloads need substantial amounts of electricity, and their operators cannot always wait for grid upgrades to arrive.The challenge involves more than generating electricity. Transformers, inverters, and other electrical equipment can also face lengthy procurement delays. Battery storage offers one way to manage available power, but it cannot replace the need for adequate generation capacity.Redwood plans to combine its battery systems with solar power and other energy sources. The company aims to develop large microgrids that can supply industrial sites and data centers.Such systems could help businesses bring facilities online without relying entirely on new grid connections. Their effectiveness will depend on local power demand, available generation, and the cost of installation.The broader strategy connects battery recovery with a pressing infrastructure problem. Retired EV packs could become part of the equipment helping American industry secure electricity as demand continues to rise.

title: 37-unit robotic material synchronizes itself without external timing
content: Researchers have developed a robotic material that can synchronize the movement of 37 connected units, turning small vibrations into a coordinated rhythm without an external timing signal.The international team built a two-dimensional honeycomb structure containing 37 active units and a separate elastic ring with 24 motorized units. Both structures developed repeating patterns of movement through interactions between their components.The researchers describe the behavior as a form of time crystallization, in which a system develops a repeating pattern in time. Unlike conventional crystals, whose atomic structures repeat in space, these experimental materials also display organized movement over time.The work involved researchers from the universities of Amsterdam, Leiden, Birmingham and other European institutions. It could eventually help engineers develop robotic materials capable of changing shape and coordinating movement without relying on a central controller.Vibrations merge into rhythmThe experimental material combines elastic structures, sensors, electronics and actuators. Actuators convert electrical energy into physical movement, allowing individual components to move and influence their neighbors.The researchers designed the interactions to be nonreciprocal. This means that when one component influences another, the second does not necessarily produce an equal response in return.That difference proved important. In the honeycomb structure, individual units initially oscillated at approximately 30 hertz, or 30 times per second. Over time, the vibrations combined into larger patterns, with longer wavelengths and periods, until the structure moved collectively.The researchers call this process “wave coarsening.” Instead of requiring an external signal to synchronize each component, the system develops an organized rhythm through the interactions built into the material.The team also tested a ring-shaped structure containing 24 motorized units. Higher-frequency deformation patterns initially appeared around the ring before gradually merging into larger movements. Eventually, the ring settled into a slower, repeating cycle.The experiments showed that the collective patterns could remain stable despite random disturbances. The researchers also used mathematical modeling to examine how the ordered movement behaves as the size of the system increases.Materials coordinate their movementsThe findings suggest a possible approach to building robotic structures that coordinate their movements through their physical design rather than through instructions issued to every component.“Our research provides a striking example of spontaneous organization—tiny vibrations organizing themselves until an entire material moves in a coordinated way,” said Jack Binysh, a co-lead author from the University of Birmingham.The experimental structures incorporated more than 100 sensors and actuators, along with 3D-printed components and custom-built Lorentz actuators that use electromagnetic forces to generate mechanical motion.Researchers envision future materials that could switch between different stable movement patterns. Such structures might eventually change shape or move in different directions without requiring separate mechanical systems for every function.However, the experiments demonstrated coordinated oscillations, not a robot capable of performing multiple practical tasks. The researchers have yet to demonstrate controlled switching between different movement modes for useful robotic operations.The team plans to investigate three-dimensional structures that could support more complex movements, including bending, twisting, and shearing. The findings were published in the journal Nature.

title: Scientists develop novel route to produce nanoporous ceramic materials
content: A team of Japanese researchers has obtained Silicon Carbide (SiC) crystals at approximately 1,472 °F, two-fold less than the temperatures at which commercial production begins.​Typically, in an industrial setup, the purest form of SiC is obtained at temperatures reaching 4,500 °F. However, at such high processing temperatures, formation and control of its porous structure at the nanometer scale becomes a challenge.​Scientists at the Institute for Materials Research (IMR) at Tohoku University circumvented the problem.​Low temp LMD forms SiC crystalsUsing the age-old technique of liquid metal dealloying (LMD) under milder thermal conditions (1,472 °F), they generated SiC nanomaterial crystals with a distinct porous architecture.​In LMD, a solid precursor is dipped into multiple molten metals for selectively remove a specific element.​”LMD is a method that has been previously applied mainly to metals, intermetallic compounds, and semimetals, but our research expands the scope to strongly covalently bonded ceramics,” said Hidemi Kato, professor at the Institute for Materials Research, Tohoku University. ​Researchers took molten bismuth and immersed Mn5SiC, a layered solid precursor, into this liquid bath. They discovered that Manganese melted away and got mixed with the molten metal, while the Solid SiC precursor rearranged to form crystalline β-SiC.​3-D nanoscale platesThe newly formed structure comprises nanoscale plates that were interconnected in the three-dimensional space.​The findings were recently published in Scripta Materialia, showing that first-principles energy calculations confirmed the stability of the framework obtained by this innovative technique.​Scientists proposed that the layered crystal structure of the precursor may have influenced the formation of the nanoplate architecture. However, they cautioned that further studies would be needed to ascertain the role of precursor structure in the growth and crystallographic orientation of the nanoplates.Expressing hope from the modified LMD method, Kato in a statement said, “We think this approach could provide an exciting new strategy for designing nanoporous ceramics.”​The method adopted by Japanese researchers is likely to benefit the silicon carbide industry in the USA, which was valued at $1.80 billion in 2025, projected to reach $1.93 billion in 2026, according to a report published last year.​Much like a heavy-duty electric truck, it can handle much higher voltages, temperatures, and power with less energy loss and is one of the most critical semiconductor materials that powers modern electronics.​From powering AI data centers to improving electric-vehicle battery efficiency, Silicon carbide is a widely adopted material. ​In an earlier study, scientists made significant progress in exploring ways of substantially enhancing the design of silicon carbide power devices that are slated for use in electric vehicles, trains, and many other vehicles.​With the expanding use of silicon carbide, including in robotics, defense, electric vehicles, solar power plants, renewable energy, and battery storage systems, experts have estimated its market to grow at an approximate 7.1% Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) and reach up to  $3.83 billion over the next decade.​
