title: New 360-degree air defense radar offers 205-mile detection range
content: Leonardo DRS has launched its new cxMHR radar and begun initial production of the system, which is designed to help military forces detect and track drones, cruise missiles, rockets, and other aerial threats as part of integrated air and missile defense networks.The company announced the milestone at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 12. The radar is intended to provide continuous 360-degree coverage while combining long-range detection, target tracking, and a transportable configuration in a single system.Called the C-Band Extended Multi-Mission Hemispheric Radar, or cxMHR, the system uses four active electronically scanned array (AESA) panels integrated with identification friend-or-foe (IFF) equipment, command-and-control components, and supporting hardware.The entire assembly is housed in an International Organization for Standardization (ISO) container, allowing Leonardo DRS to transport it by air, land, or sea and deploy it on a single vehicle.Radar designed to track multiple aerial threatsThe cxMHR is designed to detect, track, and identify multiple aerial targets simultaneously, including unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), loitering munitions, cruise missiles, rockets, and tactical ballistic missiles.Leonardo DRS reports detection ranges exceeding 90 kilometers (56 miles) against UAS and loitering munitions, and more than 330 kilometers (205 miles) against transport aircraft. These figures apply to different target categories; the company has not provided equivalent range figures for every threat listed.The radar uses C-band radio frequencies and a digital AESA architecture. Unlike a conventional mechanically rotating radar antenna, an AESA system electronically directs its radar beams, enabling it to scan and revisit areas of interest without relying on physical antenna rotation.This approach supports rapid updates to target tracks, an important capability when monitoring multiple aerial threats that may be moving at different speeds and altitudes.The cxMHR also incorporates AI-enabled tracking and classification, which the company says helps produce what is known as fire-control-quality tracking. In air defense, this refers to sufficiently precise and timely target information to support the systems responsible for engaging a threat. The radar itself is a sensor, not an interceptor.Built to integrate with existing air defensesLeonardo DRS says the cxMHR is designed to meet Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) standards. This approach uses standardized interfaces and modular components to make it easier to integrate equipment from different manufacturers and upgrade systems over time.The radar supports interfaces including FAAD, Medusa, SAPIENT, Lattice, ASTERIX, MICAD, and RAFT, among others, according to the company.Such interoperability matters because modern integrated air and missile defense relies on multiple layers of sensors, command systems, and weapons rather than a single radar or interceptor operating independently. A radar that can share information with existing networks can help commanders build a broader picture of incoming threats and coordinate responses.Leonardo DRS already markets a family of Multi-Mission Hemispheric Radar systems for missions including counter-drone operations, very-short-range air defense, and hemispheric surveillance. The cxMHR adds a C-band variant specifically positioned for integrated air and missile defense.“The cxMHR gives our customers a deployable, single-vehicle capability that delivers persistent 360-degree surveillance, long-range detection, and fire-control-quality tracking against today’s most challenging air threats,” said Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager of Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies.The company is displaying the radar alongside its wider Multi-Mission Hemispheric Radar family at AUSA Annual 2026, which runs through October 14. The start of initial production marks a manufacturing milestone for the cxMHR, but Leonardo DRS has not disclosed production quantities, customer orders, delivery schedules, or a timeline for operational deployment in its announcement.

title: 3D-printed US mandrel dissolves in water to make hydrogen storage tanks
content: Scientists have created a new 3D-printed mold that dissolved in water to produce linerless, lightweight tanks for storying hydrogen in addition to other gases under high pressure. The mold, also known as mandrel, was designed by a group of researchers at the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). As part of the project, the team worked together with aerospace firm Infinite Composites, additive manufacturing company JuggerBot 3D, and Oklahoma State University. Ahmed Arabi Hassen, PhD, who led the project, revealed that the technology uses a specially tailored water-soluble polymer to create the mandrels. These are then used to manufacture Type V composite pressure vessels. These vessels are entirely made from composite materials. They also do not need a permanent internal liner. On top of that, they can store hydrogen, compressed natural gas, nitrogen, and helium for the aerospace, defense, transportation, and energy industries. A water-soluble mandrelLightweight gas storage tanks can be difficult to produce especially when creating and removing the internal molds used to shape them. Engineers rely on expensive metal molds or complex tools that must be disassembled before removal.Hassen discussed the significance of Type V composite pressure vessels, and their potential. “Type V linerless composite pressure vessels represent the next frontier in lightweight, high-pressure gas storage, but their manufacturing remains extremely challenging, particularly when it comes to producing and removing complex internal tooling,” he added. A lightweight Type V composite pressure vessel for high-pressure gas storage. Credit: Logan Korn / ORNL, U.S. Dept. of EnergyTo tackle the challenge and create a temporary mandrel, the researchers turned to large-format additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing. They used a specially formulated polymer that can dissolve in water, which serves to print the mold in the desired shape of the tank. The engineers then wound carbon fiber around the mandrel to create the vessel’s outer structure. Once the composite material cured, they dissolved the temporary mold in water. As a result, the team designed a hollow carbon-fiber tank without a permanent internal liner. They then applied a gas-barrier coating to the vessel.Making gas tanks lighterThe research team pointed out that the technology does not require complicated mechanical systems to remove the internal tooling. It can also eliminate the need for solvents during mold removal, and simplify the production of large pressure vessels. Hassen explained that the method could also ensure high dimensional accuracy. “Our water-soluble, 3D-printed mandrels represent an important step toward overcoming this barrier and enabling scalable, cost-effective manufacturing of Type V vessels,” he continued. The design also reduces the tanks’ overall weight and prevents problems caused by permanent internal liners. Additionally, replacing conventional metal tooling with 3D-printed molds could cut manufacturing complexity, shorten production times, and lower costs.This could be useful for industries that require lightweight gas storage systems capable of operating under high pressure. “This achievement demonstrates how advanced manufacturing and strong industry partnerships can help bring these technologies closer to commercial reality,” Hassen concluded in a press release.The team carried out its research at the Department of Energy’s Manufacturing Demonstration Facility. The project was backed by the DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation.

title: NASA battery survives -274°F cold in test for future Moon missions
content: NASA has tested a solid-state battery that survived temperatures as low as minus 274 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 170 Celsius) without damage, a step toward developing power systems for future missions to the Moon’s South Pole.The prototype cells also operated at temperatures as low as minus 112 F (minus 80 C), although with reduced performance. NASA said the batteries worked well between minus 76 F (minus 60 C) and 176 F (80 C) during recent thermal vacuum testing.The results come from NASA’s Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS) project, which is developing batteries capable of surviving the Moon’s extreme temperature changes without requiring continuous heating.The technology could eventually power lunar rovers, scientific instruments and emergency equipment used by astronauts under NASA’s Artemis program. However, the batteries remain small laboratory prototypes and have not yet been demonstrated in space.Surviving extreme lunar temperaturesTemperatures near the Moon’s South Pole can fall to minus 328 F (minus 200 C). Such conditions present a major challenge for conventional lithium-ion batteries, which depend on liquid electrolytes to transport charged particles between electrodes.These liquids can freeze in extreme cold, while excessive heat can affect battery performance. Exposure to the vacuum of space also creates problems for conventional liquid-based systems.NASA’s SPEARS batteries instead use solid ceramic- or polymer-based electrolytes. The design aims to improve resistance to temperature extremes while reducing the fire hazards associated with flammable liquid electrolytes.Researchers conducted thermal vacuum tests at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Virginia to examine how the prototype cells performed under conditions relevant to lunar operations.“We proved for the first time that these cells can work down to minus 80 degrees Celsius,” said Yi Lin, SPEARS testing and research lead at NASA Langley.The tests also showed that the cells could withstand exposure to temperatures ranging from 212 F (100 C) to minus 274 F without sustaining damage.However, the batteries cannot generate power at the lowest temperature tested. Instead, they must be warmed to an operating temperature before use.Less heating between missionsThis ability to survive deep cold without continuous heating could reduce the need for heavy thermal management equipment aboard lunar spacecraft and rovers.Small heaters could bring the batteries back to operating temperature when power is needed, rather than keeping them warm throughout the lunar night.NASA researchers are also exploring different electrode materials to adjust the batteries’ energy capacity, power output, and durability for specific applications.The SPEARS project began in 2026 with funding from NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Ohio leads the effort, while Langley researchers are conducting materials development and testing.NASA’s Ames Research Center in California is developing test boards and electronics to help prepare the technology for future spaceflight testing.The agency sees potential applications beyond lunar exploration, including aircraft, drones, vehicles, and portable electronic devices. However, further development and testing will be required before the batteries are ready for operational use.

title: Agile bicycle robot hops sideways, jumps, and performs front flips
content: Researchers have developed a bicycle-inspired robot capable of performing acrobatic maneuvers while maintaining balance at high speeds.The Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV) uses a moving reaction mass to control its stability and execute complex movements. The robot can perform jumps, wheelies, flips, and other maneuvers inspired by mountain biking and trials cycling. The researchers trained the machine using reinforcement learning, enabling it to navigate obstacles and perform dynamic movements.Robot bicycle jumpsResearchers at the Robotics and AI Institute (RAI Institute) have developed the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle-based robot designed to combine fast wheeled movement with the agility of legged machines. The 51-pound (23.5-kilogram) robot can drive at speeds of up to 8 meters per second (18 mph), balance on its rear wheel, hop sideways, perform wheelies, and execute front flips. Its design uses a movable reaction mass and reinforcement learning to achieve these maneuvers with just five actuated degrees of freedom (DoF), reducing mechanical complexity compared with conventional legged robots.The UMV consists of three main structural components: a head, a neck, and a bicycle frame. Unlike conventional bicycles, its head houses most of the robot’s mass, including its computing hardware, batteries, and powerful jumping actuators. A spatial linkage connecting the head to the bicycle frame allows the robot to shift its mass and change its orientation during movement.The linkage consists of the neck and two tie rods, which work together to control the head’s position relative to the bicycle. Two actuators drive the primary movement, while another pair works through the tie rods to enable lateral motion. These mechanisms help the robot generate the forces needed for jumping and maintain balance when operating on a single wheel.Two additional actuators control steering and rear-wheel drive, enabling conventional bicycle-like movement. The complete system uses five actuated degrees of freedom, allowing it to perform a range of dynamic maneuvers without reaction wheels, kickstands, or other dedicated static stabilization mechanisms.AI-powered robot acrobaticsThe researchers used reinforcement learning (RL) to train the UMV to perform different movements in simulation before transferring the learned control policies to the physical robot. The training process used NVIDIA Isaac Laboratory and the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm.During training, the simulation varied parameters such as mass distribution, friction, motor strength, control delays, and sensor noise. This domain randomization was intended to help the learned policies handle differences between simulated and real-world conditions.The researchers developed four main control policies for driving, wheelies and hopping, flipping, and jumping. The policies control the robot’s joint movements through lower-level proportional-derivative controllers. The resulting behaviors transferred from simulation to hardware without additional training.The robot can maintain balance while moving forward or backward, turn in place around its rear wheel, and perform track stands with minimal movement. During rear-wheel hopping, it can move laterally in different directions, overcoming the directional limitations of conventional wheeled platforms.In one experiment, the UMV autonomously approached a 1-meter-high platform, jumped onto it, drove across the surface, and jumped down. It repeated the sequence 15 times, demonstrating consistent jump trajectories during ascent.The robot also performed front flips by jumping and drawing its body into a tighter configuration. This movement reduces its rotational inertia, allowing it to spin faster. During the maneuver, its pitch angular velocity reached approximately 17 radians per second, and the robot completed the rotation and landed in less than half a second.The researchers tested the system in a laboratory using motion-capture equipment to improve state estimation. Future development will focus on more robust hardware, improved batteries and motor drivers, and onboard sensing that reduces reliance on external motion-capture systems. The team sees potential applications in urban delivery and long-distance reconnaissance across rough terrain, where speed, maneuverability, and obstacle clearance are important.

title: OpenAI alleges ex-employee took 100 files before Apple product pitch
content: OpenAI has accused a former employee of taking confidential product information to Apple after transferring approximately 100 files to a personal account. A new court filing alleges that the employee later presented details about an unreleased OpenAI product to a senior Apple executive.The allegations add another layer to a growing trade secrets dispute between the two technology companies. OpenAI claims Apple could use the information to guide its own hardware development, raising questions about how companies protect proprietary engineering work during recruitment.OpenAI raises product secrecy concernsAccording to Reuters, the filing was submitted in San Jose, California. OpenAI alleges that the presentation occurred months ago and claims Apple’s recent release of its Home View product adds to its concerns.The company warned that confidential material could already be circulating among Apple’s engineering teams. OpenAI said it was “very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple.”The filing argues that access to such information could give Apple’s engineers insight into OpenAI’s upcoming products. However, the allegations do not establish that Apple used any allegedly misappropriated material to develop Home View.Apple rejected OpenAI’s claims. The company said it maintains procedures to prevent new hires from using confidential information belonging to previous employers. Apple also said it has found no evidence supporting OpenAI’s allegations.Neither the product presentation nor the alleged file transfer independently establishes that Apple misused trade secrets. The dispute will require the parties to substantiate their competing claims through the legal process.Apple expands access to recordsThe new allegations intersect with a lawsuit Apple filed against OpenAI in July. Apple accused former employees of taking proprietary information from the iPhone maker to OpenAI’s consumer hardware division.OpenAI has denied those accusations. Apple alleges that some departing employees downloaded confidential files using company laptops and brought knowledge of unannounced technologies into their new roles.The dispute also concerns how OpenAI recruited former Apple employees for its consumer hardware and robotics teams. Apple claims some recruits received guidance about presenting information from their previous jobs during interviews.A federal judge has granted Apple expedited access to certain OpenAI hiring records. The materials include interview guides, technical presentations, and documents that could reveal discussions about Apple technologies or components.U.S. District Judge Edward Davila also approved depositions for three former Apple employees. They include OpenAI chief hardware officer Tang Yew Tan, along with employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.Hardware ambitions raise stakesOpenAI’s hardware ambitions help explain why the dispute extends beyond employee departures. The company is developing a consumer device that could eventually compete with smartphones if it becomes a central way for people to access software and services.Apple’s legal requests seek information that could clarify whether OpenAI’s recruitment process featured Apple’s proprietary technology. However, the judge rejected several broader requests, including expedited access to OpenAI’s hardware research and development work on specific engineering areas.Those denied requests covered subjects such as metal finishes and power management. The court also declined to grant Apple broader access to OpenAI’s hardware research and information about work former Apple employees performed after joining OpenAI.The proceedings now put employee mobility, confidential engineering knowledge, and product development under scrutiny. Both companies face the challenge of proving their claims as they compete for talent and pursue new hardware opportunities.

title: Lake Powell Just Hit Its Lowest Level Ever
content:
Lake Powell stood at one of its highest levels in the past decade on September 1, 2017, in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin
Snow drought and record warmth have pushed Lake Powell to its lowest level on record, deepening pressure on the Colorado River system.
Snow drought and exceptional warmth across the Colorado Basin in 2026 helped push water storage in major Western reservoirs to historic lows.
Satellite Images Show Lake Powell’s Dramatic Decline
Satellite images captured a striking comparison between Lake Powell in 2017 and 2026. The images show an area just upstream from Glen Canyon Dam as seen by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the NASA USGS Landsat 8 satellite on September 1, 2017 (above), and September 10, 2026 (below).
When the 2026 image was acquired, Lake Powell’s water elevation measured 3,517.24 feet. Roughly a month earlier, the reservoir had already fallen below the previous record low of 3,519.92 feet, which was set on April 13, 2023. Water levels continued declining into early September. By contrast, the 2017 image captures Lake Powell during one of its highest water levels of the past decade.
Lake Powell stood at a record low on September 10, 2026, in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin
The Colorado River flows into Lake Powell before continuing downstream toward Lake Mead. Lake Mead also reached record low levels in August 2026.
The river system, managed by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) and other agencies, is critical to the Southwest. It supplies water and electricity to more than 40 million people, including residents of Las Vegas, Phoenix, Los Angeles, and San Diego. It also provides irrigation water for about 5 million acres of farmland.
A Snow Drought Starved the Colorado River
Because much of the Colorado Basin is arid or semi arid, snow in the surrounding mountains serves as an important natural water reservoir. A substantial share of the Colorado River’s water begins as snow that accumulates at high elevations before melting during spring and early summer.
During winter 2025-2026, however, the Upper Colorado Basin received unusually little snow. Similar conditions affected mountainous regions across the U.S. West, creating what scientists call a snow drought.
Periods of record warmth made the situation worse by further reducing the snowpack. When spring arrived, there was far less snow available to melt and flow into rivers and reservoirs. As a result, the seasonal runoff that normally helps replenish Lake Powell provided relatively little relief.
Officials Move Water to Protect Hydropower
The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation began taking action in April 2026 to
stabilize Lake Powell
. Without intervention, the agency warned that the reservoir could fall below the elevation required for hydropower generation as early as August 2026.
To help maintain water levels, USBR began sending additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir in northern Utah and southern Wyoming into Lake Powell.
Officials also reduced the amount of water being released from Lake Powell toward Lake Mead. Other planned water releases were altered as well. The agency
canceled
a “controlled flood” planned for April that was intended to rebuild sandbars used as fish habitat. It also skipped a “cool mix” release in August that had been designed to help protect native species.
Decades of Drought Continue to Strain the Southwest
The latest reservoir decline comes against the backdrop of a much longer water shortage.
Drought in the U.S. Southwest
has persisted since around the beginning of the 21st century. Researchers have described the prolonged dry period as a
megadrought
Those conditions continue to put enormous pressure on the Colorado River system and the communities, farms, ecosystems, and power infrastructure that depend on it.
NASA-supported projects are helping water managers better understand changing conditions across the basin. Many combine satellite observations with ground measurements and computer modeling to track drought, snow, soil moisture, and water storage.
At the headwaters of the Colorado River, a dashboard built around the Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS) provides current visualizations of soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and evapotranspiration. The information helps support Colorado’s drought task force and contributes to weekly
U.S. Drought Monitor
NASA Tools Track Drought Across the Basin
Closer to Lake Powell, the
Drought Severity Evaluation Tool
, developed in collaboration with the
Navajo Nation
, allows leaders to track local drought indicators, changes in precipitation, and vegetation health across tribal lands. (With funding from NOAA’s
National Integrated Drought Information System
, its adoption expanded to Oklahoma’s Chickasaw and Choctaw Nations in 2025.)
Researchers at Arizona State University, in partnership with the Central Arizona Project, created another resource: the Colorado River Integrated Assessment tool. It brings together improved modeling and information validated with NASA satellite observations in a single interactive platform.
The system includes data on snowpack, surface water,
groundwater
storage,
soil moisture
, and other conditions across the Colorado River Basin, giving decision-makers a broader view of how water supplies are changing throughout the region.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the
U.S. Geological Survey
and lake elevation data from the
U.S. Bureau of Reclamation

title: For Decades, the Arctic Melt Season Kept Growing. Then It Stopped
content:
The Arctic melt season lengthened dramatically for decades, but its average duration has barely changed since around 2010. Scientists think changing clouds and increasingly thin sea ice may be behind the shift, though the pause could prove temporary. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison based on data from Boisvert, L., et al.
For much of the satellite record, the Arctic sea ice melt season kept getting longer. Then, around 2010, that long-running trend unexpectedly flattened.
Over several decades, Arctic sea ice generally began melting earlier in the spring and refreezing later in the fall. That extended the time each year when ice was melting and contributed to major reductions in sea ice across the Arctic. A new NASA-led study now shows that while the melt season has lengthened dramatically since satellite monitoring began, its average duration has changed relatively little since about 2010.
Arctic Melt Season Is Now About 40 Days Longer
The researchers found that the Arctic sea ice melt season is now approximately 40 days longer than it was in 1979.
Most of that increase occurred before 2010. Since then, the average length of the melt season has remained fairly steady, even though conditions can still differ substantially from one year to the next.
To track the change, researchers analyzed satellite observations spanning 1979 through 2023. They identified when sea ice began to melt each spring and when freezing resumed in the fall.
Their analysis showed that the longer melt season was caused primarily by later fall freeze-up, rather than by a major shift toward much earlier spring melting.
“Previously, there was more of this multiyear ice that didn’t melt away each summer,” said Linette Boisvert, a co-author on the study and ice scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “Now that the ice is thinner and there’s less of it, there’s a lot more variability.”
On average, however, the rapid decline in Arctic sea ice thickness and extent that characterized the 2000s appears to have paused for the time being.
Since the start of the satellite record, the Arctic sea ice melt season has lengthened in most decades, particularly in the 2000s. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison based on data from Boisvert, L., et al.
Why the Arctic Melt Trend Slowed
To understand what may have caused the change, the researchers examined the Arctic’s energy balance. This describes the difference between the heat entering the region from the Sun, atmosphere, and ocean and the infrared energy escaping back into space.
During the 2000s, rapid losses of sea ice exposed larger areas of dark ocean water. Bright ice reflects much of the Sun’s energy, while darker seawater absorbs more of it.
That additional stored heat helped keep the ocean warmer later into the year, delaying fall freeze-up and extending the melt season.
In the left map above, the darkest red areas identify places where the melt season increased most rapidly during that decade. In some locations, it lengthened by as much as 5 days per year.
At the same time, the Arctic ice cover itself was undergoing a major transformation. Much of the sea ice that remains today is younger and thinner than the multiyear ice that once covered a much larger share of the Arctic Ocean. Thinner ice reacts more strongly to short-term changes in clouds, storms, and winds.
Since 2010, the melt season appears to have stabilized. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison based on data from Boisvert, L., et al.
Changing Clouds Are Influencing Arctic Sea Ice
Since 2010, shifts in cloud patterns have reduced the amount of sunlight reaching certain parts of the Arctic Ocean.
Researchers say that change has contributed to a melt season that still fluctuates considerably from year to year but has shown relatively little long-term change over the past decade or more.
The right map above illustrates that shift. Lighter reds and blues represent much smaller rates of change during that period.
The findings do not suggest that climate change has stopped reshaping the Arctic.
The region continues to warm nearly four times faster than the global average, and the remaining sea ice is far thinner than it was several decades ago.
Instead, the study suggests that the Arctic may have entered a different stage, with year-to-year weather conditions now playing a larger role in determining the duration of the melt season.
“Melt season length is much more dependent on atmospheric effects,” Boisvert said. “They seem to be playing a bigger role because the ice is generally thinner and more vulnerable to begin with.”
The Current Pause Could Be Temporary
Researchers caution that the recent leveling off may not continue indefinitely.
Thick Arctic sea ice still survives year-round in areas north of Greenland and around the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.
If that remaining thick ice continues to thin, the Arctic could move into another period of rapid sea ice loss. Such a shift could cause the melt season to begin lengthening again.
For now, the findings highlight the importance of continued satellite monitoring of Arctic sea ice, as well as the energy balance that controls how the ice forms, melts, and refreezes.
Scientists still do not know whether the recent stabilization represents a lasting shift in the Arctic melt season or only a temporary pause before another period of rapid change.
Reference: “A recent stabilization in the lengthening of the Arctic sea ice melt season into a highly variable regime” by Linette Boisvert, Chelsea Parker, Elina Valkonen and Rachel Tilling, 23 April 2026,
Communications Earth & Environment
DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-03534-8

title: Scientists Discover a Mysterious Giant Deep-Sea Creature Hiding in Plain Sight for 40 Years
content:
Underside of the exoskeleton of the newly discovered giant isopod species Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis, showing several pairs of legs. Credit: Julie Klaess
A newly identified giant isopod species offers clues to how these deep-sea crustaceans spread around the world, including a possible return to the Americas via Antarctica.
A giant crustacean brought from Puerto Rico to Germany as a teaching specimen has turned out to belong to a species unknown to science. Tübingen paleontologist Professor Dolf Seilacher (1925–2014) acquired the animal at a research station in Puerto Rico in the 1980s. The dried specimen, rediscovered in storage at the University of Tübingen’s Paleontological Collection, represents a species still living today.
Paleontology student and isopod expert Benedikt Kästle and the collection’s curator, PD Dr. Ingmar Werneburg of the university’s Senckenberg Center for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment, examined the animal using advanced imaging techniques. They identified it as a new species of giant isopod and compared its anatomy with that of other giant isopods around the world.
Rear view of the exoskeleton of the newly-discovered giant isopod species Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis. Credit: Julie Klaess
Deep-sea giants that resemble woodlice
These marine crustaceans resemble the much smaller woodlice found in caves and damp basements. Their bodies are armored with an exoskeleton made of calcium-rich, scale-like segments. Members of their genus,
Bathynomus
, inhabit all the world’s oceans, living as omnivores at depths reaching 2,500 meters, or about 8,200 feet. They can grow up to 50 centimeters, or nearly 20 inches, long and weigh several kilograms, placing them among the largest invertebrates.
“Our Tübingen specimen from Puerto Rico, measuring 32.2 centimeters in length, falls into the category of ‘colossogiants’,” says Kästle.
The researchers named the species
Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis
, combining a reference to their university town with Boríken, the Indigenous Taíno name for Puerto Rico. Werneburg points to the discovery as evidence of the value of natural history collections as global archives of nature. Their study and species description, published in
Scientific Reports
, are expected to help scientists understand the broader evolution of deep-sea isopods.
Mouth parts of the newly-discovered giant isopod species Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis. Credit: Julie Klaess
When Panama was a seaway
To investigate that history, Kästle and Werneburg carried out a phylogenetic analysis, reconstructing evolutionary relationships among species. Their results suggest that
Bathynomus
originated in what is now the Gulf of Mexico during the Miocene, more than 15 million years ago. The route out of that region was different from the geography familiar today.
“At that time, the Isthmus of Panama was open, leaving a strait between North and South America, and the marine animals were able to spread westward, initially as far as Japan,” says Werneburg.
Researcher Ingmar Werneburg (left) and Benedikt Kästle in the Tübingen Palaeontological Collection archive, with Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis surrounded by fossil crabs. Credit: Julie Klaess
As they spread through the Indian and Pacific Oceans, the isopods diversified into many new species. “This gave rise to the so-called ‘giant’ isopods that are up to 15 centimeters long, and the ‘supergiants’ with a body length of more than 15 centimeters,” adds Kästle. Their expansion also took them to Australia and East Africa, and, before the collision of the Arabian and African continental plates, to Europe, where they became extinct at the end of the Miocene.
Colossogiants emerge as Earth cools
A distinct group emerged in the Indo-Pacific as Earth cooled at the boundary between the Miocene and Pliocene epochs, 5.333 million years ago. “These veritable colossi grew to more than 25.2 centimeters in length and were physiologically perfectly adapted to the new climatic conditions,” says Werneburg.
The researchers propose that these larger isopods spread from Australia via Antarctica to South and Central America. There, they encountered smaller, more distantly related isopods whose ancestors had remained behind during the genus’s original westward expansion. The Puerto Rican specimen belongs to this larger group, and its anatomical relationships connect it to another species in the region.
“The new species is very closely related to another giant species found off the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico,” Kästle says.
Reference: “A new Caribbean species of the giant isopod genus Bathynomus (Crustacea, Isopoda, Cirolanidae) with notes on its evolutionary history” by Ingmar Werneburg, and Benedikt Kästle, 8 October 2026,
Scientific Reports
DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-69097-y

title: What’s Really Inside Breast Milk? Scientists Discover 7 Molecules Linked to How Babies Grow
content:
Scientists analyzing human milk from diverse populations identified seven molecules linked to maternal nutrition, infant growth, and the biology of milk production. Credit: Shutterstock
Seven molecules in human milk could help explain how a mother’s nutrition connects with her baby’s growth, offering a window into the biology of milk production.
Human milk contains thousands of nutrients, metabolites, proteins, immune factors, and other molecules, yet researchers have often studied those components one at a time. Much remains unknown about how the gland that produces milk shapes this mixture and how differences in its composition relate to infant growth.
The mammary gland prepares for milk production during pregnancy, undergoing hormonal changes that guide cell specialization, tissue and immune remodeling, and metabolic programming. Lactation becomes the main expression of that preparation after delivery. Like the placenta during pregnancy, the gland then serves as an interface between mother and child, connecting maternal biology and nutrition with the developing infant.
“Human milk gives us a rare, non-invasive window into the biology of the lactating mammary gland,” said Liat Shenhav, PhD, the study’s senior author and an assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, with appointments in the Institute for Systems Genetics, the Department of Microbiology, and the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. “By looking at molecular patterns across diverse populations, we can begin to identify shared features of mammary function and understand how maternal nutritional and metabolic state relates to milk composition and infant growth.”
Nutrition changes some milk components
The study is one of two complementary papers published in
“Human milk gives us a rare, noninvasive window into the biology of the lactating mammary gland,” said Liat Shenhav, PhD, senior author of the study. Credit: NYU Langone
For the NYU-led analysis, researchers integrated measurements of metabolites, proteins, micronutrients such as vitamins, macronutrients such as carbohydrates, and human milk oligosaccharides, a group of complex sugars. This approach, called multi-omics, examines several types of molecules together to build a fuller picture of a biological system. The team analyzed these measurements alongside infant growth data using computational tools, including machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence.
In two randomized nutritional trials, maternal supplementation promoted recovery or stability in growth among infants at higher risk of poor growth. The molecular analyses also revealed a shared pattern in milk composition associated with both supplementation and infant growth.
The companion study examined which milk components could be changed through maternal nutrition. It found that supplementation during lactation increased several B vitamins in milk, while many other components remained comparatively stable.
“The studies show that human milk is neither fixed nor simply a reflection of what a mother eats,” said Shenhav. “Some components respond to maternal nutrition, while others remain stable or appear to reflect broader biological states within the mammary gland. Understanding that distinction is essential if we want to design interventions that meaningfully support maternal and infant health.”
Seven molecular clues to mammary function
Mammary cells make and release milk components, while an epithelial barrier regulates what passes between the bloodstream and milk. Tissue remodeling reshapes the milk-producing tissue, and immune and repair processes protect the gland and help it recover from stress or injury. The researchers mapped milk’s molecular patterns onto these interconnected functions.
Seven molecules contributed most consistently to the patterns associated with maternal nutritional status and infant growth. Four were short-chain acylcarnitines, called C2, C3, C4, and C5, which help cells process nutrients for energy. The remaining three were the amino acid lysine, the complex sugar 6′ sialyllactose, a human milk oligosaccharide, and the mineral selenium. Together, these candidate biomarkers captured complementary aspects of mammary function, extending beyond established measures of blood-milk barrier permeability, or how readily substances cross that barrier.
The acylcarnitines showed the strongest links across the gland’s different functions, particularly C5. Higher C5 levels were associated with molecular signatures of reduced milk synthesis and with patterns related to tissue remodeling and immune activity.
A possible vitamin B5 bottleneck
C5’s prominence prompted the researchers to examine how maternal nutrition might influence acylcarnitine levels. Acylcarnitine metabolism depends on coenzyme A, or CoA, a molecule central to energy and fat metabolism. The body makes CoA from pantothenic acid, better known as vitamin B5. Drawing on this established biology and associations across the cohorts, the researchers proposed that too little available vitamin B5 may restrict CoA-dependent metabolism and alter acylcarnitine profiles, potentially allowing C5 to accumulate.
“Our findings demonstrate the intimate link between maternal nutrition, metabolic health and mammary function, highlighting the importance of an integrative approach to supporting maternal and infant health,” said first author Dr. April Jauhal of the Shenhav lab at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “One plausible route linking maternal nutrition to mammary metabolism in our data is via the pantothenic-CoA-C5 metabolic pathway, and we are currently investigating the functional role of this pathway in mammary biology and lactation.”
The Shenhav Lab is developing a framework that combines computational and experimental work to test potential nutritional bottlenecks that may constrain mammary metabolism and milk production. These include the proposed pathway involving vitamin B5, coenzyme A, and C5.
“Ultimately, we want to understand milk in the context of the biology that produces it,” said Shenhav. “The mammary gland sits at a critical interface between maternal physiology and the developing infant. By understanding how maternal metabolism influences mammary function and milk composition, we can begin to uncover the biological pathways linking maternal nutritional status with infant growth.”
Milk can be collected repeatedly without invasive procedures, allowing researchers to follow mammary biology over time. The lab is also studying colostrum, the earliest milk, and transitional milk, which precedes mature milk. Researchers want to understand how mammary functional states emerge during the transition from pregnancy to mature lactation, and whether early molecular changes in milk reflect the development of the gland’s metabolic, barrier, and secretory functions.
Reference: “Shared patterns of human milk composition link mammary gland function to infant growth” by April Jauhal, Bianca Cordazzo-Vargas, Daniel Sunko, Pratima Niroula, Lishi Deng, Laeticia Celine Toe, Ameer Muhammad, Aneela Pasha, Yasir Shafiq, Naveed Iqbal, Waqasuddin Khan, Andrew Mertens, Kelsey Fehr, Joann M. McDermid, Melissa B. Manus, Chi-Hung Shu, Daniela Hampel, Setareh Shahab-Ferdows, Megan R. Beggs, Kim A. Lagerborg, Mohit Jain, Carl Lachat, Mark D. DeBoer, Jennifer Van Eyk, Natalie Rodriguez, Theo J. title: Scientists Discover a Surprisingly Simple Way To Relieve Stubborn Carpal Tunnel Pain
content:
Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when a nerve in the wrist becomes compressed, causing numbness, tingling, pain, and weakness in the hand. Often associated with repetitive hand movements, the condition can interfere with everyday activities and may be difficult to treat effectively. Credit: Shutterstock
A brief procedure using saline could offer lasting relief for stubborn carpal tunnel symptoms without steroids, a small clinical trial suggests.
The numbness, tingling, weakness, and pain of carpal tunnel syndrome arise when the median nerve, a major nerve running from the forearm, is compressed inside a narrow passage in the wrist. Corticosteroid injections can reduce swelling and ease that pressure, but the relief may be temporary. Associated with repetitive hand and wrist movements, the condition affects roughly 5% to 10% of people over their lifetimes, and its incidence is rising.
A randomized trial of 63 patients now suggests that injecting saline around the nerve under ultrasound guidance can provide relief that lasts through six months of follow-up. Adding steroids to the procedure did not significantly improve its long-term benefits. The study was published in
Radiology
, a journal of the
Radiological Society of North America (RSNA)
Photographs depict the in-plane technique of needle insertion for the US-guided hydrodissection procedure using the (A) ulnar approach in right wrist carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) and the (B) radial approach in left wrist CTS. Credit: Radiological Society of North America (RSNA)
Using saline to free the nerve
The procedure, called nerve hydrodissection, uses carefully injected fluid to free the nerve from surrounding adhesions, tissue attachments that can restrict its movement. Ultrasound allows clinicians to guide the injection around the affected nerve. Hydrodissection is generally combined with steroid treatment, so its effectiveness without steroids has remained uncertain.
Study lead author Anindita Bose, M.D., assistant professor in the Department of Radiology at Mahatma Gandhi Medical College and Hospital in Jaipur, India, and colleagues studied patients with confirmed carpal tunnel syndrome who had not responded to conventional treatment.
Ultrasound images depict the procedure of hydrodissection in a patient with carpal tunnel syndrome using an in-plane approach. (A) The needle is placed below the median nerve (white dashed oval) with fluid (blue × symbols) dissecting the nerve from the underlying flexor tendons (green stars). (B) The needle was placed above the median nerve with fluid dissecting the nerve away from the flexor retinaculum (yellow star). (C) Image at completion of procedure depicts the dissected median nerve with fluid all around. Red arrows indicate the needle position. Credit: Radiological Society of North America (RSNA)
“Most of our patients had been suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome for months to years and did not get much relief despite trying various treatments like pain medications, splints, lifestyle modification, and corticosteroids,” said study co-author Anupama Tandon, M.D., professor in the Department of Radiodiagnosis and Imaging at University College of Medical Sciences and Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital in Delhi, India. “It came as a pleasant surprise to find that a simple procedure of dissecting the median nerve under ultrasound guidance with normal saline provided them long-term relief.”
To compare the treatments, the researchers randomly divided participants into three equal groups. One received hydrodissection with normal saline, a saltwater solution. Another received hydrodissection with saline and a corticosteroid, while the third received a corticosteroid injection alone. All three treatments were guided by ultrasound.
The team tracked symptoms, function, and pain using standardized clinical scores. Ultrasound measurements of the median nerve’s cross-sectional area allowed the researchers to assess changes in swelling. Follow-up assessments took place four, 12, and 24 weeks after treatment.
Less nerve swelling, longer-lasting relief
All three groups improved significantly by four weeks, but their outcomes diverged as follow-up continued.
“At 12 weeks and 6 months, both hydrodissection groups demonstrated further improvement in clinical symptoms and function, whereas patients who received corticosteroid injection alone experienced a recurrence of the symptoms, suggesting that the initial benefit was short-lived,” Dr. Tandon said.
The ultrasound measurements supported the symptom and function results. The median nerve’s cross-sectional area decreased by approximately 43% to 45% after hydrodissection, compared with approximately 15% after steroid injection alone, indicating a greater reduction in nerve swelling.
Group comparison of trend in (A) Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire Symptom Severity Scale, (B) Functional Status Scale, and (C) Visual Analog Scale scores at different time points. Group 1 underwent US-guided hydrodissection with normal saline (NS), group 2 underwent US-guided corticosteroid injection alone, and group 3 underwent US-guided hydrodissection with NS plus corticosteroid. Clinical improvement was sustained in both hydrodissection groups, whereas participants treated with corticosteroid injection alone showed symptom recurrence after the initial response. Credit: Radiological Society of North America (RSNA)
The lack of a significant additional long-term benefit from steroids in the hydrodissection groups matters because those drugs carry risks beyond the possibility that symptoms will return.
“Traditional steroid injection for carpal tunnel syndrome often provides only temporary relief, thus requiring repeats of the procedure,” Dr. Tandon said. “Further, steroids carry risk of localized skin changes, fat thinning and tendon weakening.”
A 15-minute procedure without hospitalization
Hydrodissection took an average of 15 minutes, and patients tolerated it well, with no significant immediate or delayed complications observed. Questionnaire responses indicated high satisfaction with the procedure. It was low-cost, required neither anesthesia nor hospitalization, and allowed patients to return to work within an hour.
Ultrasound images of the median nerve (yellow dashed oval) in participants with carpal tunnel syndrome who underwent US-guided interventions. Images show (A) hydrodissection with normal saline (NS) only in a 33-year-old female participant, (B) US-guided corticosteroid injection in a 35-year-old female participant, and (C) US-guided hydrodissection with NS and corticosteroid in a 29-year-old male participant at baseline, 4 weeks, and 12 weeks. Median nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) decreased progressively following hydrodissection, but there was no significant improvement after corticosteroid injection alone. Credit: Radiological Society of North America (RSNA)
“Overall, the study suggests that ultrasound-guided saline hydrodissection is a safe, minimally invasive treatment that can provide sustained clinical and morphological improvement in patients with refractory carpal tunnel syndrome,” Dr. Tandon said. “Thus, hydrodissection merits to be a minimally invasive option for mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome and can defer and even alleviate the need for surgery.”
The researchers said larger studies across multiple centers, with longer follow-up, are needed. They have already launched a study comparing the long-term effectiveness of different fluids used for hydrodissection in carpal tunnel syndrome, including dextrose versus saline.
“This trial features an extended follow-up period to track long-term patient outcomes and establish the true durability of the treatment,” Dr. Tandon said.
Reference: “Efficacy of US-guided Hydrodissection for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial” by Anindita Bose, Anupama Tandon, Gopesh Mehrotra, Siddharth Maheshwari and Ayush Khandelwal, 6 October 2026,
Radiology
DOI: 10.1148/radiol.260185

title: Same Calories, Same Nutrients – but One Meal Triggered a Surprising Reaction in the Body
content:
Researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC found that two meals with the same carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, calories, salt, and weight — but that differed in their level of processing — produced different metabolic responses. Credit: Zach Hutelin/Virginia Tech
Two meals looked nearly identical nutritionally, yet the ultraprocessed option triggered more insulin release in healthy adults, hinting at differences nutrition labels may miss.
Ultraprocessed foods supply more than half of the average American’s daily calories, and their place in diets worldwide is growing. Formulated to be convenient, accessible, affordable, and highly palatable, they can be easy to overeat. Understanding their effects on health, however, requires untangling the influence of processing from that of the nutrients they contain.
Meals with the same basic nutritional profile are generally expected to affect blood sugar in similar ways. Yet in a Virginia Tech study, healthy adults expended more energy and burned less carbohydrate after eating an ultraprocessed meal than after a minimally processed one. Both meals contained 300 calories and were closely matched for carbohydrates, fat, protein, water, salt, and weight. The findings appeared in
Nature Metabolism
“We know that the majority of ultraprocessed foods are high in fat, they’re high in sugar, they’re low in fiber, and they’re low in protein,” said Alex DiFeliceantonio, an associate professor at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC whose lab led the study. “But if we artificially hold all of those things constant, is there something about the processing that leads to a different outcome?”
Neuroscientist Alex DiFeliceantonio (left) and researcher Zach Hutelin at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC unexpectedly found that two meals with the same carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, calories, salt, and weight — but that differed in their level of processing — produced different brain and metabolic responses. Credit: Stephanie Klein-Davis for Virginia Tech
Matched nutrients, a stronger insulin response
The researchers selected foods using NOVA, a classification system that divides foods into four groups according to their level of industrial processing. Their ultraprocessed meal included a bite of a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, deli turkey, veggie chips, a cookie, cereal, instant mashed potatoes, and a little water. The minimally processed meal consisted of sliced banana, dried cranberries, cheese, and egg.
“The two meals are matched within 1 percent of carbs, fat, protein, calories, water, and salt,” said Zach Hutelin, a researcher at the institute and the study’s first author. “If these meals had a nutritional label, they would be practically identical.” The study formed part of his doctoral research through Virginia Tech’s Translational Biology, Medicine, and Health Graduate Program.
The full study involved 57 healthy adults ages 18 to 45, including 32 who completed both the metabolic testing and brain imaging sessions. Participants ate the two types of meals in separate sessions at least three days apart, allowing the researchers to compare each person’s responses.
Alexandra DiFeliceantonio is a neuroscientist who works to understand the basic mechanisms of food choice — why we eat what we eat. Credit: Virginia Tech
For the metabolic tests, participants arrived after fasting overnight and settled onto a twin-size bed inside a metabolic chamber, a sealed, airtight room used to measure energy expenditure and metabolism. Researchers took baseline measurements, then waited an hour before giving participants 10 minutes to eat one of the meals. Blood samples were collected immediately afterward and six more times over the next three hours. The team tracked energy expenditure, carbohydrate oxidation, or the burning of carbohydrates for fuel, and the response of insulin, a hormone that helps cells take up glucose from the blood.
“We were shocked when every single metabolic metric differed,” Hutelin said. “What we noticed with the ultraprocessed food is that insulin response was much higher and blood sugar stays a little bit higher for a little bit longer.”
Matching the amounts of nutrients did leave some differences unresolved. The meals contained different protein sources, which could have influenced the results, and the ultraprocessed meal contained more additives. Although the researchers measured total fiber, they did not explicitly measure the foods’ physical and chemical structures.
Carbohydrate burning linked to brain responses
DiFeliceantonio, a neuroscientist who studies the basic mechanisms behind food choice, also wanted to know whether the metabolic responses were connected to how the brain responded to food cues. On a separate day, participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, while viewing pictures of nutritionally matched highly and minimally processed foods. These included the foods served during the metabolic tests. The scans measured brain activity by tracking changes in blood flow across different regions.
For each food pictured, participants reported how much they would be willing to pay for it. Their answers gave researchers a measure of subjective value to compare with brain activity. Participants did not report being willing to pay more for either the ultraprocessed or minimally processed foods.
Zach Hutelin, a researcher conducting experiments at the metabolic kitchen at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute and the study’s first author, said the two meals are matched within 1 percent of carbs, fat, protein, calories, water, and salt. Credit: Virginia Tech
Differences in how participants burned carbohydrates after the two meals were nevertheless linked to differences in their brain responses to food pictures. One notable result involved the ventral striatum and nucleus accumbens, brain structures involved in learning, motivation, and reward. The association suggests a connection between the body’s response to the meals and the brain’s response to food cues, although it does not establish that those differences cause people to eat more.
“A key debate in the literature is whether [ultraprocessed food] associations with poor health outcomes are driven by nutrient composition rather than processing,” Carlos A. Monteiro of the University of São Paulo told
Nature Metabolism
. Monteiro is a Brazilian epidemiologist whose obesity research led to the development of the international NOVA classification used in nutrition and public health studies. He highlighted the Roanoke team’s examination of brain activity alongside metabolism. “This is a novel and important contribution, as the brain ultimately regulates eating behavior.”
Untangling the health risks of ultraprocessed foods
Whether these short-term responses help explain the health effects associated with ultraprocessed foods remains unresolved. Chronically elevated blood sugar increases the risk of conditions such as diabetes, but measurements taken over three hours after a meal cannot establish long-term consequences.
“If you look at that population-level data, people who consume large amounts of ultraprocessed foods have higher rates of poor health outcomes — obesity, cardiac events, type 2 diabetes, and even some metrics of mental health,” DiFeliceantonio said.
The experiment tested only one pair of matched 300-calorie meals in young, healthy adults. DiFeliceantonio, who also holds an appointment in the Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise in Virginia Tech’s College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, would like to examine other populations, follow responses over longer periods, and test larger meals and more pairings of minimally and highly processed foods.
“We want to examine specific factors, such as commercial additives or specific processing steps, that might lead to different metabolic responses,” DiFeliceantonio said.
Reference: “Metabolic and neural responses to ultraprocessed foods: a randomized, controlled, crossover study” by Zach Hutelin, Monica Ahrens, Mary Elizabeth Baugh, Emmanuel Nartey, Delbert L. Herald III, Alexandra L. Hanlon and Alexandra G. DiFeliceantonio, 5 October 2026,
Nature Metabolism
DOI: 10.1038/s42255-026-01619-4
The research was funded by a National Institutes of Health research grant through the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and a National Science Foundation graduate research fellowship.

title: Researchers Map the Brain’s Mysterious “Blue Place” and Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron
content:
Topography of locus coeruleus norepinephrine neurons in the mouse brain. Approximately 100 fully reconstructed neurons are superimposed. Neurons are colored by their locations. Dorsal neurons (purple) project to the front of the brain, ventral (yellow) neurons project to the back. Credit: Allen Institute
Scientists exploring the brain’s “blue place” discovered the longest neuron ever measured in a mouse and uncovered new clues about how the brain learns.
When mice in a decision-making experiment switched their choices after a negative outcome, neurons near the top of a tiny brainstem region became active. Just before the mice ignored cues that might lead to a reward, neurons near the bottom fired more rapidly.
These neighboring groups belong to the locus coeruleus (LC), Latin for “blue place.” This small cluster accounts for a tiny fraction of the brain’s cells but releases norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention and learning, activates the body’s response to stress or excitement, and affects heart rate.
Scientists long viewed the LC as a single loudspeaker broadcasting a uniform signal throughout the brain. In a new study published in
, Allen Institute researchers combined brain imaging, neural recordings, genetic tools, and behavioral experiments in mice to examine how the region’s connections and activity relate to what an animal experiences.
“The findings suggest the brain’s norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn,” said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.
Reconstruction of 70 cm LC neuron in mouse, the longest ever measured. Credit: Allen Institute
Separate routes for learning and engagement
Tracing those connections revealed distinct destinations. Neurons in the upper, or dorsal, LC connected mainly to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Those in the lower, or ventral, LC connected to the brainstem and spinal cord. These routes determine where the neurons send the signals that prompt norepinephrine release.
The work included whole-brain imaging of almost 35,000 neurons, genetic profiling of nearly 400,000 cells to examine gene activity, and complete reconstructions of some of the brain’s most complex cells. The researchers could therefore compare the neurons’ physical connections with their genetic characteristics and activity during behavior.
“What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all,” said Svoboda. “We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns.”
A 27.7-inch axon skips brain regions
Reconstructing individual LC neurons also revealed how extensive their connections could be. Their axons, the long projections that carry signals to other cells, averaged about 35 centimeters, or 13.8 inches, in length. One measured 70.32 centimeters, about 27.7 inches, making it the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.
“This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets,” said Jeremiah Cohen, a scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. “But this neuron doesn’t release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord.”
Sue Su, scientist at the Allen Institute. Credit: Allen Institute
The learning-related activity also led the researchers to draw parallels with dopamine, another major chemical messenger that carries signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in habit formation. They propose that the norepinephrine and dopamine systems work together as a learning platform, allowing the brain to learn multiple complex and abstract concepts simultaneously.
Norepinephrine drugs could target specific circuits
Norepinephrine’s roles in mood and attention already make it a target of common medications for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. LC neurons are also among the first to degenerate in Alzheimer’s disease.
The organization uncovered in mice could eventually help researchers develop treatments that target particular parts of the system, reducing the possibility of helping some circuits while negatively affecting others.

title: Scientists Discover a New Cousin of Diamond That Was Thought To Exist Only in Theory
content:
Chemistry
A shimmering diamond represents one of carbon’s most familiar forms. Scientists have now created a new, porous, diamond-like structure that reveals another surprising way carbon atoms can arrange themselves. Credit: Shutterstock
Diamond and graphite have a new carbon cousin called diamondiyne, with a crystal structure confirmed so far only in microscopic patches.
A carbon structure proposed 35 years ago has finally taken shape in a thin film where two liquids meet. Using relatively inexpensive equipment, researchers at the
University of Gothenburg
have created diamondiyne for the first time, adding a new three-dimensional structure to the forms carbon can take.
Diamondiyne is a carbon allotrope, a form of the element distinguished by how its atoms are arranged. Diamond and graphite are familiar examples. To create diamondiyne, the researchers joined carbon atoms through triple bonds. The material crystallizes into a network of tetrahedra, shapes with four triangular faces, connected corner to corner in all three dimensions.
“The structure creates voids between the tetrahedra. The carbon allotrope can therefore be compared to a porous diamond. But unlike diamonds, diamondiyne does not require high pressure to make the carbon atoms bond to one another,” says Karl Börjesson, professor of physical chemistry at the University of Gothenburg, who leads the research team.
Crystal patterns confirmed in tiny patches
Electron microscopy at Stockholm University confirmed the crystal structure, although only in patches on the film’s surface. Many things can go wrong during formation and prevent the carbon atoms from assembling into diamondiyne.
The carbon allotrope is called diamondiyne and it creates a porous material with the basic shape as a tetrahedron. Credit: Yizhou Yang
“We have at least managed to produce repeating patterns of diamondiyne in a volume measuring 10 nanometers on each side, 10 × 10⁻⁹ meters, and the images of the patterns correspond well with the theoretical models,” says Börjesson.
Carbon frameworks without metal ions
The discovery grew out of the team’s longstanding effort to create porous materials in which carbon-based molecules bind together without metal ions. These materials are called covalent organic frameworks, or COFs. They differ from metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs, which combine carbon-based molecules with metal ions and whose development earned the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Karl Börjesson has spent many years working to produce diamondiyne, which had previously only been described in theory. Credit: Erika Hoff
A colleague told Börjesson about a website where theoretical chemists had compiled an almost endless list of carbon allotropes that should be possible to create. Diamondiyne’s tetrahedral structure had been described theoretically decades before the team succeeded in making it.
“It has taken us an incredibly long time, but we finally succeeded. I am very pleased,” says Börjesson.
For many years, known carbon allotropes were limited to diamond, graphite, and three artificially produced forms: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, and graphene. The development of fullerenes and graphene was recognized with Nobel Prizes, largely because the idea that these materials could exist was itself new. Researchers have created many additional allotropes in recent years, with diamondiyne the first of this newer group to have a three-dimensional structure.
“We will now investigate the properties of diamondiyne and how it might be used. One exciting aspect of the porous structure is that several diamondiyne structures could potentially be interwoven through each other’s voids,” says Börjesson.
Reference: “Diamondiyne: A 3D Carbon Allotrope With Mixed sp–sp3 Hybridization” by Yizhou Yang, Jie Xu, Yanyan Chen, Yu Xia, Sami Zeliouche, Clara Schäfer, Martin Ratsch, Ebba Matic, Martin Rahm, Lars Evenäs, Angela Beth Grommet, Tom Willhammar and Karl Börjesson, 14 September 2026,

title: A Missing Molecule May Explain Why Muscles Weaken With Age
content:
Aging muscles may sacrifice strength to protect themselves from cellular damage. Researchers discovered that disrupting this natural defense can have surprising consequences. Credit: Stock
Restoring just part of a depleted mitochondrial fat began reversing muscle wasting in mice, suggesting a possible route toward treating age-related muscle decline.
As muscles weaken with age, they shift toward fibers built for endurance rather than quick, powerful bursts of movement. These slow-twitch fibers contain more mitochondria, the structures that supply cells with energy, than fast-twitch fibers, which tire more quickly. Yet mitochondria also become less effective with age, leaving older muscles increasingly dependent on machinery that is struggling to do its job.
Experiments in mice and cultured muscle cells suggest that this shift, also seen in many muscle-wasting diseases, helps cells withstand damage from their strained mitochondria. Researchers at the
University of Copenhagen
traced the response to a shortage of cardiolipin, a fat molecule found almost exclusively in the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin maintains the membrane’s distinctive folded structure, which mitochondria need to supply enough energy, metabolic signals, and building blocks for cells.
The researchers found that cardiolipin levels declined in muscle mitochondria with aging and disease, leaving the structures distorted and functioning poorly. Human muscle samples confirmed that cardiolipin also falls with age in people, while experiments in mice and cultured muscle cells explored the consequences. To establish whether the loss could cause muscle changes rather than simply accompany them, the team reduced cardiolipin in young mice to mimic the decline associated with aging. Their muscles developed the same shift from fast-twitch to slow-twitch fibers seen in older mice and humans.
Sugar redirected toward muscle defenses
The altered muscles also handled sugar differently. Mice deficient in cardiolipin drew much more glucose from the bloodstream, but tracing labeled sugar through their muscles revealed that it was being used to manufacture the cells’ own antioxidants rather than being burned for energy. Those antioxidants helped the remodeled slow-twitch fibers protect cells against reactive oxygen species, or ROS, molecules that can damage cells.
“The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That’s also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better,” says Fabian Finger, an assistant professor at the University of Copenhagen and the study’s first and co-corresponding author.
ROS also act as a signal that helps set this protective response in motion. As cardiolipin levels fall, stressed mitochondria produce far more ROS. Removing them with an antioxidant in cardiolipin-depleted muscle cells blunted the shift toward slow-twitch fibers. The response operates through a protein called ERRγ, which prompts cells to remodel their mitochondria and change fiber type. Blocking ERRγ in cultured muscle cells stopped the switch completely.
Restoring cardiolipin reduces wasting in mice
Restoring the missing fat addressed the mitochondrial problem more directly. When the researchers brought cardiolipin back to roughly two-thirds of its normal level in the mice, muscle wasting began to reverse, and the animals’ early deaths were prevented entirely.
“What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies,” says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, an associate professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen.
A drug proposed to stabilize cardiolipin, elamipretide, recently received accelerated FDA approval for Barth syndrome, a rare genetic disorder. That approval provides an existing example of a treatment directed at cardiolipin, although the muscle recovery reported in this study was demonstrated in mice.
ERRγ offers another possible route for drug development. It belongs to a class of molecules called nuclear receptors, which are targeted by roughly 10 to 15 percent of all FDA-approved small-molecule medications. Compounds that activate ERRγ are already in preclinical development for other conditions.

title: Antibiotic Resistance Is Making This Dangerous Gut Bacterium Even Harder To Kill
content:
Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is a bacterium that can cause severe diarrhea and inflammation of the colon, particularly after antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal gut microbiome. It spreads through hardy spores that can persist on surfaces, making it a persistent challenge in hospitals and other healthcare settings. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
An antibiotic resistance gene helps a dangerous gut bacterium build tougher spores that can survive hospital disinfectants.
A hospital surface can be disinfected and still harbor dormant spores of
Clostridioides difficile
, a bacterium that causes diarrhea that can be deadly for already sick patients. Researchers have now found that an antibiotic resistance gene can help the bacterium produce tougher spores, allowing them to survive hospital-grade cleaning products and high laundry temperatures.
Monash University
researchers traced this added resilience to a change in how the bacterium builds its spores. Their study, published in
Nature Communications
, reveals how acquiring a gene that protects against an antibiotic can also strengthen the form the bacterium uses to spread.
A protein swap builds tougher spores
C. difficile
spores behave much like plant seeds, waiting for suitable conditions to become active again. The human gut provides one such opportunity, making survival outside the body a crucial part of the bacterium’s journey between patients.
“Spore survival matters because spores are the main way these pathogens spread between people and through hospitals, homes, and the environment,” said first author Dr. Yogitha Srikhanta, a postdoctoral research fellow at Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.
Antibiotic resistance is supercharging dangerous gut bacteria to withstand even hospital-grade disinfectants intended to kill them. Credit: Desirel Ng/Monash University
The resistance gene produces a protein that takes the place of a key protein used to build spores. With that replacement in place, the bacterium can continue making spores despite an antibiotic that would otherwise block the process. The resulting spores are also tougher, extending the gene’s effects beyond resistance to the drug itself.
“Antibiotics are helping bacteria evolve in ways we hadn’t anticipated,” said lead researcher Professor Dena Lyras, director of Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and interim dean of Monash’s Sub-Faculty of Biomedical and Psychological Sciences.
Spore survival could help resistance spread
Bacteria that stop responding to antibiotics can leave infections difficult or impossible to treat. The World Health Organization identifies antimicrobial resistance as a major global health threat and estimates that it contributes to millions of deaths each year. The Monash team describes its study as the first to uncover a link between antibiotic resistance and bacterial spores, connecting treatment resistance with the ability to survive outside a patient.
Antibiotic resistance is supercharging dangerous gut bacteria to withstand even hospital-grade disinfectants intended to kill them. Credit: Desirel Ng/Monash University
Srikhanta cautioned, “A resistance gene that changes how spores are built could make infections harder to control and help resistant strains spread more easily.
“We are now investigating ways to deal with this new type of antibiotic resistance.”
Targeting the spores could offer a way to interrupt that spread, although the researchers have yet to establish a solution. Lyras said, “Our new research shows just how sophisticated their evolution is, with the potential to have disastrous impacts on humans.
“They are not only better at building tolerance to drugs we develop, but making new versions of themselves that can survive better in particular environments, like surfaces where cleaning products are commonly applied.”
