title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Trigger That Keeps Inflammation Alive
content:
A newly identified cellular structure may be a more promising target for controlling runaway inflammation than the immune receptors scientists have focused on for decades. Credit: Stock
Inflammation persists after proteins detach from immune receptors, revealing a potential target for autoimmune treatments.
Since a Nobel Prize-winning discovery in the 1990s identified molecules called Toll-like Receptors as the guardians of the human immune system, researchers have pursued a straightforward strategy for treating autoimmune diseases. By developing therapies that interfere with these receptors, scientists hoped to suppress runaway inflammation. Yet those efforts have seen little success.
Research from
Boston Children’s Hospital
suggests that a crucial part of the inflammatory response depends on what happens after signaling proteins separate from those receptors. The team found that the proteins had to break free before they could assemble a structure that activates inflammatory genes. Published September 23, 2026, in
, the study points to that structure as a potentially more effective treatment target for autoimmune diseases.
Inflammation persists beyond the receptor
To understand why that separation matters, consider how receptors are generally thought to work. They detect changes around a cell, including signals associated with other cells, infections, or cancer, and bind to signaling proteins in the cytoplasm, the cell’s interior. Those proteins then prompt changes in cell function, such as inflammation. This process, called receptor-mediated signal transduction, has shaped scientists’ understanding of cell communication and the changes in cell behavior that drive disease.
The Boston Children’s team observed the familiar beginning of that process, with Toll-like receptors bringing signaling proteins together. But the receptors then released the proteins, and inflammation continued. Under the conventional model, losing the connection to the receptor should have stopped the inflammatory signaling.
Instead, being released allowed the proteins to assemble an organelle called the myddosome, a structure within the cell that stimulates inflammation. The separation was essential to its formation. Without release from the receptors, myddosomes could not form or activate inflammatory genes. The receptors therefore helped initiate the process, but the proteins needed to leave them behind to carry out this later step.
Jonathan Kagan, PhD, the study’s senior author and director of basic research and Shwachman Chair in Gastroenterology at Boston Children’s, described the finding as an expansion of the ways scientists understand cellular signaling.
“The discovery of this receptor-free signaling transduction underscores the value of exploratory science as a means to expand the lexicon of life,” said Kagan.
Myddosomes could offer a better treatment target
The distinction between starting the response and assembling its inflammatory machinery could help explain why treatments aimed at Toll-like receptors have struggled. Kagan believes targeting the myddosome itself may offer a more effective way to intervene, and the team has evidence from drug experiments in mice to support pursuing that approach.
“New strategies to manipulate the TLR pathway, central to so many aspects of inflammation, are now possible,” said Kagan. “We have already found pharmacological evidence that disruption of myddosomes (rather than disrupting receptor function) resolved inflammation in mice. Our hope is to develop new classes of small molecules that manipulate myddosomes as a means of therapeutic treatment for autoimmune diseases, and beyond.”
Reference: “TRAM promotes Toll-like-receptor-free myddosome signal transduction” by Daniel Fisch, Vaani Ohri, Eleni Anastasakou, Lucia J. Wesemann, Joon H. Choi, Katherine E. Lindblad and Jonathan C. Kagan, 23 September 2026,

title: Scientists Tested Diet Drinks for 2 Years. The Results May Surprise You
content:
Diet drinks offer sweetness with little or no sugar and far fewer calories than regular soda. Credit: Stock
Water had no clear weight-loss advantage over diet drinks in a two-year trial, with both groups keeping weight off after program support ended.
Replacing a sugary soda in the refrigerator with a diet version keeps the sweet taste while cutting sugar and calories. The harder question has been whether the sweeteners used in that swap might disrupt appetite and make lost weight harder to keep off.
University of Liverpool
researchers put that concern to a two-year test, randomly assigning 493 adults with overweight or obesity to drink either water or commercially available diet beverages daily. Both groups took part in a structured behavioral weight-management program, and at 104 weeks, those drinking diet beverages had maintained weight loss similar to those drinking water.
Diet drinks keep pace with water
The diet beverages contained low- or no-calorie sugar substitutes, specifically aspartame, acesulfame potassium (acesulfame-K), and sucralose. Participants consumed these sweeteners at levels well within the European Food Safety Authority’s established safety thresholds.
Following participants through a second year extended earlier findings from the SWITCH trial, published in the
International Journal of Obesity
in 2023. The latest results, reported in the
British Journal of Nutrition
, included:
Weight loss averaged 4.8 kilograms, about 10.6 pounds, in the diet-beverage group and 3.7 kilograms, about 8.2 pounds, in the water group. The difference was not statistically significant.
Both groups sustained weight reductions over two years, including the final year without assistance.
Waist and hip measurements decreased in both groups, alongside improvements in body composition and several measures of metabolic health.
Blood pressure and cholesterol outcomes showed no clinically meaningful differences between the diet-beverage and water groups.
Sugar intake fell in both groups, with slightly greater reductions among participants assigned to diet beverages.
Participants maintained those reductions after the assisted portion of the program ended, giving researchers a longer view of how the two beverage choices fit into weight management. The findings did not support concerns about disrupted appetite regulation or metabolic harm under the conditions studied, although the weight losses occurred within a broader behavioral program and cannot be attributed to the drinks alone.
Professor Joanne Harrold, dean of psychology at the University of Liverpool, led the research alongside Professor Jason Halford of the University of Leeds, formerly of Liverpool. The American Beverage Association funded the peer-reviewed study. The research team worked independently of the funder and retained full control over the analysis and reporting of its findings.
Two-year results could inform WHO guidance
The World Health Organization has advised against using non-sugar sweeteners for weight control amid uncertainty in observational evidence. By assigning participants to beverage groups and following them over two years, the SWITCH researchers tested the question directly over an extended period.
Harrold said, “The University of Liverpool is one of the UK’s leading research-intensive higher education institutions, with a key focus on public health. These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomized trial. We hope this evidence informs future WHO guidance and public health policy.”
Reaching for a drink from the refrigerator remains one part of a broader effort to lose weight and keep it off. Halford said, “This study provides the long‑term clinical evidence that has been missing from international discussions. For people trying to manage their weight, non‑nutritive sweetened beverages offer an effective alternative to sugar‑sweetened drinks—and perform equivalently to water over two years.”
Reference: “Effect of non-nutritive sweetened beverages v. water on body weight: long-term results of a randomised controlled trial” by Joanne A. Harrold, Scott Hill, Cristina Radu, Paul Thomas, Paula Thorp, Charlotte A. Hardman, Paul Christiansen, Una Masic, Lauren McGale, Dan J. Cuthbertson and Jason C.G. Halford, 4 August 2026,
British Journal of Nutrition

title: Scientists Unlock 700,000-Year-Old Secrets Hidden Inside a Giant Elephant Tooth
content:
The elephant remains were discovered alongside basalt handaxes and cleavers, hallmark tools of the Acheulian tradition, one of the earliest and most widespread stone-tool technologies in human history. Credit: Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and Hannah Farrell, University of Haifa
A giant elephant’s tooth has preserved clues to the watery world that sustained early humans nearly 700,000 years ago.
Researchers studying elephant remains from Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (GBY-NBA) in northern Israel have reconstructed a Pleistocene environment rich in water, vegetation, and wildlife. Published in
Quaternary Science Reviews
, the study reveals the landscape shared by enormous mammals and some of the region’s earliest human toolmakers.
Led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University), the research examined molar and tusk fragments excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues. The site, Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), sits in the Jordan Rift Valley, south of today’s Hula Valley.
Rather than studying the elephant alone, researchers used the tooth as a biological archive to reconstruct the broader ecosystem shared by large mammals and early human toolmakers. Credit: Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and Hannah Farrell, University of Haifa
The fossils belonged to
Palaeoloxodon antiquus
, the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Nearby basalt handaxes and cleavers place early humans in the same setting. These tools belong to the Acheulian tradition, among the earliest and most geographically widespread stone tool technologies in human history.
An Elephant Tooth Holds Environmental Clues
The tooth offered more than a way to identify the animal. Its structure, microscopic wear, and chemical composition provided different lines of evidence about its life and surroundings. The team combined CT scanning, 3D reconstruction, microscopic wear analysis, isotope geochemistry, and pollen studies to piece together the broader ecosystem.
The remains belong to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Credit: Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and Hannah Farrell, University of Haifa
The results point to an enduring landscape of woodlands, grasslands, marshes, rivers, and shallow-water habitats. Carbon isotope values suggest that the elephant lived where water remained consistently available. Pollen recovered from sediments added detail to that picture, revealing reeds, sedges, willows, tamarisks, and aquatic plants.
Together, the findings suggest that the Hula Valley region was a stable ecological refuge within the Levantine Corridor, the land bridge connecting Africa and Eurasia. Reliable water and biological resources likely made this landscape a valuable stopping point or habitat for wildlife and human groups moving through the region.
The research focuses on a giant elephant molar and tusk fragments discovered alongside Acheulian stone tools at Gesher Benot Ya’aqov in northern Israel. The remains belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Credit: Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and Hannah Farrell, University of Haifa
According to Sharon, “understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species.”
“The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive,” Sharon says. “The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world’s earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago.”
Reference: “Elephant dental remains from the Acheulian site at North Bridge Acheulian–Gesher Benot Ya’aqov: hominin behavior and environmental implications” by Hannah Farrell, Gonen Sharon, Minji Jin, Dafna Langgut, Cheryl A. Makarewicz and Nimrod Marom, 14 September 2026,

title: EneCoat completes new perovskite plant as Japan’s solar makers race to scale up
content:
EneCoat completes new perovskite plant as Japan’s solar makers race to scale up
recently held a ceremony for its new headquarters and manufacturing plant in Uji, Kyoto Prefecture. Production there begins next year, with full operation scheduled from 2028 and annual capacity expected to exceed 10 MW. The cells will be used mainly on building exteriors, vehicles and watches. At the ceremony, CEO Naoya Kato said the company wants to make perovskite cells a “power source found anywhere.”
Other Japanese companies are also moving toward production.
Panasonic
, which makes glass-type cells for use as building materials, is about to open a mass-production technology development facility in Nagahama, Shiga Prefecture, using government subsidies. It targets mass production around fiscal 2030 and is discussing bringing that date forward.
Sekisui Chemical
launched its film-type Solafil cells
, and plans to start up a 100 MW plant in Sakai, Osaka Prefecture, in fiscal 2027, equivalent to the annual electricity use of about 31,000 households.
The government has named perovskite solar cells a key product among 17 strategic fields under the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Most solar cells are silicon-based, and China is the largest silicon producer, while perovskite’s main raw material is iodine, of which Japan is the world’s second-largest producer after Chile. That has raised hopes of a carbon-free power source with fewer economic security risks. The push follows Japan’s recent
plan to shift subsidies from silicon panels to perovskite
and the launch of the
JPSC industry alliance

title: Stage-dependent additive strategy enables deep-red perovskite LED with 21.7% EQE
content:
Stage-dependent additive strategy enables deep-red perovskite LED with 21.7% EQE
Researchers at the Institute of Solid State Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed a stage-dependent additive incorporation strategy for mixed-halide perovskite films, producing deep-red perovskite LEDs (PeLEDs) with a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 21.70% at an electroluminescence peak of 734 nm.
Deep-red PeLEDs are of interest for long-wavelength optoelectronics, but their development is hindered by defect-assisted non-radiative recombination, ion migration, and insufficient spectral and operational stability in mixed-halide perovskites. To address this, the team introduced 4-vinylbenzylammonium iodide (VBAI) into the perovskite precursor and octylphosphonic acid (OPA) into the antisolvent, so that each additive acts at a different step of film formation and the two exert complementary effects.
Experimental characterization and theoretical calculations indicate that this approach improves film morphology and crystallinity, reduces trap density, suppresses non-radiative recombination, and enhances thermal and spectral stability. The optimized devices reached an operational lifetime (T50) of 26.39 hours. The researchers say the method offers a practical route to high-quality deep-red perovskite films and to efficient mixed-halide PeLEDs with improved spectral and operational stability.

title: 浙江虚拟电厂 2.0 版新规发布 运营管理与市场化响应细则深度解读-索比光伏网
content:
2026年9月23日，浙江电力交易中心同步发布《浙江电力领域新型主体市场化响应实施细则（试行2.0版）》与《浙江省
运营管理实施细则（试行）》，标志着浙江
正式进入2.0市场化运营阶段。这是继2025年4月1.0版细则发布后，浙江时隔一年多对
制度体系的系统性修订，覆盖准入门槛、聚合分类、价格机制、考核评级等全维度规则调整，其中用户侧储能可单独以储能类聚合单元身份参与市场，成为本次新规最受关注的突破点。
本次2.0版规则呈现 “放管结合” 的鲜明特征：准入端整体放宽，聚合用户立户时间从6个月缩短至3个月，用户绑定窗口延长至每月1—20日，平台等保要求降至二级及以上，审核时限压缩至5个工作日，降低增量资源入市门槛；交易端分类细化，首次将聚合资源划分为发电类、储能类、负荷类三类单元并支持独立入市，解决此前打包聚合导致高价值资源收益被稀释的问题；价格端与现货脱钩，调节型、局域型按响应出清价格结算，快速型按固定价格结算，不再执行 “三者取高” 规则；考核端差异化调整，调节型有效响应率要求降至70%、处罚方式优化，快速型仍保留严格能力约束，同时建立按月评级机制，能力与执行指标按3:7权重分级，行业竞争从规模扩张转向质量比拼。
截至2026年上半年，浙江
可调节能力已突破190万千瓦，聚合用户超4400户，填谷需求已超过削峰需求，市场结构持续演化。新规落地后，用户侧储能、
、工商业可调负荷等资源的收益路径将进一步清晰，
运营商的竞争逻辑也将随之重构。
运营商、储能投资主体、工商业负荷方全面吃透2.0版规则变化、明确资源分类界定、测算收益空间、规避运营风险，索比光伏网结合两份细则原文、浙江
运行数据及行业实践，推出深度解读报告，覆盖规则逐条拆解、三类单元界定、价格机制分析、考核评级规则、分主体影响评估、实操落地建议等全维度内容。
以下为报告节选内容，完整聚合单元分类标准、收益测算模型、申报准入清单、评级规则细则及风险避坑指南，可扫码跳转小程序查看全文完整版报告。

title: 河南一地分布式光伏反向送电，引发频繁停电-索比光伏网

通报中提出3个典型案例（一）焦作市山阳区群众投诉频繁停电问题。经核实，反映事项属实。投诉人所在地因分布式光伏反向送电，造成配电台区配变容量越限引发设备故障停电。供电企业已采取临时措施消除频繁停电隐患，并承诺改造配变提升台区承载力。
（二）郑州市金水区群众投诉光伏上网电费转错账户问题。经核实，反映事项属实。投诉人申请办理更换银行账户收款信息业务后因供电企业系统原因导致上网电费结算至投诉人旧账户。供电企业已纠正错误，并向用户道歉。

title: Record-breaking cable operations completed at East Anglia TWO
content:
ScottishPower Renewables has completed a major construction milestone at
its 960MW East
Anglia TWO offshore wind farm
with the installation of two cable ducts that will provide a pathway for
high-voltage export cables.
The ducts were installed beneath the Suffolk coastline using Horizontal
Directional Drilling (HDD), allowing engineers to drill beneath the coastline
and seabed without disturbing beaches, dunes, cliffs or sensitive coastal
habitats.
The work involved installing two continuous polyethylene ducts, each measuring
at an estimated 1,800 metres in length and 800mm in diameter.
According to the announcement, the ducts form the UK's largest electricity
transmission landfall of their kind based on the combination of length
and diameter.
The pipes were manufactured by Pipelife. Project Manager in Pipelife Norway,
Martin Myhre, said “Producing the pipe through continuous extrusion meant
we could manufacture it as one uninterrupted length, without the need for
welding.”
The HDD programme is being delivered by OCU Group, supported by Peter McCormack
& Sons. The construction contract is expected to support more than
80 jobs during the construction phase of the project.
The first export cable is expected to be installed in summer 2027, with
commercial operations targeted for late 2028.

title: UK confirms standard timetable for AR8 process
content:
The government have announced the decision not to apply the Pending Applications
process to AR8 of the Contracts for Difference (CfD) scheme. As a result,
the auction will proceed under a standard timetable rather than an accelerated
schedule.
According to the government, the decision was made to support maximum competition
in the auction, deliver value for money for consumers and provide participants
with sufficient time to prepare their bids.
The sealed bid window will open following the conclusion of the appeals
process for all non-qualifying AR8 applications. The exact timing will
be confirmed by the National Energy System Operator (NESO) in its Notice
of Auction, due to be published on 19 November.
The government will also publish the AR8 Contract Budget Notice on 19 November,

title: Cognition’s Plan to Limit Tokenmaxxing to the Most Efficient Engineers
content: To rein in AI spending, large companies are capping employees’ usage, turning to cheaper and smaller models and using routers to send only the hardest requests to the most expensive models. Cognition , the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin , is adding a new trick to the book: measuring how efficiently different engineers use AI so companies can allocate more resources toward their most efficient employees, Cognition told The Information exclusively. “The limits that a user should have should not be static. They should be dynamic based on the efficiency of your usage and the value that you're getting out of it,” said Calvin Giroud , a vice president of customer engineering at Cognition. By looking at an engineer’s coding session using Devin, Cognition can estimate the equivalent number of hours it would have taken a human to do the same amount of work. Dividing by the costs of that session, Cognition gets a measure of each engineer’s efficiency. Then, when engineers run into usage limits, their limits can automatically increase if they have a “healthy” or “satisfactory” grade. “This is how credit cards work, for example,” said Giroud. “You have a set credit limit, and as you prove that you are a good steward of the credit card and you're paying back things on time, you get higher and higher and higher limits.” Helping customers rein in token use could seem paradoxical for Cognition given it charges based on usage. But the company argues that in this hyper-competitive market for AI coding tools, it is incentivized to build trust with customers that will deliver long term loyalty rather than maximizing spending now. Unrestrained tokenmaxxing is “not a sustainable long-term approach, and many of our customers are large public companies that have to answer to their shareholders and public markets around the efficiency of the tools that they're using,” he said. Cognition is also rolling out Devin Coach , an AI system that gives feedback on engineers’ requests to encourage them to work more efficiently. The coach is prompted to spot the top 20 to 30 most common mistakes, such as an ambiguous request or a user selecting an unnecessarily expensive model for their task. For example, if a user tries to combine multiple distinct tasks in the same request, the coach might notice that those tasks could more quickly be completed in parallel and suggest splitting them into separate sessions. The coach will also notice if employees are using Devin for personal tasks, such as planning a vacation. That was motivated by worries from a customer of Cognition’s that found some employees using Devin for non-work tasks, though it was a “relatively trivial percentage” of usage, according to Giroud. Here’s what else is going on… Big Number Anthropic’s revenue in the third quarter hit $16.8 billion, the company on Wednesday told prospective investors in its initial public offering, The Information reported. That marked a jump of about 45% from the second quarter, and was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year. Katti, who joined OpenAI after four years at Intel , announced that he would be “moving on to build something new” in a post on X. title: Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training
content: In the weeks before SpaceX’s AI unit in August introduced Grok Bot, its version of a personal AI agent, engineers at Cursor discovered a potential problem. Cursor, the AI coding startup SpaceX was then in the process of acquiring, was developing Grok Bot, and as part of that process, employees across Cursor were using the tool extensively for testing and as a part of their everyday work. In late July, engineers raised concerns that Cursor might have sent data from that internal testing—potentially including confidential information about its customers, suppliers and business partners—to SpaceX’s AI unit. One of Cursor’s lawyers warned that if word got out that the company was using the data for training, that could cause a “huge trust problem,” according to internal communications viewed by The Information. Cursor began an investigation to understand what, if any, sensitive data employees had sent to SpaceX’s AI unit, now known as SpaceXSI, according to internal communications viewed by The Information and two people familiar with the project. While the outcome of Cursor’s internal investigation couldn’t be learned, the company took steps to ensure that in the future, training models would not include employee usage data. The episode spotlights a challenge AI developers face, especially amid the rising popularity of agent tools like Grok Bot. By design, those agents are supposed to have wide latitude to roam across files and applications on a user’s computer so they can accomplish tasks autonomously. But that freedom introduces new security risks, including the possibility of unintentionally sharing sensitive information with models for training purposes. In general, AI companies have said they will not train off access to connected tools like Gmail and Google Drive. In Grok Bot’s terms and conditions , for example, SpaceXSI says the company does not use Google Drive for model training and that users can opt out of sharing their data for that purpose. The Grok Bot investigation isn’t the only time Cursor has faced issues with data security. During the summer, its employees inadvertently exposed some customer information through publicly accessible websites built for internal use, according to internal communications viewed by The Information. SpaceXSI didn’t respond to a request for comment. Even before SpaceX completed its $60 billion acquisition of Cursor in mid-August, Cursor was working to expand its offerings beyond coding-focused tools. Since then, Grok Bot, an always-on AI co-worker that can handle a broad range of tasks, has become a key part of SpaceXSI’s effort to nab a bigger piece of the lucrative enterprise market for AI tools. To improve early versions of Grok Bot, Cursor tested the product with both Cursor and SpaceXSI employees, as well as people and companies outside Cursor, according to the two people familiar with the project. The startup collected records of how people used the agent. Cursor could then use that data to train AI models by showing them how an agent carries out a task, including the actions it takes and the information it accesses while performing the task. Inside Cursor, employees first got their hands on Grok Bot—then code-named Sand—around June. The product quickly became a hit around the office, Roman Ugarte, Cursor’s former head of growth, said in a podcast interview . He said employees used Grok Bot for sales, recruiting, research and other tasks, often giving the software access to company systems and asking it to carry out work independently. That meant they might use the agent in work involving external customers and with prospective hires, potentially exposing it to sensitive information from sales conversations, customer records and recruiting conversations, one of the people said. But in July, shortly before Cursor released Grok Bot publicly, some of its engineers used a Slack incident channel to flag their concern that there could be confidential information in the training data the company had been collecting from internal usage of Sand, and that it might have sent that information to SpaceXSI. As part of its investigation, Cursor reviewed which users were included in the training data it sent, according to internal communications and people familiar with the issue. Some Cursor employees had been using Sand with their personal email addresses, which made it harder for the company to identify them and exclude their data from the training process in the future, one person said. As a result, Cursor made it so employees could no longer access Sand without using their Cursor email addresses. It also moved to exclude any data coming from Cursor employees in future training. “From a legal standpoint because of the broad general purpose use of Sand, the datasets involved are going to include confidential information that belongs to customers, partners, vendors etc.,” the Cursor lawyer wrote in a company Slack channel. “Legally, we arguably don’t have the rights to train on this data.” This isn’t the first time Cursor has had to deal with the aftermath of potentially sloppy handling of user data. Earlier this year, in a previously unreported incident, Cursor sales and marketing staff inadvertently exposed customer information to the internet, according to internal communications viewed by The Information. The issue involved websites the staff had built using Vercel, a platform for creating websites and apps. The sites helped the Cursor sales and marketing team  manage its relationships with current and prospective customers. One of those websites allowed Cursor to manage its customer relationship with Verizon: It included an organizational chart of some Verizon technology leaders, and listed a handful of Verizon’s top users of Cursor’s tools, along with how much they were spending on the product and the email addresses for each user, documents show. While the Verizon website was password protected, that password and all of the Cursor customer information was embedded in the underlying code, according to Cursor’s internal communications. That meant anyone on the public internet looking at the code could have seen the password and information. The company faced similar issues with other companies’ data, including those of Bosch and Coupa, internal communications show. Upon discovering the issues, Cursor engineers scrambled to take down the websites. They even gave a lengthy name to a Slack channel in which they communicated about the growing number of issues: “A ton of gtm sites that leak customer/internal data” (GTM stands for go to market). Bosch referred questions to Cursor, while Coupa declined to comment. Verizon didn’t respond to a request for comment. Vercel declined to comment. Well before Cursor became a part of SpaceXSI, the rocket company’s AI unit faced similar problems. In an incident in March 2025, a SpaceXSI employee exposed a Grok application programming interface key, which gave access to unreleased xAI models, after they accidentally sent a test script to a public GitHub repository. And this summer, a researcher discovered that SpaceX’s Grok Build developer tool uploaded entire Git repositories to company-owned Google Cloud storage, potentially exposing proprietary source code or credentials developers had not intended to share. In response, xAI disabled repository uploads and made the tool open source. Elon Musk wrote on X , “All user data that was uploaded to SpaceXAI before now will be completely and utterly deleted.”

title: Anthropic’s Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation
content: Anthropic reported rapid-but-slowing revenue growth in a meeting with potential investors in its planned initial public offering, leaving some attendees expecting the company will need to keep its valuation target in check. At a private investor meeting Wednesday in San Francisco, the company said revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to people briefed on the numbers. That was a jump of about 45% from the second quarter. The figure was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year. Anthropic also said it had an adjusted operating margin of 11% for the year through the latest quarter, one of the people said. While that figure excludes major costs such as stock compensation, it suggests the company is having some  success in moving toward profitability. At the same time, the company acknowledged some challenges, the people said. It estimated 5% to 7% of its revenue comes from distillation—a practice that involves other companies using Anthropic’s AI to glean data on how it works so they can train their own models. Anthropic has repeatedly accused Chinese AI labs of distilling its models and has said it is working to fight those efforts. The company told investors Wednesday that distillation revenue will decline and continue to weigh on its numbers in the current period, the people said. Overall, the readout offered a bit of a mixed picture for a company whose record-setting growth rate this year has raised expectations to extraordinary heights. The investor meeting came as economic and market forces already are weighing on Wall Street sentiment toward AI companies . Such concerns have started to cool once-red hot sentiment about Anthropic’s giant IPO. Anthropic’s private valuation ballooned to $965 billion in May from less than $20 billion two years ago. And while investors still expect the offering to succeed, the revenue figures were met with some disappointment by some potential investors, who thought it should prompt Anthropic’s bankers to lower valuation expectations to perhaps even less than $1.5 trillion in the IPO, rather than the $2 trillion that some bankers have floated privately. Anthropic’s IPO—expected to take place next month before the Thanksgiving holiday—will be by far the biggest test of investor attitudes toward an AI boom that has powered the U.S. stock market and the economy for several years. Investors have already soured on the prospects and valuation expectations of some other companies connected to that boom. Borrowing costs have jumped and shares in some publicly listed AI data center operators have fallen recently. Firmus Grid, an AI data center company backed by Nvidia, last week pulled what would have been Australia’s biggest IPO in almost 30 years, citing market volatility, and other AI cloud company’s offerings are also hitting headwinds. While demand for Anthropic’s Claude Code and Cowork tools for businesses have enabled it to surge past rival OpenAI in revenue this year, competition is intensifying. OpenAI has beefed up its own enterprise AI offerings and undercut Anthropic on price. OpenAI and rivals including Google and Meta Platforms have come out with new AI models that rival the performance of Anthropic’s models in some categories, and some businesses—increasingly concerned about surging AI costs—have been turning to cheaper options including open source models. In Wednesday’s meeting, Anthropic notably didn’t provide an update for its annualized revenue, a measure of monthly sales multiplied by 12. That figure, which hit $65 billion in July, has been closely watched as a growth barometer but has also come under scrutiny—in part because of confusion over the number for OpenAI .

title: CoreWeave Co-Founders’ Stock Sales Aren’t Helping Investor Confidence
content: This was not the day to be a publicly traded neocloud (as young AI data center firms are known). As the market sold off on bad inflation data—reinforcing certainty of another interest rate hike—neoclouds tanked. These companies typically are borrowing a lot to finance expansion. The worst hit in the stock sell-off was CoreWeave, whose stock fell 15.5%, fueled by chatter that its bonds were falling to worryingly low levels. CoreWeave CEO and co-founder Michael Intrator was defiant. He told his staff, according to a spokesperson: “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” Yeah, right. The issue may be more that Intrator doesn’t understand investors. He sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. That can’t help but undermine investor confidence in the company. Intrator could win some brownie points by pledging to stop selling his stock for a while. CoreWeave said in a statement that the company’s co-founders were “making personal financial planning decisions that any responsible founder with concentrated holdings would make.” Still, Intrator will have noticed the impact: In May, he was selling at $128 a share, and last month, he sold at $86. If he wanted to sell now, his shares would only fetch $65. The reason for CoreWeave’s stock slide is that it has borrowed a lot of money to finance its expansion, including by issuing $4.2 billion in convertible notes last month. It also announced it may sell as many as 35 million shares over time. Its aggressive capital raising not only exposes it to rising interest rates but means it has to contend with shrinking investor appetite for AI-related debt. And yet CoreWeave doesn’t seem to be at all concerned about those anxieties. In an interview with the Financial Times , published on Wednesday, CoreWeave co-founder Brannin McBee said the company hopes to borrow from insurers, whom he said had “unlimited” capital. He also said, “We are in a period where you have to be huge. You have to be one of the biggest players.” To be sure, CoreWeave is surely better off than less-developed neoclouds Nscale and SB Energy, both of which are trying to go public—so far without much success. Intrator isn’t wrong that the market can overreact. But we’re in an anxious time, and the least Intrator could do would be to hold off on unloading more shares for a while. Investors’ Bending Spoons Euphoria Whoa! Investors got ahead of themselves on Wednesday when they bid up shares of Bending Spoons 41%, lifting the stock to close at $53.46. That exuberance was a result of the Italian digital conglomerate’s disclosure that revered investor Berkshire Hathaway (run until his recent retirement by Warren Buffett) had agreed to invest $330 million in the company in a private stock placement. Even better, Bending Spoons revealed that Berkshire bought a slug of stock in the company’s July IPO and now owns about 4%, making it one of the biggest outside holders apart from the company’s co-founders. We understand why investors would enthusiastically follow Berkshire, but if they were thinking logically, they’d only pay what Berkshire is paying—$33 a share. That’s a slight discount to where the stock has been trading for the past week, although it’s in line with where it has traded for much of the time since the IPO. Paying $20 more than Berkshire makes no sense at all. In Other News • Anthropic told investors its third quarter revenue had risen 46% to $16.8 billion from $11.5 billion in the June quarter, the Financial Times reported. • Nvidia and ChipAgents, a startup that helps customers automate chip design, on Wednesday released a benchmark that measures how different AI models perform a specific task. • Data center operator AirTrunk is postponing its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore as higher interest rates and volatile markets dampen investor demand, Bloomberg reported . • Anthropic has struck an agreement to license technology and hire some engineers from Opaque Systems, a five-year-old startup that sells software for securing confidential data to use with AI agents, according to an Anthropic spokesperson. • Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick said on Wednesday that he expects the AI build-out will encounter bottlenecks and periods of overbuilding, but investment will continue at a massive scale over the next several years. • Sachin Katti, vice president of compute strategy at OpenAI, said Wednesday he was leaving the role on November 15 after about a year at the company. title: Ahead of a Public Listing, ZincFive Talks of Replacing Supercapacitors in Data Centers
content: In the first age of commercial batteries—in the early 1900s—Thomas Edison thought their best use would be to power long-range electric vehicles, and he patented EV batteries combining nickel with iron and zinc. That was a decidedly wrong-way bet—the internal combustion engine, powered by gasoline, rapidly eclipsed Edison’s batteries, which found only narrow use in mining and on railroads. But Edison’s nickel-zinc battery is back, updated to resolve flaws with the original version, and it is now powering AI data centers, thanks to its ability to deliver power in lightning-fast bursts. Oregon startup ZincFive says it’s on track to generate $105 million in sales of nickel-zinc batteries to AI data centers this year, up 60% from 2025, and it plans to go public in a reverse merger by December. The company earned a 9.5% gross margin in the first half of the year, a substantial swing from negative 14% in the same period in 2025. ZincFive’s much-improved financial picture this year, and the return of nickel-zinc batteries, are products of the dramatic upturn in the previously struggling next-generation battery industry, a result of the AI and drone booms. Almost all the batteries used in major tech products like EVs, electronic devices and drones have cathodes made of nickel mixed with cobalt and often manganese, or of iron mixed with phosphate. Almost all have graphite anodes, sometimes mixed with silicon. Zinc features in none of these popular batteries. But ZincFive CEO Tod Higinbotham said a zinc anode along with a pure nickel cathode make for a battery able to completely discharge the energy held within it in 4 minutes, up to five times faster than conventional batteries can. Such a battery would be too large and expensive to use in an EV and wouldn’t last very long, which is why no one deploys them in any commercial cars. But they are highly useful in AI data centers, where they provide an instant jolt of uninterrupted power when the electricity suddenly goes down, as it’s increasingly prone to do. In a typical blackout, nickel-zinc batteries will deliver power in milliseconds so a data center’s graphics processing units do not lose an iota of data, and the batteries continue to deliver this power for up to 5 minutes. At that stage, the data center’s diesel or natural gas generators take over. That ability is crucial in a data center, where even an instant of lost power can be extremely expensive, given the cost of compute. “It’s Edison technology with some new twists on the chemistry, and it allows it to cycle at very high rates,” Higinbotham told me. Higinbotham said the company has shipped 1.3 gigawatts of these nickel-zinc batteries to customers, enough to temporarily power some of the world’s largest data centers. They look a lot like the standard lead-acid batteries found in combustion autos. ZincFive stacks up to 39 of them in a 7-foot-tall cabinet, placed on sliding trays within it. The company then positions multiple battery cabinets side by side in a data center. Higinbotham said ZincFive was developing a battery that will operate even faster, discharging all its energy in only 2 minutes and then recharging just as quickly. Data centers frequently require such fast power because GPUs often demand power in large pulses lasting just 50 milliseconds. Such pulses can be 70% greater than a server’s normal power demand. A data center will require such pulses millions of times over a period of months, Higinbotham said. “That’s been the big new challenge for AI and GPUs,” he said. To obtain this power, data centers typically rely on supercapacitors, devices that deliver a small amount of power extremely fast. ZincFive is seeking to deploy a nickel-zinc battery that will deliver twice the number of bursts of power as a supercapacitor at roughly half the cost, he said. He expects the battery to be ready for commercial sale by 2028. In June, ZincFive filed documents with the Securities and Exchange Commission to go public in a merger with a special purpose acquisition company. Higinbotham said he expected the merger process to finish by the middle of December.

title: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
content:

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.
The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.
Dissect what the breakthrough means for organ transplantation.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How much more can nuclear power plants give?
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that.
Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. But just how much additional power can we count on?
—Casey Crownhart

The company has more than 150 electric buses on the road in Kenya and Rwanda, with a reservation list of 1,200 customers. Now it’s targeting another major source of pollution on the roads: trucks.
Here’s how BasiGo is working to electrify public transport in Africa.

title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.
Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US,
announced plans
to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy
awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra
for previously announced upgrades at three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?
Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission
approved
over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33.
But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again.
Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment.
Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded.
The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019.
Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes.
Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO,
told the
New York Times
: “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.”
Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has
already signed on
to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal.
A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant.
Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere
three and
eight additional
gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032.
It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about
30 gigawatts
of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that.
Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors.

title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
content:
Have you ever thought about what makes you
? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.
EDDIE GUY
Head transplant
An entirely new body
Key Tech Required
Spinal-cord fusion
Mired in technical and ethical issues
n 1970, the neurosurgeon Robert White removed the head of a rhesus monkey and transplanted it onto the body of another. The patched-together primate lived several hours before succumbing to its injuries. White, a professor at Case Western Reserve University, tried the surgery several times. Remarkably, the reattached heads could move their eyes and mouths, but because he’d severed the monkeys’ spinal cords, those heads never gained control of their new bodies.
White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.
The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and
got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.
Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed
MIT Technology Review
to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared
in the journal
PLOS One
, all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily.
Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.”
“There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email.
Mindclones
Conscious software avatars
Key Tech Required
Artificial intelligence
Available in unconscious formats
n her 2014 book
Virtually Human: The Promise—and the Peril—of Digital Immor­tality,
the futurist and biotech executive Martine Rothblatt put forward an argument for what she called “mindclones.” People would upload their diaries, recordings, social media histories, and other personal data into a digital filing cabinet. Then, via software she termed “mindware,” they would create realistic digital avatars of themselves. In Rothblatt’s view, as technology advanced, mindclones would inevitably be considered conscious and even “afforded human rights” after passing psychological screening.
Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building
avatars of their aging parents
in order to preserve their personalities.
While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.”
Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality.
What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and
it answered
, “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less
a diagnostic test
they could apply to an avatar.
Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not
you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.
Brain in a jar
Disembodied brains
Key Tech Required
Life-support perfusion
Jars, yes—alive, not so much
n the 1983 comedy The Man with Two Brains, Steve Martin plays a scientist who falls in love with a brain that he keeps alive in a jar filled with a fictional life-sustaining fluid and that talks to him via telepathy.
So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists
human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood.
The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ.
Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.
What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks.
EDDIE GUY
Gradual brain replacement
Extreme life extension
Key Tech Required
Lab-grown cortical tissue
Now funded by your tax dollars
ow would you like to replace your brain, little by little? The process would go slowly enough to avoid your notice, but quickly enough to undo the inevitable damage that aging brings. In 2026, this wild idea got a massive endorsement from the US government when ARPA-H, a health agency that backs high-risk projects, committed up to $175 million to a program it calls FRONT, for “functional repair of neocortical tissue.”
On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book,
Replacing Aging
, that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones.
We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue.
Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied.
Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body.
We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too.
Brain upload
Whole-brain emulation
Key Tech Required
Connectome maps
Give it another century
ou are your connectome.”
That’s the famous hypothesis of the Princeton neuroscientist Sebastian Seung. It states that memory and identity reside in the brain’s impossibly complex network of hundreds of trillions of synapses—delicate junctions between neurons.
Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says.
Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research  will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere.
Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A
of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in
PLOS One
, estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125.
That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated.
But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer.
EDDIE GUY
Synthetic neocortex
An extra brain
Key Tech Required
Bio-hybrid interfaces
Stealth mode
he futurist Ray Kurzweil likes to say evolution’s key innovation was the creation of the neocortex—the thin extra sheet on the outermost portion of the brain, where we humans do math and recognize patterns. And he’s predicted what the next evolutionary jump could be. Someday, he says, advanced nanobots will wire up our brain cells to a “synthetic neocortex” in the cloud.
That’s right: an extra brain.
Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language.
The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.”
Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine.
Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-­funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-­engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts.
The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.”
Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”

title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.
The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server
and has not yet been peer-reviewed.
The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field.
“Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.”
“Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.”
Buying time
Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have
saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years
. But there’s plenty of room for improvement.
One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs.
People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer.
The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand.
“With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger.
Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder.
Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through.
Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.
When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.
The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in
work published in 2023
. Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats.
Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100.
It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.”
Deep-freezing kidneys
The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab.
There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours.
The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it.
It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof.
Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack.
After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year.
Pink right up
The real test of these kidneys comes when they’re taken out of the freezer, rewarmed, and flushed of their chemicals and nanoparticles. Can they support life? So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways.
In one set of experiments, the researchers put rewarmed kidneys on
perfusion devices
—systems that are already used in transplant surgeries both to provide organs with nutrients and to help doctors assess them while they’re out of the body.
In another set of experiments, Finger and his colleagues transplanted rewarmed kidneys into pigs and monitored them for two hours. In both experiments, the rewarmed kidneys seemed to recover, says Finger. “They pink right up,” he says.
The team see blood flow into the rewarmed, transplanted kidney, allowing it to "pink up."
COURTESY OF THE RESEARCHERS
There are lots of ways to measure the function of a kidney, but one key test is whether or not the organ can make urine. By this measure, the rewarmed kidneys did well, although they produced around two-thirds of the amount that would normally be expected. “They produce urine … within a minute or so,” says Finger. “We know that they work.”
Most of the rewarmed kidneys had been banked for days or weeks. But one had been in the freezer for just over a year. When Finger and his colleagues rewarmed it and put it on a perfusion machine, they found that it produced urine “immediately.” “It actually looked better than many of the [other] kidneys,” says Finger. “We’re comfortable now saying we can store them for a year and rewarm them with excellent function.”
“It’s a very big deal to go a year,” says Kevin Myer, president and CEO of
LifeGift
, an organ procurement organization based in Texas. Being able to store organs for that length of time would transform organ transplantation. He envisions banks of organs that could be used on demand in emergency cases where people can’t wait, such as for some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds.
Final hurdles
But the procedure isn’t ready for prime time just yet. As well as producing less urine than expected, the rewarmed kidneys also showed signs of injury. The damage seems to be caused by the cryoprotectant chemicals, say the researchers.
“This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem,” as Kilbride puts it.
The team has shown that the rewarmed kidneys can regain blood flow, which is “very important," says Greg Fahy, a cryobiologist who is considered a pioneer in the field. But he’s worried about the extent of the damage to the organs. “We can’t tell from these experiments whether these kidneys might have supported life or not.”
But Fahy, who is chief scientific officer at the biotech companies Intervene Immune and 21st Century Medicine (where he is also executive director), acknowledges that it’s not clear how these kidneys might fare once they’re inside a living animal for the long term.
Finger also hopes to find ways to repair the damage seen in the kidneys. Other research has shown that the health of transplant organs
can improve while they’re on perfusion machines
. And damaged kidneys might undergo some level of self-repair once they’re in a body. At any rate, human kidneys may cope better with the process than pig kidneys, says Finger.
The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs over longer periods of time. The team, along with many other researchers in the field, will continue the search for less toxic cryoprotectants, too. Finger, Bischof, and their colleagues are also planning experiments with human kidneys.
Finger is optimistic. “We’re going to see that there’s injury, and it’s not perfect ... but now we’ve got to the point where it works,” he says. “These are big, historic milestones in our field, and we’re excited about it.”

Wie lassen sich Studium, gesellschaftliche Verantwortung und konkrete Stadtentwicklung miteinander verbinden? In der erstmals angebotenen Lehrveranstaltung „Stadt- und Raumpolitik (Service Learning)“ bearbeiteten Studierende der HafenCity Universität Hamburg im Sommersemester 2026 reale stadtplanerische Fragestellungen für zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen. Dabei ging es von Barrierefreiheit über Erinnerungskultur bis hin zu Stadtteilzentren.
Gefördert wurde die Entwicklung und erste Durchführung des Formats von der Claussen-Simon-Stiftung in der Förderlinie innovativer Lehrkonzepte.
Das innovative Lehrformat verband fachliches Lernen mit gesellschaftlichem Engagement: Studierende bearbeiteten reale stadtplanerische Fragestellungen von zivilgesellschaftlichen Organisationen und wendeten ihr Wissen in konkreten Praxiszusammenhängen an.
Studierende arbeiten an realen Fragestellungen und begegnen realen Herausforderungen
Ziel des Kurses ist es, Studierenden die Möglichkeit zu geben, im Rahmen ihres Studiums gesellschaftliche Verantwortung zu übernehmen und zugleich zentrale Herausforderungen planerischer Praxis kennenzulernen. Dazu gehört auch das Verständnis dafür, warum Stadtplanung häufig ein langwieriger Aushandlungsprozess ist, welche Hürden und gegenläufigen Interessen auftreten können und wie Interessenvertretung in Organisationen funktioniert.
Im Kurs arbeiteten die Studierenden unter anderem zu Fragen von Barrierefreiheit, Fußverkehr, Erinnerungskultur, Stadtteilentwicklung und Teilhabe. Zu den Aufgaben gehörten beispielsweise die Untersuchung der Bedürfnisse verschiedener Nutzungsgruppen in der Langen Reihe sowie die Erarbeitung von Potenzialen zur Verbesserung von Teilhabe für das Kompetenzzentrum für ein barrierefreies Hamburg. Weitere Projekte befassten sich mit der Verankerung von Denkmälern im Quartier (Stadthaus & Hannoverscher Bahnhof, Stiftung Hamburger Gedenkstätten und Lernorte zur Erinnerung an die Opfer der NS-Verbrechen), den Bedarfen von Nutzer:innen und Zielgruppen von Stadtteilzentren (Bürgerhaus in Meiendorf, Freizeitzentrum Schnelsen) sowie mit der Entwicklung eines Fußverkehrskonzepts für Eißendorf (fuss e. V.).
Die Studierenden lernten dabei nicht nur die fachliche Arbeit der beteiligten Organisationen kennen, sondern erhielten auch Einblicke in Formen demokratischer Teilhabe – etwa durch die Teilnahme an Gremiensitzungen, Gespräche mit Akteurinnen vor Ort oder eigene Erhebungen, beispielsweise in Fußgängerzonen. Die Arbeit fand sowohl selbstorganisiert als auch im direkten Austausch mit den Kooperationspartner:innen statt.
Studierende und beteiligte Organisationen profitieren
Auch die beteiligten Organisationen profitieren von dem Format: Sie erhalten zeitlich und inhaltlich klar umrissene fachliche Zuarbeit, die sie für ihre eigene Arbeit nutzen und weiterentwickeln können. Die HCU übernimmt dabei die Rolle, Aufgabenstellungen gemeinsam mit den Partner:innen vorzubereiten, zwischen Studierenden und Organisationen zu vermitteln und die Arbeit fachlich in den Kontext stadtplanerischer Praxis einzuordnen.
Die erste Sitzung fand am 7. April 2026 statt, der Kursabschluss war bereits am 10. Juli 2026. Einzelne Projekte wurden im Anschluss weitergeführt. Bereits 2025 hatte die konzeptionelle Vorbereitung des Formats begonnen.
Zu den Kooperationspartner:innen gehörten unter anderem der Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland e. V., das Freizeitzentrum Schnelsen e. V., FUSS e. V., das Kompetenzzentrum für ein barrierefreies Hamburg, das Kulturzentrum BiM/Bürgerhaus in Meiendorf e. V., die Stiftung Hamburger Gedenkstätten und Lernorte zur Erinnerung an die Opfer der NS-Verbrechen, die Evangelische Stiftung Alsterforf, UrbView sowie der Verkehrsclub Deutschland e. V.
Für kommende Semester ist geplant, das Format weiterzuentwickeln. So soll Service Learning langfristig dazu beitragen, fachliche Ausbildung, gesellschaftliche Verantwortung und praxisnahe Stadtentwicklung an der HCU enger miteinander zu verbinden. Im Wintersemester 2026/27 bietet die Lehrveranstaltung „Stadtplanung in der zivilgesellschaftlichen Praxis“ wieder Studierenden ab dem 5. Bachelorsemester Stadtplanung die Möglichkeit, ihr Wissen direkt in gemeinwohlorientierten Organisationen einzubringen.

Datenschutzexperte Thomas Köllmer vom Fraunhofer IDMT erläuterte dem Publikum, wie digitale Wasserzeichen Copyright- und Herkunftsinformationen sichern, Manipulationen erkennbar machen und KI-generierte Inhalte kennzeichnen können.
